THE PLOUGHMAN. Clear the brown path to meet his coulter's gleam; Lo! on he comes behind his smoking team, With toil's bright dew-drop on his sun-burnt brow, The lord of the earth, the hero of the plough! First in the field, before the reddenin7, sun, Last in the shadows when the day is done; Line after line along the breaking sod Masks the broad acres where his feet have trod. Shill where he treads the stubborn clods divide, The smooth, fresh furrow opens deep and wide; Matted and dense the tangled turf upheaves, Mellow and dark the ridgy cornfield cleaves. Up the steep hillside, where the labouring train Slants the long track that scores the level plain; Through the moist valley, clogged with oozing clay', The patient convoy breaks its destined way. At every turn the loosened chains resound, The swinging ploughshare circles glistening round, Till the wide field one billowy waste appears, And the wearied hands unbind the panting steers. These are the hands whose sturdy labour brings The peasant's food, the golden pomp of kings; This is the page whose letters shall be seen, Changed by the sun to words of living green; This is the scholar whose immortal pen Spells the first lessons hunger taught to men; These are the lives that Heaven-commanded toil Shows on his deed—the charter of the soil. OLIVER WENDELL HOLVES.

LOVE'S POWER. If I were blind, and thou sbouldst enter E're so softly in the room, I should know it, I should feel it, Something subtle would reveal it, And a glory round the centre That would lighten up the gloom, And my heart would surely guide me, With Love's second-sight provide me, One amid the crowd to find. It I were blind If I were deaf, and thou hadst spoken Ere thy presence I had known, I should know it I should feel it, Something subtle would reveal it, And the seal at once be broken By Love's liquid undertone. Deaf to other stranger voices, And the world's discordant noises,— Whisper, whosoe'er thou art, 'Twill'reach my heart! If I were dead, and tttou .houldst venture Near the coffin where I lay. I should know it, I should feel it, Something subtle would reveal it, And no look of modest censure Rest upon that face of clay. Shottldst thou kiss me, conk:elms dashes Of Love's fire through Death's cold ashes Would give back the cheek its red, P 1 were dead!

THE STANLEY CREST.—We ought not to omit a reference to—whether we can quite explaia is another matter—the singular and so often prominent crest of the Stanley or Derby family, the eagle and the child. It seems to hold a mysterious tradition, and several attempts have been made at a solution of it. Perhaps our readers know something of the story of Sir Thomas La.thom, of the reign of Edward 111. It is said that in the old age of this ancient knight, finding himself heirless and childless, he and his wife the Lady Isabel Stanley, discovered in an eagle's nest, hard by their mansion, a child; this child was adopted by them, and became, by the name and title of Sir Oskatel D'Latlaom, the inheritor of these great estates. But another version of the story is that Sir Thoinas Lathom, as he drew towards the close of life, confessed that Sir Oskatel was only his natural sun, that he had placed him in the eagle's nest, and that the daughter of Sir Thomas Lathom, the Lady Stanley, in con- tempt and derision of the spurious brother, took the eagle and child for the crest, in token of conquest over him and of his claims. There is, no doubt, much of the mythical and fabulous about the story, but it seems probable that, amidst the variations with which the tradition is presented, there is something like a probable air of truth in that con- cise version which we have summarised from the lengthy pages of Seacome for our readers. ht the same time a little circumstance, quoted from Jones of Tynemouth by Dr. in his learned Life of King Alfred, appears to have escaped notice. One day, when Alfred was hunting in the forest, he heard the cry of an infant, which appeared to come from a tree. He despatched his huntsmen to seek for the voice. They climbed the tree, and found on the top, in an eagle's nest, a wondrously beautiful child, clothed in purple, and with golden bracelets on its arms. The King commanded that it should be cared for, baptised, and well educated. In remembrance of the singular discovery, he caused it to be named Nestingus. It was added that the great-granddaughter of this foundling- was a great favourite at the Court of King Edgar. Thus there was clearly the tradition of an eagle and child before those to which we have alluded. Is it possible that the Stanleys derive their crest from the Saxons, as they derive their name ?—Leisure Hour. A SCSSEX HEROINE.—Phoabe Hassell was a celebrated character, born of respectable parents, at Stepney, in March, 1713; her maiden name was Smith. When about 15 she formed a romantic attachment to Samuel Golding, a private in Kirke's Lambee.giSuch was her passion for this man that on his regiment going to the West Indies, in 1728, she donned male attire and enlisted in the sth Foot, under General Pearce; there she served in the ranks five years without her sex being suspected. Soon after her re- turn to England the troops were ordered abroad, and she was present at the battle of Fontenoy, May Ist, 1743, com- manded by the Duke of Cumberland; there she received a bayonet wound in her arm. Golding haying been wounded also at Gibraltar, the forces were invalided to Plymouth. rhcebe there told Lady Pearce her history, and obtained her discharge at the military hospital. She nursed her lover, and when he was convalescent they were married, and lived happily for over a score of years, Golding having a pension from Chelsea Barracks. Phcebe was chiefly instru- mental in the capture of James Rock and Edward Howell, for highway robbery of the mail cart, driven by John Ste- plaenson, on the night of November Ist, 1792, at Goldstone Bottom, where they were gibbeted April 26th, 1793, the de- tection occurring through Hassell being in the Red Lion alehouse, Old Shoreham, and overheard the plan, of which she gave information to Bartholomew Roberts, the constable, who made a clean capture of the fellows, with the stolen property upon each. About 1790 she married William Hassell, a fisherman, and became excessively poor. Hassell died in 1792, and Phcebe took to hawking fish for sale, the basket being borne by a in 1797 she became an in- donheeey. mate of the poorhouse, from which, on August 14th, 1806, she was, at her own request, discharged to take toesheurt oaken ei azt the foot of the marine parade, leaning on he staff, and offering her basket of fruit, bull's eyes, and pin- cushions to passers-by. ,There, hard by the Old Steine, she attracted great attention, her homely garb, a brown, coarse serge dress, clean white apron, surmounted by a black cloth c',oak, with a hood, over which was a red spotted and white handkerchief, her headgear being a black antique .fashioned velvet bonnet, over a mole washing cap; her hands and arms were encased in a long pair of woollen mittens her fine strong features were animated, and her hobnailed strong shoes were made more for service than ornament. Phoebe had nine children; her eldest son was a seaman. On April 12th, 1814, she was noticed as the oldest inhabitant at the Peace Rejoicings, and at the coronation of George IV. she joined in the National Anthem and procession. Flambe had received 10s. 6d. a week from the King for some years. She expired December 12, 1821, aged 108 years, and was buried in St. Nicholas Old Churchyard, at Brighton.

M. Solomon Reinach starts next month for an a logical tour in Tunisia. Ile will first visit Jerbah, the island. of the low-eaters, and do a little digging there. His excavations on the site of Carthage will not begin till next February. Mr. W. F. Duncan, of Stafford, sends us (.4Menzeurn) a pamphlet in which he recommends the exploration of Southern Europe and Sub-tropical Asia for the fossil re- mains of man. His arguments tend to the conclusion that these regions were the probable area of man's evolution. The original trust-deed of Shakspere's Blackfriars estate, executed in 1618, and ratifying the uses of that estate given in the poet's will, has been lately added to the Shaksperian rarities preserved at Hollinbury Copse, near Brighton. Amongst other recent additions to the same collection is a hitherto unknown family settlement of 106, one to which the poet's father was a witness, his name, however, being merely registered by the scrivener, not attested by his mark. Another interesting acquisition is a contemporary manu- , script of the "Return from Parnassus," confirming Dr. Nicholson's date of 1602. In the last-named volume there are some curious variations in one of the passages which refer to Shakspere. Hysnm Sazaros-Tuot-r.—"l have experimented for years in crossing the breed of the various fish, and am still working upon it. We cross the female salmon-trout with the male brook trout, and thus preduce a hybrid. Then we cross the hybrid with the brook trout, which gives us three-quarter brook trout and one•cluarter salmon-trout. This makes one of the finest fishes in the world. He has all the habits of the brook trout, lives in both streams and lakes, develops vermillion spots on his sides rises readily to a fly, is far more vigorous and fully one-third larger than ordinary brook trout of the same age. The possibilities of development in the fish world are great, and we are rapidly ascertaining what they are."--Ifr. AS:,llz Green, in "Turf, Field, and Farm."

_ , BCTYRIC FRIMENTS IN TILE Som.—There is no doubt I says the Brewers' Guardian, that the soil or uppermost crust of the earth swarms with organisms of the bacteria type, and that by percolation these organism find their way into wells, and thus contaminate the water derived from such sources. In a recent paper, Kessrs. Deherain and Ma.cquenne recorded some observatienc on the action of a microscopical organism presenting the characters of the butyric ferment of Pasteur, which was found to be present, in garden soil, and capable of reducing-the nitrates occurr- ing in it. They now report the results of experiments in another direction, and state that when the ferments of arable soil are allowed to act upon eau sugar in aqueous ' solution, at a temperature of 35deg C., in the presence of calcium carbonate, and sheltered from contact with air, there are produced small quantities cf ethyl alcohol and still smaller quantities of superior alcohols ; together with acetic, butyric, and proponic acids in proportions represent- ing nearly one half of the sugar employed, the acetic and butyric acids being by far the more abundant. These results therefore confirm the inferences drawn from the previous experiments that the dominant ferment in the soil belongs to the class of butyric ferments.

PRIMARY ELECTRIC BATTERIES.—An invention has re- cently been completed which goes far to solve the question of independent house and railway carriage lighting. This is the primary battery of Messrs. Holmes and Burke, which is being exhibited at No. 31, Lombard-street. by Colonel J. D. Shakespear. The foreign patents not being quite com- pleted, the detailed construction of the batteries cannot yet be described. It may, however, be stated that carbon and zinc are employed, and that the patent consists in the mechanical arrangements of the battery and the nature of the chemicals used in on•-rdising the zinc. It is stated that a 16-cell battery is equal to the supply of 18 incandescence lamps of five-candle power each. A number of Swan lamps el this power were arranged in a room at the address and produced a very good effect, the light being pure white and v:.-ry brilliant. The lamps were supplied from a battery placed in an adjoining apartment. A lamp for lighting railway carriages was alsc shown, and, the other lamps being extinguished, gave an excellent light. About a month ago one of these:batteries was fitted in one of the carriages of the 5 40 p.m. Great Northern express train (Kings Cross to Leeds), and I.lEs been successfully running ever since. With regard to duration of lighting, it is stated that Vas batteries will remain active for 24 hours in• full work without being touched, and that the light can be produced at an average cost of id. per light per hour. The system has also been tried on the South-Western Rai:way and approved, and some carriages have been ordered to be fitted with the batteries on this and other lines. The ap- plication to domestic lighting appaars to be very simple, and the system is said to be perfectly free from danger to users.

DISTRIBZ.77ION OF ELECTRICITY.—L practical demonstra- tion of a nes-7 mode of distributing .electricity is now being given at Edgware-road and several .other stations on the Metropolitan P.ailway. The distributing medium is nailed the Gaulard-Gibbs Secondary generator. The primary generator used in the present demonstration is a Siemens alternating current dynamo. A current-from this dynamo is sent round a wire cable, which connects Notting-hill- gate, Gower-street, King's-cross, and Ahlgate, and returns to - Edgware-road, where, in technical phrase, the circuit is me- tallically closed with the generating dynamo. The circuit may be touched at any point without danger. How to utilise this current for lighting or other purposes at a strength variable at the will of the consumer is a problem which the Ganlarcl.Gibho Secondary generator is intended to solve. This so-called generator, for the name is hardly ssccurate, consists of close coils of smaller insulated wires, so brought into relation with the primary circuit, that by the influence of induction a powerful secondary current is set -up in them. It is the secondary current so obtained that the consumer utilises in a circuit of his own premises, whether for lighting or for motive power. The sufficiency of the primary current being taken for granted, the poten- tial obtainable will depend upon the size of his secondary generator, and also on his manipulation of it; for it is pro- vided with a contrivance for modifying the strength of the current. This contrivance is verss similar to that which, on a smaller scale, is seen in the familiar medical machines for administering shocks the strength of which is inten- sified by the withdrawal Of a brass cylinder separating the coil from its iron cone. By the use of these secondary gene- rators stations so far apart as those abovo mentioned can be independently lightt d without the intervention of any other dynamo than one in the circuit, which in this case is as long as 15 miles. The great advantage claimed by the in- ventors for this system of distribution is that the loss of electricity by transport remains constant on a line of given length whatever the power transported may be. They claim that it demonstrates the possibility of distributing natural forces over great distances at an unlimited number of points.

CITINA GRAss.—An article in The Times calls attention to the utilisation of China grass, or rheea, sometimes called ramie, a textile plant indigenous to China and India. The writer says—" It is perennial, easy cf cultivation, and pro- duces a remarkably strong fibre. The problem of its culti- vation has long been solved, for within certain limits rheea can be grown in any climate. India and the British colonies offer !unusual facilities, and present vast and appropriate fields for that enterprise, while it can be, and is, grown in most European countries. All this has long been demon- strated ; not so, however, the commercial utilisation of the fibre, which up to the present time would appear to be a problem only partially solved, although many earnest wozkers have been engaged in the attempted solution." On t o occasions the Indian Government has offered a prize of £5,000 for a machine that would deal satisfactorily with the plant, and several inventions have been tried. The diffi- culty was to decorticate the plant, and, until recently, all machines tried failed in this respect. The prize was for a second time withdrawn, and yet inventors did not slacken their efforts. And no wonder, since we are told that the strength of rheea fibre from Assam, experimented with in 1852 by Dr. Forbes Boyle, as compared with St. Petersburg hemp, was in the ratio of 280 to 160, while the wild rheea from Assam was as high as 343; besides which rheea iJ de- clared on good anthority to possess the widest range of pos- sible applications of any fibre. Last year, M. Favier suc- ceeded in decorticating the plant in a green state, after subjecting it to the action of steam. His invention, how- ever failed to separate the fibre from the refuse matter, and it was not till Professor Fremy took the matter up that this difficulty was met. The two processes of Messrs. Favier and Fremy have been combined, and machinery has been set up in France. This has recently been tried successfully before a number of gentlemen from various countries. The rheea dealt with was grown near Bordeaux; but some grown by the Duke of Wellington at Strathfieldsaye has also been ex- perimented on. Great results are expected from the solu- tion of the difficulty of manufacturing this valuable textile I material. The Times of Thursday last says :—Within the past two or three weeks, however, it has been demonstrated that there is a machine of recent invention which effec- tually separates the fibre from the woody stem of the green rheea, and at the same time cleanses it from all extraneous adherent matter, producing it in good condition for the market, and this without any previous or subsequent treat- ment. A private demonstration of the process took place on Friday last at Messrs. George Jenning's works, Stangate Wharf, Lambeth, upon which occasion there were present General Hyde, of the India Office, the Hon. Hy. Berkeley, Mr. C. E. Collyer, and the representatives of some of the leading firms in the fibre trade. The experiments were con- ducted by Dr. Forbes Watson, and amply demonstrated that the main object of the experiments—the treatment of the rheea plant—had been fully and fairly accomplished, and that the prospects of the utilisation of this valuable, but hitherto useless, plant are now fairly established. The in- vention is in the hands of Mr. C. E. Collyer, of 141, Fen- church-street, London.

In the rotation experiments the wheat aressed with the larger dose of nitrate did more harm than good, and produced 34-8 bushels of head wheat, weighing 59.41b5. per bushel; and nearly 10 bushels of tail wheat, weighing only 51-81bs. per bushel; and the enormous qaantity of 2 tOns 15 cwt. 3 us. 131-lbs. of straw and chaff. With the smaller qus.ntity of nitrate of soda a better result was obtained than with the larger, the produce amounting to 409 bushels of head wheat, weighing 59.51b5. per bushel, and 51 bushels weigh- ing 51-Blbs. per bushel, or, together, 464 bushels per acre, and 2 tons 13 cwt. 3 era. of straw and chaff. The results once more prove the great advantage of using nitrogenous manures, and the comparative uselessness of mineral ma- nures only. They also s'llow, to those who need to be At the time of going to press last week we were contend- ing with a frost of unusual severity for the seasCm, and making provision for its continuance. During the corre- sponding week last year the registered degrees were 7,6, and 5. This year nine degrees of frost was registered twice, and 11 degrees once, on the morning of the 14th. We may expect a recurrence, and with as little warning as we received of this. In our last week's notes we referred to ridging the ground, and as it is next in importance to trenching, we shall give directions how to proceed with the work, and after a little practice it will be found very simple. Most people have seen our farm men plough. If the ploughman placed two furrows one against the other, as he usually does the two first, and continued the process, the land would be ridged. The cottager can do the same but much more effectually, if he is provided with a good spade. After marking with the fine the direction he intends taking, he will turn his spadefals of soil right or left as is most con- venient for his hand, and when he reaches the end he will work backwards on the opposite side, and turn his soil well up against the other, and thus the ridge is formed. From the centre of one channel to the other there will be a space of nearly two feet, and if the spade has been thrust into the ground its full depth, the hollow will be sufficiently deep for planting early potatoes in at the proper time, and the manure can then be placed on the top or underneath the sets as the planter fancies. •••••••••••04110.01111MINIME•

FOUR CALVES AT A BIRTIL—Four calves at a birth is a rare event. Mr. J. Matthews, Verde Creek, Kerr County, Texas, owns a cow that gave him four calves on the 18th August. Three of the calves are heifers. They all lived, and at the age of one month were perfectly healthy. The cow was a good milker, only had single calves hefore, and was bringing all the four up without assistance. These facts are vouched for by Frederick Lawrence, Summer-place, Maidstone, who was in Texas at the time the calves were born. I THE GROUND GAME _A.cr.—ln Cheshire landlords haVe been much affected in their shooting by the operations of this Act. Lord Tollemache and the Marquis of Cholmonde- ley have both appealed to the Assessment Committee of the Nantwich Union for a reduction in their assessments fdr I game. Mr. Cawley, on behalf of Lord Tollemache, said that in one township they had been assessed at £5O and had received £l2, but in consequence of the Ground Game Act (they were now unable to get any offers whatever. The Marquis of Cholmondeley's appe.al will be heard next month.

A CHEESE AND BUTTER FACTORP.—We believe that Captain Adcock, North Lodge, Melton Mowbray, purposes building a butter and cheese factory, with the necessary ad- juncts of piggeries for the consumption of the buttermilk and whey. He proposes making a basement, and three up- per rooms, sbout GOft. by 241 t. The factory will be fitted with separators, the motive power being furnished by an Otto gas-engine. It is intended that in the making of cheese the best known and most modern appliances will be used, and that the factory system will be applied throughout each department. The premises adjoin the joint London and North-Western and Great Northern Railways, and it is pro- I posed to send the daily produce each night by a late train, for delivery in London early on the following.morning. A FRENCH SILO.—M. Turckein has lately given some valuable information to French agriculturists upon the alimentary value of green forage, such as maize, trifoliam, and grass, and of the same forage ensilaged and fermented. It is now ten years since, in common with other agricul- turists of France and Wurtemberg, he commenced to en- silage maize for the winter, and to supply the want of forage which several consecutive bad yeare had caused. He obtains from the same cows a superior supply of milk and of excellent quality, as well as better manure. M.Turckein , has this summer constructed a silo in the ground, in which . . . .

he ensilaged during August and September-60 loads of grass of his second cutting, sprinkled with a pretty strong addi- tion of salt, and a little powdered lime to neutralise the acids v. hich might be produced by a bad fermentation. Ac- cording to the experiments made, these CO loads would re- present about 30 loads of dry return, deprived of all its I flowers and fine leaves of trefoil, consequently the most nutritious and delicate parts of a grass which has been of quite the best quality this year. SOme epecimena of this fermented fodder as well as fermented maize will be sent for comparative analysis by the specialists of the aloe of the Commission of Assay. THE SHORTHORN " CO&T" IN AMERTCL—In an article on the influence of soil and climate on the coats and "handling" of animals, the National Lire Stock Journal (Chicago) remarks that it is the custom to refer to the back of the shorthorn as the home of a mossy coat, whereas the mossy coat is the product of a moist climate, and goes on to say:—lt does not belong exclusively ,to the short- horn. While perhaps this breed more generally has a mossy coat than any other is observed to have, still, the Hereford bred and reared in the humid atmosphere of England will show more of the mossy coat than a shorthorn bred and reared in the dry atmosphere of the States. We doubt if men in general keep watch of the regularity with which the mossy coat disappears upon English-bred cattle when brought to tile States. This change, like all changes upon animal organisms, the outgrowth of climatic influences, sets in so insidioualy, and progresses so slowly, that both the beginning and the daily progress escape observation. A like change has taken place, it is believed, ly close ob- servers, upon the head-covering of the American people, the hair having become straight and stiff as compared with the head-coverings of our forefathers, who were reared under different influences. With regard to our cattle, no natural procedure will cause them to retain the mossy coat.

ABORTION AMONGST ENVIES —A letter from PrO.-:08SOT J. Wortley Axe on the abject of abortion amongst ewes was read before the recent meeting of the Council of the Royal Agricultural Society, in which it was pointed out that the practice of winter-feeding, ntore or less general in this country, condemns the breeding ewes to subsist exclavely on roots during the most trying months of the year. and over the period when the demands of pregnancy call for a liberal and sustaining diet; nor is it in this alone that the worst feature of our winter-feeding exists. "The custom of restricting the diet of the ewe to the filth-laden or residue of roots, left after the folding of the hogge," he says, "is even still more to be condemned, not only as a fruitful cause of abortion, but of other diseases even more serious and fatal. While as a matter of expediency it may be allowable to continue to fold ewes after hoggs, as is generally practised, it is at the -came time indispensable to the health and vigour of the flock that a fair amount of fresh roots be also given, as well as wholesome dry food, in quantities according to the nature: of the season. From the time ewes are placed on turnips to-the time when they lamb down,.l am of opinion that wholesome dry food is impera• tively demanded, and that disregard of this rule of diet ex- poses both parent and progeny to many fatal disorders. I would also advise that salt be kept constantly in the fold, so as to be accessible at all times. When the lair is bad, the flock should be removed to higher and drier ground. The practice adopted by many of our best sheep-farmers, of changing the fold for the open pasture once or twice a week, cannot he too highly estimated as a rneana of maintaining a healthy condition of body and warding off disease. Where foot-rot prevails, the affected animals should be withdrawn from the fold as soon as observed, and placed on dry clean litter, and receive such other treatment and attention as the nature of the Ca&E may indicate."

A GOOD START.-Whatever may be the result of last har- vest-and in England as a whole the crops, with the excep- tion of wheat, were generally superior to those of most recent seasons-we may at least congratulate farmers and the country upon a good start for next harvest. With the ex- ception of the late districts, in which harvest was unduly prolonged by wet weather, autumn work is forward, and what has been done has been done well. The cleaning of stubbles has been carried on under fairly favourable cir- cumstances, the land turned up well for wheat and worked well when the seed was sown, and early crops have come up thick and strong, while later pieces have recently been put into an excellent seed-bed. Throughout-the greater portion of England and in the early districts of Scotland wheat sow- ing is nearly finished, while in forward counties nearly all the wheat isabove ground. A fortnight ago there was some fear that early wheat on good land would become too stout before winter had set in; but the recent frosts applied a salutary check in such cases. The plant might be a little less thick with advantage in many fields that we have seen, as there was not enough allowance made for a combination of circumstances favourable to growth. The seed corn was remakably sound, the land was in a fine state for receiving it, and the weather following early sowing was unseason- ably mild. Under such circumstances nearly every grain grew and flourished, and a peck or more of seed might have been beneficially saved. But an over-thick plant is a fault on the right side, and a long aad severe winter would do something to correct it. The later wheats are not so thick as early pieces. Winter beans and autumn-sown fodder crops have also come up well, and the young clovers are thick and strong.-llfark-Lane Express. EXPERIMENTS AT WOEURN.-Dr. Voelcker has drawn up the following abstract, for the Royal Agricultural Society, of the results obtained fronlbthe experimental corn crops at Woburn in 1883 t-One of the untnanured quarter-acre wheat plots in the series of experiments on the continuous growth of wheat yielded 16 bushels of clean wheat, weighing 58.91b5. per bushel, and 7cwt. 2qrs. 161bs. of straw; the second unmanured quarter-acre produced 18-5 bushels of wheat, weighing 58-81bs. per bushel, and 18cwt. 2qrs. 41bs. of straw and chaff. Mineral manures alone gave only 17.3 bushels, weighing 58 4lbs. per bushel, and 17cwt. 3qrs. 101bs. of straw and chaff per acre, or no more than the average produce of the two unmanured plots. Ammonia salts (2001b5.) alone gave 241 bushels, weighing 58 21bs. per bushel, and 1 ton 7cwt. of straw and chaff per acre; and ' 2751b5. of nitrate of soda alone, 27:1- bushels, weighing 54.11 b. per bushel, and 1 ton Bcwt. 3qrs. 161bs. of straw and chaff. With minerals and 2751b5. of nitrate of soda per acre, the yield of wheat amounted to 381 bushels, weighing 58.61b5. per bushel, and 1 ton 17cwt. 3qrs. of straw and chaff; whilst mineral manures gave a corresponding amount. 2001bs. of ammonia salts produced 34-2 bushels, weighing 58.71b5. per bushel, or about four bushels less wheat per acre than the adjoining plot, manured with minerals and nitrate of soda. One-half of plot 8-which last year was manured with minerals alone, and yielded in 1882 13-3 bushels of wheat, weighing 581bs. per bushel, and 17cwt. 2qrs. 61bs. of straw and chaff, and in the preceding five years was heavily manured with mixed mineral and ammo- niacal manures-was dressed with minerals and ammonia salts' at the rate of 4001bs. per acre, and. in 1883 yielded 458 bushels, weighing 60-31bs. per bushel, and 2 tons 7cwt. lqr. 121bs. of straw and chaff; whilst on the second half of the half-acre plot, the minerals, without ammonia salts, gave only 17.3 bushels, weighing 57.61b5. per bushel, or not more than 'the average produce of the continuously cow-manured plots. Similar results were obtained with nitrate of soda and minerals on the half of the plot which, with minerals alone, in 1882 yielded only 12.2 bushels weighing 561bs. per bushel, this year, with the addition of nitrate of soda to the mineral manure, produced nearly 44 bushels, weighing 57.81b5. per bushel, and 2 tons 7 cwt. of straw; whilst the second half of this plot, manured in 1882 with minerals and nitrate of soda, and yielding 35.8 bushels, weighing 58 Sibs., and 2 tons 9 cwt. 2 qrs. 221bs. of straw and chaff, this year, with minerals alone, produced only 18-6 bushels, weighing 591bs. per bushel, and 17 cwt. 31 qrs. of straw and chaff. On the plots upon which good rotten dung is ap- plied every year, at the rate of about four tons per acre on one plot and eight tons on the other, the produce amounted to about 28 bushels and 331 bushels, weighing 50-71bs. and 60-51bs. per bushel respectively. On the plots upon which good rotten dung was applied for five previous years in suc- cession, and left without dung in 1882 and in 1883, the pro- duce amounted to 19 9 bushels and 21 bushels respectively, weighing 59•61b5. and 60 Sibs. per bushel; showing that the farmyard manure of previous years, after a lapse of two years, still had left in the land some unexhausted fertilising matters which told upon the produce of the wheat crop in 1883. The rotation experiments yielded almost iden- tical results on the acre of seeds, fed off with decor- ticated cotton cake, as on the acre of clover, fed off by sheep, having had maize as additional food. One of these plots yielded 39.6 bushels of headcorn weigh- 601bs. per acre, 2 tons 5 cwt. 1 qr. of straw and chaff,

EPub3ished by Mr. E. J. Kibblerchite, 31, Tavistock-strect, London, TV.C., and reprinted by permission]. THE WEL LESLE VS. Having already noticed every English dukedom save one I now turn to our lastest military dukedom—that of Wellington. To sketch the military and political career of Arthur, first Duke of Wellington, would be quite super- fluous, even if I had sufficient space at my disposal. My business is with his rewards rather than his work. Suffice it to say that I am one of those who regard the great French War as avoidable in its inception, but unavoidable when Na- poleon had made himself master of France. The Allies, and especially England, made Bonaparte almost a necessity to the French nation; but when once he had seized supreme power and embarked upon his career of conquest, resistance to the death became necessary. I hold, therefore, that Wel- lington was engaged in a war wherein the independence of Europe was at stake, that his victories were of vital impor- tance to Europe at large, and to England in particular. I consider, too, that it would have been the better for the Duke's reputation if he had never meddled in politics—that he was soldier, but a bad statesman. Successful generals proved wise administrators of dependencies like ah agvoeo tl of ten our Indian Empire, but the atmosphere of militarism is not that in which wise governors of free peoples are nurtured. Since the days of Marlborough we have usually kept the professions of the soldier and the statesman far apart. Texception is that of the Duke of Wellington, results are not such as to induce us to repeat the and he solitarythe experiment. The Wellesleys were formerly Cowles's, or Colloys, and appear to have been office-holders in Ireland almost unin- terruptedly from the dayS of Henry VIII. to the middle of the last century. A daughter of the house married into the family of Wesley, or Wellesley, whose ancestor had accom- panied Henry 11. to Ireland, and received from that monarch considerable grants of confiscated lands in Meath and Kil- dare. The Wesley estates ultimately reverted to Richard Colley, who assumed the name of Wesley, and was created Lord Mornington. His son was advanced to an Earldom. The eldest son of the Earl became Governor-General of India, and, under his administration, the empire of Mysore, paled by Tippoo Sahib, was conquered. Thus it was that he was created Marquis of Wellesley. At his death the Marquisate expired, but the Earldom of Mornington passed from him to his next brother, thence to that brother's son and grandson, and, at the death of the latter, it passed to the second and present Duke of Wellington. The first Duke of Wellington was the third eon of the first Earl of Mornington. I have found it somewhat difficult to sum up the pecuniary I rewards of the great Duke of Wellington, and can only pre- tend to approximate aecnraey. We need not trouble our- selves about presentations of services of plate, of jewelled swords, gold vases, and such showy but unprofitable rewards. In the year 1810, shortly after the battle of Talavera, the Duke was awarded an annual pension of £2,000 by vote of the House of Commons. In 1812 he was voted another annual pension of £2,000. After the close of the great war in 18144 Parliament voted £300,000 for the purchase of an estate for him, and such further sum as would make up his income to £17,000 per annum. Besides this, he had a grant of an estate in Spain, of the estimated value of £lO,OOO a year. After the battle of Waterloo, Parliament voted him an additional £200,000 for the purchase of an estate and mansion; and he also obtained the grant of an estate in the Netherlands, of the estimated annual value of £2,000. With ' the Parliamentary grants the estate of Strathfieldsaye, in Hampshire, was purchased—a bargain of which the Iron Duke had no favourable opinion, for he declared that it would have rained any other man than himself. How far his estimate of the folly of his trustees was well founded I cannot say; but, if it was a bad birgain, unquestionably a grateful nation did its best to repair any deficiency in that respect. I find that, in 1830, the various pensions which the Duke received from the Consolidated Fund amounted to no less than £8,296 a year. He also drew, as Constable of the Tower, £950; as Colonel of the Rifle Brigade, £238; as Colonel of the Ist Regiment of Foot Guards, £2,605; and as Lord Warden of the Cinque Porte, £295 annually. Sub- sequently he held the offices of Chief Ranger and Keeper of Hyde Park and St. James's Park. Leaving out of sight the Duke's military pay, his emolu- ments during the time when he held civil offices, as Prime Minister, &c., and his salary during the many years that he held the poet of Commander-in-Chief, the Duke of Welling- ton must have received from the public purse, in one way or another, upwards of a million of money; and, if he retained -the estates in Spain and the Netherland, and their actual , value proved to be equal t o the estimate, he must have _ _ _
_ received from these sources nearly a half 'a million more. Nor must we forget that the two Parliamentary pensions of £4;000 per annum descended to the two next inheritors of the <title.

It was not merely the Duke of Wellington himself who was rewarded by a grateful nation, the whole family parti- cipated in his success and in that of the Marquis Welles- ley. it was estimated in the year 1823 that the Wellesleys obtained no less than £99,000 annually, either from Church or State. The Marquis Wellesley had a pension of £5,000 from the East India Company, held a place as Lord Steward of the Household, with a salary of £1,540, and another as Joint Remembrancer of the Court of Exchequer in Ireland, with a sa/i.ry of £5,387. The Marquis had no legitimate issue, but it was stated by an Irish newspaper in his life- time that hi i; numerous family were all provided for in the _

public eervice. The, mother of the Duke of Wellington— the Countess of Mornington—had a pension of £OOO per annum, dating from 1813. A brother of the Duke, the Rev. G. V. Wellesley, vent into the Church, where, beside a Royal Chaplaincy, he held a Prebendary in Durham ,Cathedral, value £2,000 ; the rectory of Bishop Wearmouth, value £2,000 and a residence ; the rectory of Chelsea, value £1,400 and a residence ; and and the rectory of Tiler- field, value £937 and a residence. Besides these, there were ether relatives, who were provided for in an almost equally lavish manner. The Duke's youngest brother, Lord Cowley, for instance, held in succession a number of lucrative diplomatic anpointments, and one of his eons, who went into the Church, became Dean of Wineisor and Lord High Almoner of the Queen, offices which he sill continues to hold. The first Lord Cowley, who at one time held the post of Ambassador at Vienna, with a salary of £12,000, retired on a pension of £2,500. The Duke of Wellington also had another brother, Lord Maryborough, who for a great number of years was a place-holder, and seems to have been under the special care of his yet more fortunate brother, the Duke. He began in 1802 with the office of Clerk of the Ordnance. Successively he held the places of Chief Secretary for Ireland, Master of the Mint, Master of-the King's Buckhounds, and Postmaster-General. Leaving the less important relatives of the great Duke, I think, from the examples I have given, that the estimate that the family must at one time have drawn nearly a hundred thousand pounds a year from the public revenue is not far from correct.

At the death of the Great Duke, in 1852, he was succeeded by his eldest son, who is a lieutenant-general in the Army (tho.ugh his military achievements are nit), and Lord- Lieutenant of Middlesex. The present Duke of Wellington owns in—
Total with a rental of £31,233.
The present Duke is over seventy years of age, and has no children. His nephew ia presumptive heir to the dukedom and to the pension of_£4,ooo _

How far the prodigious rewards of the Marlboroughs, Nelsons, and Wellingtons serve as an incentive to those who are engaged in the profession of arms it would be difficult to say; but there can be no comparison between the material prizes of the soldier and those which are offered to those who serve the nation by other than destructive arts. In litera- ture our mightiest Englishmen—Shakespeare and Milton, and others of later time—have met with scanty recognition from the State. Our greatest inventors—Arkwright, and Watt, and Stephenson—died commoners. Even our greatest statesmen met with scant reward. Since the accession of the House of Hanover, not one of them has climbed from the House of Commons to the highest rank in the Peerage. It is on!y the successful general who, commencing at the lowest round of the ladder, can hope to aspire to the position of a Duke. In future times, our children may reach a more just estimate of the value of the services rendered by men to their fellows.

I should think the grandmother would have been enough for it. She would, if she was as large as mine:" MATECEMATICAL.—A gentleman of Fall River who testi- fied before Senator Blair's committee as to the cost of living in Massachusetts succeeded in attracting the attention of mathematicians. He declared that he earned only. a hun- dred dollars last year, of which he paid seventy-two dollars for rent. "Now, says the Boston Herald, "as the records show he paid forty-seven dollars in fines for drunkenness daring the time, he had nineteen dollars less than nothing left with which to support his family and buy whisky; and if he spent it all for whisky, there is still a frightful dis- proportion to be explained between nineteen dollars less than nothing's worth of whisky and forty-seven dollars' worth of fines."

TENNYSON.—In her paper on Tennyson in the Christmas number of Harper's Magazine, says the New lark Critic, Mrs. Thackeray Ritchie closes with this pleasant paragraph. "It is a gain to the world when people are content to be themselves, not chipped to the smooth pattern of the times, but simple, original, and unaffected in ways and words. Here is a poet leading a poet's life; where he goes there goes the spirit of his home, whether in London among the crowd, or at Aldworth on the lonely height, or at Farringfard in that beautiful bay. The last I went to see him he was smoking in a top room in Eaton-square. It may interest an American public to be told that it was Durham tobacco from North Carolina, which Mr. Lowell had given him. I could not but feel how little even circumstance itself can contribute to that mysterious essence of individuality which we all recognise and love. In this commonplace London room, with all the stucco of Belgravia round about, I found the old dream realised, the old charm of youthful impression. There sat my friend as I had first seen him years ago among the clouds."

DASTARDLY PLOT ON THE LIFE OF THE PREMIER. A most timely discovery was made on Monday night, upon the Great Western Line, about six-and-a-half-miles from Wolverhampton, on the Chester side. About 7-40 p.m., as the Great Western express meat train from Birken- head was running between Albrighton and Codsall, some pieces of timber upon the line awoke the suspicion of the driver and guard, for they caused the engine to leap a little. The guard's light soon showed that this minor obstruction was part of a much more serious business. There were great quarry stones upon the down-line. With as much speed as practicable the train shot a mile and a half ahead to Codsall Station and there pulled up, that the signala might be put on to stop all traffic on the down rails. It was known that the next train to pass on that side was no other than that celebrated passenger express which leaves Paddington at 4-45 p.m., which has been designated the "Zulu." This train, which in the over 140 miles from London to Wolverhampton stops only at Oxford and Birmingham, would in a few minutes be passing at the rate of sixty miles an hour into the pitfall which had been laid for it. Indeed, it had already started from Wolver- hampton, but the signals brought it up, after a five-mile run, at Codsall Station. Here the express was kept for nearly an hour. During the interval the stationmasters and their men, from Codsall and Albrighton respectively, were, with as much rapidity as possible, clearing the line of the ob- structions. These were so formidable that it took two men to move some ef them. They had been got from the com- pany's new red sandstone quarry on the side of the line; and the pieces of timber which first awoke the suspicions of the men in charge of the meat express had probably been used as levers in the moving of the stone blocks by the miscreants who had made so determined an attempt to perpetrate one of the foulest crimes in modern railway history. There is reason to fear that no less an offence was aimed at than the death of the Premier. It had been reported that Mr. Gladstone, after closing his visit to her Majesty at Windsor, would later in the day leave London for Hawarden, there to spend Christmas; and it is known that the Premier, after transacting business in Lon- don, frequently travelled by this same "Zulu " express. Happily, if Mr. Gladstone had not remained, as he did, at Oxford on Monday night, the timely discovery of the con- templated slaughter would have saved the oountry from the horror which had otherwise threatened it.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

RASPBERRIES.—If the old canes have not been cut out this should now be dcne, and the young ones reduced to five or not more than seven in number, and tied to stakes, if such are already in use. These supports are not essential, if the canes belonging to one stool are bent over, and those of its neighbour brought over to meet them, and the whole tied at their points with tar string or a twig of willow so as to form an arch. In this way sufficient stability is given to them to carry the crops safely. If, in very bleak situations, it is found that there is not sufficient strength in the arch (though we have not met with any instance yet) a stake may be driven in the centre and the whole secured to it. This will reduce the number of stakes to one-half. We have discarded the use of wood stakes for years, their first cost, and the annual labour of replacing decayed ones, being an important item of expenditure. Next to arching the canes one-inch iron rods are more economical. Some growers of the Raspberry make a practice of digging between the plants aanually, but in our opinion it is most reprehensible, and the plant's rooting habits forbid it. IVlay they thus dig, they are at a loss to reply, at any rate satisfactorily. The answer usually given is "We always have done it, and we get good crops." Granted; but it is not proof that much better crops may not be procured if they were left alone, and the labour of digging avoided, Our custom is after they are tied, and the weeds and dead canes cleared, to wheel sufficient manure to cover the whole of the ground they occupy. The rain will wash most of the nutriment out of it downwards, and the roots will find their way upwards to the particles and take possession of them. Tire FRONT GARDEN.—Resuming our notes on Creepers ! so far as they are serviceable for covering the nakedness of our dwellings, we shall enter into a few details as to -how they should be treated. Soil such as will grow good pota- toes will suit most Creepers, and if there is a borderelgin. wide, and the same depth, it will be a fair provision, though a greater width would be better, and to secure it the walk or path near the front may be filled with good soil. In exca- vating for the walk the depth should be at least 181 n., 10in. or •12in. of which may be filled with soil, and trodden moderately firm. The remaining space should be tilled with broken bricks or clinkers, with a surfacing of cinders or gravel. The roots will find their way through and underneath into other good scils if there are any, such as adjacent flower beds, &c. The Ivy will grow in moist soils at the rate of a few inches a year, but in rich soil it will grow a yard, providing there is a dry subsoil. Where there is not the space for the border, the walk must be taken out deeper, so as to admit of 6in. of some rough material for drainage. Considerable hoctility has been shown towards the Ivy on the presump- tion that it has a tendency to make our dwellings damp, and is apparently a nting companion to the jerry builder and kis misdeeds. So far as the Ivy is concerned the charge is fallacious. Who ever saw damp on an Ivy-covered -wall? The leaves turn off the rain almost as effectually as the slates on the roof protect overhead, and should drops be driven amongst the leaves, they have very little chance of reaching the bricks for they are thickly coated with Ivy roots, which greedily absorb every drop of moisture. We therefore ask in which way does Ivy engender damp? So convinced was a clergyman once of the absurdity of the allegation, that he planted Ivy round his vestry to cure dampness, which manifested itself during heavy driving rains. THE WINDOW.—The boxes outside the windows may be removed. Though the Geraniums are still alive in ours, they only look shabby, and tend to darken the room. If the boxes are planted with a few bulbs, they make a charm- ing display in spring. The groundwork may be Snowdrops or Crocus, with Tulips and Hyacinths dotted amongst them. The same soil will serve for them, with the addition of a little decayed manure. The bulbs will require planting 2in. or 3in. deeper than was advised for pots. Those having large windows and the means have two sets of boxes, and this time of the year they insert a few small shrubs in them, which gives a cosy appearance. The other boxes, 'being planted with bulbs as described, are put under some shed or other out of the way place, and will be brought to the windows before they come in flower. There is another advantage in having two sets of boxes—it gives an oppor- tunity to have them painted, which cannot be done when full of wet soil. B. B —We would advise you to clear ail the weeds au ay, and ;f there are any plants you wish to save, plant them thickly in one corner. Then trench and manure the ground to a depth of IBin or 2ft., according to the nature of the soil, and this should he proceeded with at once, so that the ground may have time to settle before planting time. We conclude that the nine yard borders are continuous. This, with a width of four yards, is rather inconvenient for flowers, as it necessitates the feet being put on them for the purpose of conducting the various operations of planting, tying, &c. It would; therefore, add to your convenience, and not detract from the appearance of the garden. if you intersected it mid-way by another walk a yard wide. Much depends on the nature of your boundary. If a dead fence, it can be utilised for creepers, and in this case you should have a walk 21e. wide and 21t. from the wall, and of course parallel with it. You would thus have the beds Sit. wide, which Is' as wide as any beds ought to be, and the 21t space under the wall will do for creepers. Your first duty will be to trench the whole of the ground except the centre walk and mark out your walks, &e., after the ground has subsided.— HoPaTs.

Gilbert was at an evening parfy, and coming out was with a crowd of other gentlemen at the door. One of them mis- took the dramatist for a waiter. It is a kind of blunder that is not unfrequently made, and originates in a pardonable and warranted misconception. "Oh, please," said the guest, "call me a four-wheeler." "Certainly I will," said Gilbert, "you are a four-wheeler." He then waited till the storm of indignation on the part of the mistaken guest, and of amusement on the part of all the others had subsided, before he added—" You know I cannot call you a hansom." A handsome senorita went to one of the best photo- graphers in Madrid to have her picture taken. When the posture was all settled, and the cloth was about to be drawn, the artist threw a last glance at his subject, and to his con- sternation found that sh.e was holding a pistol to her head. "What are you doing?" he cried, " you will not shoot your- self, it will ruin my business; besides, it would be wicked to mar so lovely a face." "Don't be afraid," she replied, "I have no thought of spoiling the original of one of your pictures; but my love has left me, and I'm going to send him my photograph in this posture, with the message that I'll fire if he does not return to me."

THE KING OF SHERWOOD FOREST.—Three furlongs further on, through a wilderness of tangled forest, present- ing every variety of foliage and tint, the crowning triumph of his labour is reached, and the pedestrian again sits down under the shadow of one of the mightiest oaks that exist in England. This is the famous "major" oak, the photo- graphic picture of which he will be able to purchase from the "old man of the' woods," who constantly inhabits its vicinity. He will be lucky indeed if he can sit down on the immense roots without being interrupted in his cogitations by the presence of a party bent on enjoyment. This is the "happy hunting ground" of the Nottingham lacemaker and the Sheffield grinder, and no better locale could. be imagined. The venerable oak stands in the centre of an acre of beauti- ful turf, and can be viewed in all the glory of its proud position. The size of its trunk can be imagined from the fact that seven full-grown persons can only clasp hands around it, while its hollow interior has been known to accommodate a dozen persons. The spectator is astounded with its size, and not only is it the monarch of the forest, but its branches spread out to form a picture of grace and beauty. There are no lightning-shivered branches or un- gainly growth; all the pose of the tree is exceptionally graceful, and such as many an artist has loved to delineate. Here he may rest and gaze upon the aspect of loveliness which surtiounds him, and when he has sufficiently admired the thousands of birches with their shimmering leaves, the chestnuts with their wealth of foliage, the golden-crestea gorse and undulations of woodland scenery unmatched in its beauty, he will be content to seek the quietude of the village inn, and ruminate on his wanderings through one of the most picturesque forests in the kingdom.—N. Hartley Aspden in Forestry for November.

div.head: NATIONAL LIBERAL FEDERATION.
div.p: THE NATIONAL LIBERAL FEDERATION.

SPEECH ON REFORM BY MR. CHAMBERLAIN. The annual meetings of the National Liberal Federation were held on Monday at Bristol. At the business Conference a report showing a considerable increase in the number of affiliated associations, and congratulating members upon the passing of substantial measures of reform in the last session of Parliament was unanimously adopted. A resolution con- curring with the Leeds Conference in the urgency of ex- tending the franchise and of providing such a redistribu- tion of seats as would give each vote as nearly as possible an equal value, "such measure not to maintain the present or provide any other artificial means for the representation of minorities," was carried, with lout two dissentients. The Conference also decided, by fifty-five votes to fifty, to re- quest the introduction into the new Reform Bill of a clause giving a parliamentary vote to women possessing the need- ful qualification. The extension of the hours of polling I was further urged apon Ministers, and metropolitan Liberals were assured of support from their provincial brethren in any legislation for reforming the municipal government of London.

In the evening Mr. J. Chamberlain, M.P., was present at a great public meeting in connection with the Federation, and replied to a vote of confidence in the Government. He said that much fault had been found by the Tories with the doings of the Government, but it had not been the mission of Her Majesty's Administration to please their political opponents. In spite of delays and hindrances in Parlia- ment, they had done a great deal more in the way of useful legislation than those opponents either expected or desired, and if they were to leave office to-morrow they would leave behind a record which for cmnpleteness and importance had not, with perhaps one exception, been excelled since 1832. The great task which now lay before them—the, subject which was the root of all others, and the settlement of which would give the greatest possible stimu- lus to all the reforms which a Liberal Government had it in their hearts to carry—was the extension of the franchise and the reform of representation. A Govern- ment pledged to that measure, would, in his view, be liable to a charge of betrayal of trust if it were to leave anything to hazard in a matter of such great importance. He hoped the Tories weald on this occasion give proof of greater prac- tical wisdom than they did in 1832 and 1867, although hitherto they had not been ostentatious in its display. In his judgement, the wisest course for the Government to adopt was to bring in the Franchise Bill first next session, and carry it, for thereby they would avoid all risk of the failure which might attend the endeavour to carry the franchise and redistribution measures together- For him- self, he might reply to Lord Salisbury's complaints about "tinkering with the Constntion" by saying that he would deal with the Constitution so effectually, by giving absolute manhood suffrage, that it would never again require amend- ing. The country was not, he admitted, ready for such an advance, and in the meantime he gratefnlly accepted the creation of household suff,-a,7e in counties. He was strongly in favour of an equal franchise for the three kingdoms ; see- ing no reason why this great measure of juscice should be denied to Ireland. It was better to deal with even an en- larged bind of irreconcileables in Parliament than drive the discontent below the surface and have to grapple with the hostility to imperial rule which he regretted to find in Ire- land.

div.head: MARQUIS_ OF HARTINGTON AT
div.p: THE MARQUIS_ OF HARTINGTON AT
MANCHESTER.

The Marquis of Hartington on Tuesday evening addressed a representative gathering of the Liberals of Manchester and of North-east and South•east Lancashire in the Free-trade Hall. The place was crowded, and the noble Lord had an enthusiastic reception. Mr. Leake, M.P., moved a resolu- tion sincerely thanking the Government for the measures which it had passed in the face of extraordinary opposition, and expressing unabated confidence in its future administra- tion of national affairs. The resolution was seconded by Mr. Grafton, M.P., supported by Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P., and carried by acclamation. In responding, Lord Hartington referred to a statement lately made by "one deep in the secrets of the Conservative party "—Sir R. Cross— that the present Government had not long to live. What might be the duration of its exis'ende was, however, a mat- ter of speculation which even the late Home Secretary could not solve; but it was no doubt true that the Opposition had it in their power to force a dissolution if, as seemed to be assumed, the question of Parliamentary representation occu- pied a place in the programme of the next session. If it was the will of the Conservative party that there should be an appeal to the country, they should have it. Liberals had no reason to apprehend that Conservative appeals upon ques- tions affecting the representation of the people would be more listened to than their own. The noble Lord proceeded to examine the charges brought avainst the Government by their opponents, and asked the meeting to observe, on the one hand, how vague, how general, how unfounded were the charges made against their principles and general policy, and en the other hand how narrow, how petty, and how personal were the attacks which were made upon their policy in detail With regard to Egypt, he made some reply to the criticism of the Opposition. There was notyet sufficient information as to recent events in the Soudan to enable him to speak with any certainty or assurance. He said nothing as to the policy of the Egyptian Government in undertaking the government of the Soudan, but what concerned us directly and immediately was the effect which recent events might have on Egypt proper. Ile attached no importance to the apprehensions which seemed to be felt that the victorious army of the False Prophet would succeed in invading the provinces of Egypt proper. It was, however, in strict accordance with the policy of Her Majesty's Gwerntnent that until we obtained a clear view as to the pfogress of events we shOuld retain our fore( s in the country. Adverting again to home politics, Lord Hartington said he saw no reason why Parliament should not make progress next session, both with the county franchise and local government reform, but their devotion to business would have to be much greater than it had been in previous sessions to enable them to do this. He looked upon the enfranchisement of the county occupiers, whether they were labourers or the industrial population not distinguishable from the industrial: popula- tion in the mercantile districts, as simple a matter of time; and, he added, the Liberal conferences recently held might have been more usefully employed if, instead of applying the.spur to a willing Government and a willing party, they had addressed themselves to the consideration of some of the questions which would have to be settled whenever the Franchise Bill was brought forward, and which did not seem to him as yet to have been very adequately considered. Having discussed some of the difficulties surrounding the question of the county franchise, he concluded by appealing to the country to leave the question of reform in the hands of a Liberal Government, and not in the hands of those who would at first procrastinate, and who when they found that precrastination was no longer possible, would seek to evade the difficulties of the position.—The meeting closed with a hearty vote of thanks to Lord Hartington for his address.

div.p: When a friend pointed out to Lord North an article in print containing the most virulent invective, adding that the systematic slanderer really ought to be prosecuted, for every charge from the beginning to the end was false. "Then," said Lord North, "let him alone. I don't care for that; it is the truth the fellow tells that annoys me." An Irishman, having accidentally broken a pane of glass in a window, was making the best of his way out of sight; but, unfortunately for Pat, the proprietor stole a march on him, and having seized him by the collar, exclaimed, "You broke my window, fellow, did you not ?" "To be sure I did," said Pat," and didn't you see me running home for money to pay for it ?" A convalescent invalid, Mr. B-, brought a suit lately against his doctor, and alleged that the said Esculapius had persisted in calling upon him personally after he was cured, fees for which he now refused to pay. Dr. F- dehied the , fact, and called in a nurse who attended the invalid to prove it. "Is it true," asked the Court, "that Dr. F- con- tinued his visits when Mr. B- had no necessity for them ?" "Upon my word, sir," naively answered the wit- ness, "as long as I saw the doctor with Mr. B- I thought he was in considerable danger."
IRELAND.
Lord Waterford has served notices on his Wicklow tenantry for an advance in their rent, in some cases amount- ing t 0,30 per cent.

DUBLIN MYSTERY.—On Wednesday, the dead body of a respectably-dressed woman,about 50 Years of age, was found floating in the river Liffey, opposite the London ankNor,tla., Western Wharf, at Dublin. The municipal elections in Dublin on Monday resulted in a decided victory for the Nationalists. In the principal con- test in Cork, too, the Nationalists won, defeating Sir Daniel O'Sullivan by a considerable majority. SUPPOSED MURDER —The body of a young man, named Martin Linehan, was discovered, on Wednesday, in a bog near Charleville. He was last seen in company with two men, against whom he gave information for poaching. They have been arrested on suspicion, and also a farmer, named Curtin.

The Lord Lieutenant of Ireland has reprieved the death sentence upon Private Wilson, of the West Kent Regiment, who, while on duty, for no reason that could be assigned, went to the window of one of the barrack bedrooms and de- liberately shot (lead, through the heart, his corporal. His defence was that he was insane, but the jury convicted Sim, with a recommendation to mercy. The Lord Lieutenant ordered a special medical inquiry into the case, and re- prieved him on the ground of insanity. ACCIDENT TO THE IRISH EXPRESS.—A serious accident occurred to the Irish express which left Neyland at 2-45 on Saturday morning, for London. When passing near Kid- witty, where a goods train was being shunted, the expeae dashed into some trucks which were not quite clear of the line. Several passengers were injured. The express was severely damaged, and the line blocked, so that the down mail was delayed for some hours. The express con- sisted of an engine, tender, three coaches, a guard's 'an, and four horse-boxes, and it was running at a high rare of speed. After the collision the engine ran for 150 yards,_and then turned over. The roof of the first passenger carriage was smashed by the wheels of one of the trucks, and one of the passengers had his collar-blne dislocated, this being the only one injured out of 50. Three out of nine horses were hurt.

RIOT AT KILMAINRAAL.--In consequence of information the authorities received that on Sunday several bands would march to Kilmainham Jail and play tunes outside the walls in honour of the condemned man Joseph Poole, who is et present confined there, strong forces af police were posted all along the roads leading to the prison to prevent any such procession approaching. In the evening the majority of the constables were withdrawn, and soon afterwards two immense crowds wen seen coming up from different direc- tions, headed by bands. Reinforcements of police were immediately sent for, and on their arriving Inspector Dunne, who was in charge of the force, told the leaders of the pro- cession that they could not be allowed to approach, and warned them that any attempt to do so would be prevented by force. After some hesitation the crowds turned back, but soon afterwards commenced to stone the police, zahn were obliged to charge them. They than dispersed. Ode young man, a brassfinisher named Dunne, was arrested. He NM charged at the police court on Monday and fined. TILE FACTION FEUDS: LORD ROSSSIORE Lord Rossmore has received official notice from the Lards Commissioners for the Custody of the Great Seal of Ireland that his Lordship's Commission as Justice of the Peace for the County Monaghan has been suspended in conTequence of his action at the Rosslea meeting on the IGth of October. Some correspondence had previously passed between Lord Rossmore and the secretary to the Lords Commissioners. Tne latter alleged that his Lordship, heading a procession of large numbers of men, moved towards a counter meeting, and seriously endangered the public peace. "1 RER further directed to state," he added, "that it appears to the Lords Commissioners that the line of action adopted by your Lordship on the occasion in question, holding, as you do, Her Majesty's Commission of the Peace, calls for an expla- nation, which you will be good enough at voar earliest con- venience to furnish to their Lordships." Lord RosSmore replied as follows ;—" You will be good enough to inform their Lordships that the report referred to, so far as the facts are given in your letter, seem to be substantially correct; but that I dispute entirely the conclusions arrived at, founded, as they are, on an imperfect knowledge of what occurred. ... ••• ... I may remind their Lordships that on more than one occasion the Prime Minister had gone SO far as to complain of the increased difficulty thrown spon the Irish Government in consequence of the'cowardice' and 'traditional sluggishness and incapability of the wealthier portion of society in Ireland to do anything whatever for themselves' (October 7, 1881). I believed, and still be., lieve, that the course of action I adopted on the occasion referred to was the most practical manner in which I could resp,nci to tho. Prime Minister's earnest appeal."
