div.p: THE EXAMINER, S ALTITRDAY, DECEMBER 1, 1883.
uREIGN INTEI-IF+ENOE. --
THE WAR IN THE SOUDAN.

I Private telegrams received at Cairo from Khartoura state that the panic there is increasing owing to rumours that the Matidi at the head of a large force is advancing close to the town after having cut off all supplies of grain. The telegrams received by the Government, however, do not corroborate this report, but state that the European inhabi• tants are leaving Khartoum on board boats and proceeding down the Nile. Tne Journal des Dekts, referring to the disaster in the Soudan declares that if the English were now to abandon Egypt that country would immediately be taken by the stream of barbarians now at its doors. The journal adds, we should thus gain nothing, while Europe and civilisation would suffer immense loss. The Soliel expresses appre- hensions lest England should seek to compensate herself for the loss of the Soudan by occupying the Chinese island of Hanin. The journal recommends the French Govern- ment to accept tbe co-operation of England with a view to the pacification of the far East, but at the same time act in such a manner as not to pay too dear for her assist- ance. The preparations of the Admiralty transport officers for bringing home troops from Egypt have been suspended, and the whole of the ships chartered for the return voyage are awaiting further orders. The P. and 0. steamer Poonah having been inspected by Admiral Sir Francis Sullivan, the new head of the transport • service,.has left the Albert Docks, North Woolwich, but remains at Portsmouth for in- structions. The Italy, one of the great Atlantic liners be- longing to the National Company, is still in the Albert I Dock, and her future movements are uncertain. An idea prevails about the dock that the Italy is to take out more troops to Egypt, and this conjecture is feasible, because if the army of occupation is to remain it will be necessary to furnish reliefs and provide substitutes for invalids and time- expired men. Another large ship, the Hankow, has been taken in hand by the Admiralty shipwright, but no instruc- tions have been given to expedite her preparations. The report that 300 of the Turkish gendarmerie had re- fused to go to Suakim is contradicted by Baker Pasha, who says that, on the contrary, they showed enthusiasm to serve. All the English non-commissioned officers in the force are said to have volunteered, and the troops are taking the place of the gendarmerie detachments at Suez, Port Said, Zagazig, Mansourah, and 'Cantab. Six hundred of the gen- darmerie left Cairo for Suakim on Tuesday. Two thousand altogether will be sent under the command of Baker Pasha, who leaves in a few days. It is his intention to open the road to Sinkat, Toka, and Barber with 500 mounted men. Colonel Parr, with a battalion of the Egyptian army, is to leave for Asaouan as soon as possible, and will probably be followed by two more battalions, and, in fact, by the whole Egyptian army except those occupied in police work. It is expected that they will be employed in throwing up fortifi- cations, and as Assouan is within the Egyptian frontier, English officers will be able to assist. During Baker Pasha's absence from Cairo Colonel Gibbons will take command of the remaining police force and Colonel Baker of the gendar- merie. These officers will not, however, have control over those Egyptian troops with whom the civil force may be associated. The rumour that Dongola has risen is still prevalent in Cairo, but no news has been received from Khartoum. The wire has been cut between Berber and Kassala. The Turkish papers at Constentinople on Tuesday pub- lished an official communication from the Bureau de la Presse contradicting the news given regarding the opera- tions in the Soudan and more -particularly the statement that the Mandi had massed under him a -force of 300,000 men. The Porte's communication goes on to say that if the Mandi has not hitherto been beaten, it is owing to the fact that he had established his head quarters in a region so hot and remote from the Nile as to render the approach of the Egyptian army a matter of considerable difficulty, chiefly owing to the want of drinkable water in that part of the country. The Press Association is informed that 800 men are under orders to embark for the Mediterranean, of whom half are intended for Egypt to replace time-expired men from those regiments which it is proposed to leave in Egypt.

Prince Victor Bonaparte has declined an invitation to at- tend a political banquet. The young "Pretender " remark& that at present he has no part to play in politics, and he deprecates any attempt to exalt him at the expense of his father. A daring attack has been made on a railway train on the Southern Pacific Railway in New Mexico. A- band of masked desperadoes removed some of the rails, upset the train, secured $6OO from the express car, and then took to flight. The driver of the train was killed. SUPPOSED Loss OF A STEAMER AND. ALL HANDS, Three bodies have been washed ashore near Wiarton, On- tario, with life buoys marked "Eclipse " attached to them It is believed that the steamer Eclipse, bound from Algonia to Portsarnia„has been lost with all hands. ANOTHER TERRIBLE RAILWAY ACCIDENT. —A railway accident has occurred on the Boston, Barre, and Gardner Line, owing to a carriage in the rear of a train leaving the rails and being precipitated down an embankment. Thirty- seven persons were injured, four of them being, it is feared, fatally hurt. FRANCE AND CHINA.—A more hopeful view prevailed on Thursday regarding the Franco-Chinese difficulty, and a peaceful solution, though not sanguinely expected,is regarded as a possibility. The British Government,. it is believed, is exercising all it influence on both sides, with a view to an amicable arrangement. There is still no news from Admiral Conrbet. The trial of the Marquis de Rays and his accomplices is now proceeding in Paris. The accused are charged with having induced a thousand persons to go, out in unsound hips to Port Breton' where it was pretended that a colony would be founded. Only seventy returned alive. It is said that many of the unhappy people were eaten by cannibals. The trial will occupy several weeks. ONE RU3DRED AND FIFIT LIVES.LOST.—A telegram from Milwaukee states that 60 vessels and 55 lives were lost dur- ing the recent severe gales on the lakes. The value of the wrecked shipping is estimated at $700,000. The steamer Maistee is reported to have founded in Lake Superior, all on board-37 persons—being drowned. The steamer Cone- stoga is reported to have been lost in Lake Michigan, with 17 lives. These gases on the lakes and the Atlantic sea- board have destroyed in all 150 lives. Nnw YORK FESTIVITIES.—Monday was a public holiday in New York, he occasion being the celebration of the evacuation of New York by the British. It was the last of the series of contennial ceremonies commenced in 187ee Besides a military parade there was a procession of various associations, in which " Jumbo " was a leading feature of interest. One of the peculiar arrangements provided for the commemoration was that at a concerted instant every steam whistle within several miles of the City Hall was to shriek steadily for five conslcutive minutes. FATAL COLLISION ON LAKE GENEVA: A TOUCHING STORY.—At least 15 lives were lost by a collision between the steamers Cygne and Rhone on the Lake of Geneva, on Friday. Only five of the persons on board the Rhone were saved, and of one of these a touching story is told. It is related of this passenger; a young bridegroem' that he went mad on discovering that he had saved another woman in mistake for his wife. The collision took place in the centre of the lake, where it is 600 ft. deep. None of the bodies have been recovered: The mother and sister of the captain of the Cygne were on board the Rhone at the tine% of the colltsion and were both drowned. A BISHOP STABBED BY A PRIEST.—A most serious assault is reported from Aci Reale, in Sicily. Two days ago the director of the College of San Martino, a monk of great reputation and erudition, 48 years of age. went to the , bishop's palace to complain to Bishop Genuardi, who had refused admittance to the semiaary to a young nephew of his. Father Tommasso Patent!) first remonstrated loudly, and then, drawing a digger, attacked the bishop, who de- fended himself courageously until the servants succeeded in disarming the monk. The news created great sensation in Ad i Reale. The monk was arrested. In the evening the whole of the population, with band and banners, assembled under the Winaow of the bishop's palace, and made a demonstration of sympathy with the bishop, who was for- tunately only slightly wounded. FURIOUS ATTACK BY BLACK FLAGS. Twelve hundred Black Flags, reinforced be the inhabitants of villages which had been burned by the French, made a furious attack en the French gunboat Carabine, under the command of Lieut. Bauer, which was lying anchored in the river, near Haid- zuong. An attack was also made on the citadel of Held- zuong, which would probably have been captured but for the timely arrival of the French gunboat Lynx, the com- mander of which heard the cannonading. A thousand troops have been sent from Hanoi, and a smaller number to Haiphong, where an attack was feared from the same band. It in felt at Hong Kong that this affair of the Carabine makes the withdrawal of the French almost impossible. The effect which the commencement of hostilities bAween France and China might have upon American interests has been considered by the Cabinet at Washington, and secret instructions have been telegraphed to the commander of the American squadron on the Asiatic eation. LoYE AND SUICIDE.—Young people who find that the course of their true love is running quite the reverse of smoothly are sometimes apt to do what a pair of sweethearts in France intended to do—namely, end their troubles by self-destruction. The young people in question, however, mismanaged affairs, happily for themselves; but this led to one of the two narrowly escaping punishment. Their re- spective parents refusing to consent to their union, Jean and Marie determined to be the hero and heroine of a drama. It was decided between them that Jean should first fire at Marie, and then put an end to himself. They met together in secret on a certain Sunday to carry out this plan; the young girl took a last farewell, of her lover, implored him "not to hurt her much," and received a bullet in the head. She was not killed, however, and the sight of her suffering caused the author of it to waver in his resolution to turn the pistol against himself. The mutual determination to die to- gether holding good, the wounded girl was placed on a conch, whilst her companion went out to purchase sufficient charcoal to ensure suffocation. The usual precautions of stopping up cracks and crevices were completed; the char- coal was lighted, and death seemed at band, when the girl's mother, missing her daughter, discovered their refuge, and prevented the catastrophe. Marie was taken home and nursed; Jean was arrested for attempting to kill her, and has just been tried and acqnitted by an indulgent jury—the se- quel being the consent of the parents to the marriage.
The col liers employed by Bower and Co., at Allerton and Methley, near Leeds, gave in their notices, on Thursday,.f or a 15 per cent. advance.

WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.—The Wesleyan Band of Hope and 13; ue Rioban Army held its tea meeting on S itur- day evening in the day school, followed by a public meet- ing, presided over by a gentleman from Manchester, of large experience in connection with Bands Of Hope. Ex- cellent addressee on temperance were delivered by siveral speakers, including recitationg, to a deeply-interested audience. CONCERT.—The first concert by the Tonic-sol-fa Singing Class was held in the Wesleyan Day School on Tuesday , evening. Conductor, Mr. 'I. L. Brown accompanist, Mr. E. Aspinall. The programme was one of varied interest, and included pianoforte solo by Mr. E. Aspinall, "Nelson's , victory" (air and variations); part song by the class, " CoMe and join ;" followed by "While wintry winds ;" and "The mountaineer's song :". solo, "True till death," Miss M. Aspinall, well rendered and encored; by the class' part song, "Hear the rough November blaet ;" recitation (Lan- cashire), " Th' owd bellman," by Mr. T. Yates; part song, "Weary the night winds ;" part song, " Merry laughing May;" solo and chorus, "Beautiful star," by Mr. Daven- port; ;humorous, "Pussy's in the well ;" part song, "Don't fret;" pinaforte solo, Miss M. Taft; solo and chorus, "Forth to the battle," Miss M. Owen ;" solo and chorus, "Now prav we for our Country ;" recitation, Mr. Yates, "Look eawt chips ;" part songs, "On the dell ;" "Blue bells of Scotland;" "There's music in the air;" solo and humming chorus, "Alone at midnight" song (humor- ous), "Call John" (encored); solo and chorus, "Hark, the vesper hymn," Miss M. Aspinall (encored) ; part song, "Close of day ;" finale, "God save the Queen." The various songs and pieces vi ere well rendered, the expression excellent, and the time well kept. Miss Aspinall with care and training will be an accomplished singer, her voice is very musical and can range from the highest to the lowest notes. The attendance was large, and the concert highly appreciated. Mr. Brown deserves gr eat credit for his training.

FRODSHA.M. THE LICENSE OF THE GOLDEN LzoN.—At the Eddie- bury Petty Sessions, on Monday, Mr. Mounfield applied on behalf of Messrs.Gaskarth, brewers, Altrincham, for a permit to sell at the Golden, Lion Inn, Frodsham. The present manager at the house, Thomas Earl, had been manager for the firm three years next February, but the firm had recently had occasion to find considerable fault with him with regard to his account, and they had come to the conclusion that he was not fit to hold the license any longer and that they must transfer it to another man. The firm had an agreement with their managers that at any time they made an application to them they must deliver up the licence. He told Earl that he should want him to come there that day, and that merning he put a horse and trap ip readiness for him at Frodsham, but he refused to come. —The license was transferred to the man produced by the applicant, whom the latter said the firm believed to be a very respectable person. GRAPPENHALL. ENTERTAINMENT AT GRAPPENHALL.—OD Thursday even- in an entertainment was given in the large room, Grappen- hall, a good number of people being present. The first part consisted of glees and songs (given by the choir, assisted by a few local friends), amongst which was a pianoforte duet by Messrs. Woods and Fairhurst; also two violin solos by Mr. Geo. Shakeshaft, all of which were gone through very carefully. The second part was :a farce, entitled "Turn Him Out," by local friends which was very amusing. MECkSVICK. A Dixotlious POSITION—At the Daresbury Petty Ses- sions, on Tuesday, Thomas Harmer, carter, Appleton, was summoned for being asleep whilst in charge of two horses and a dray at Keckwick on the 17th November. It appeared that defendant was found sitting on the shaft asleep, and if the policeman had not awakened him when he did the man would have fell under the wheels. The reins were on the groand. Defendant, who denied that the horses were with- out control, was fined 2s 6il and costs.

LYM M. VIOLENT CONDUCT IN A BEERHOITSE.—At Sale, On Mon- day, a man named John Collins was charged with being drunk and disorderly and refusing to quit the licensed premises of Thomas Fleming, and further with assaulting Ann Fleming, at Statham, Lymm, on the 21st November. Prisoner, on the day in question, went into the house between twelve and one and began quarrelling with a cus- tomer. Mrs. Fleming ordered him out, when he struck her, knocking her down. Prisoner then went out but he left traces of his visit by smashing the panel of the door in. —P.C. Chapman, Lymm, and Mary O'Keefe, servant at complainant's house, having corroborated Mrs. Fleming's statement, prisoner was fined 10s and costs or 14 days for the disorderly behaviour, and for the assault he was sent to gaol for a month with hard labour. BAND OF HOPE MEETING.—On Monday evening a meeting of the Lymm United Bands of Hope was held in the Mission-roam, and was well attended. The Rev. G. W. Guest presided, and there were also on the platform the Revs. H. Davis, Baptist; E. W. Lomax Jackson, Primitive Methodist; J. Bedell, Congregational • and Messrs. Thoma- son, Ashton, Mort, :Vlostyn, Brown, and Hall. Mr. Gregson, of Blackburn, attended as a deputation.—The Chairman said there was no greater truism than "unity is -strength," and for that reason it was that the various temperance societies in the parish had arranged te hold meetings during the winter, in order to make a strong effort to combat that monster evil intemperance, which held in its grasp so many of their neighbours. The meetings would have plenty of variety in them. As the question which called them into existence was a serious one, they would of necessity have an admixture. of serious things. Ho was sanguine enough to hope to have really good results; but if nothing more came of it than bringing about a better sort of charity than sometimes prevailed, their meetings would not have bees held in. vain. (Hear, hear.)— Mr. Gregson followed in an interesting address on total ab- stinence, and spoke of the advantages to be gained by avoid- ing intoxicants. He had been ateetotaller for 50 years, and one of the advantages he found from it was that of having a clear head. A man who ha lto work with his train, a man who had to use his judgment, had never too clear a head, as some of them must .now perfectly well, and there wee- nothing that led a man through his work bettee than a light heart. It was not a very difficult thing to have to carry a heavy purse. Some people told them that money was the root of all evil. Ee did not believe that, and he L told them honestly, and tl-.e.• way to get the heavier purse was to tell the publican:4 the brewers, and the spirit mer- chants that they had time with them, and then make a full stop. He had no fear that a man, when he said " I won't," and stuck to it, would ever regret it. If their Christianity was what he believed it to be, their duty was to teach that if drink was dangerous to their neighbours and friends, it was an article they ought to dispense with.—A number of glees and songs were rendered during the evening, which, altogether, was a most enjoyable one. MOORE.

DEFRAUDING A RAILWAY C,LIIFANY.—James Mullin, labourer, Moore, was summoned at the Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, for travelling on the Chester and Manchester Railway without a ticket. Defendant arrived at Moore station from Warrington on the evening of October 30th without a ticket. He tried to evade the notice of the railway officials by running round in front of the engine and clearing the railway fence, and when foand near a public•house in the village later on he said he had only Ll. There was a good deal of this kind of thing going on.—Defendant was tined in his absence 103. and costs or a month.

A BODY FOUND.—On Tuesday, the coroner, Mr. Ridgway, held an inquest at the Red Lion Inn, on the body of a man who had not been identified.—Wm. Blower, of Runcorn, captain of the steam tug Liverpool, owned by the Bridge- water Navigation Company, said that on Sunday morning he was going with his tug from Manchester to Runcorn, and when near Moore Bridge he noticed that the tug struck something. The body of the deceased then came to the top of the water. He examined it, and found a big cut on one of the arms and on the bead. The fan of the steamer would cause some of the cuts.—P.C. Boyle said he had ex- amined the body, and be thought the wounds, which were fresh, had been caused by the fan of the steamer. The deceased was 51t. 4in. in height, he had dark-brown hair, sandy whiskers and`moustache; he was about 30 years of age, and had evidently been a labourer.—The jury returned an open verdict of "Found drowned." OVER.

BRASS BAND.—An entertainment of a mixed character I took place on Wednesday evening at the Town Hall, Wins- ford, for the purpose of buying new instruments, and so , contributing to continue the credit which this band has gained for careful and well prepared musicar performances. The mixed character of this entertainment, and the ardour with which it was undertaken, gave great satisfaction to the audience present. Songs were sung by the following : The Misses Percival, Atherton; and songs or duets by Messrs. Mason, Parry, Davies, J. 0. Gleave, and Timperley. More were also some good glees by the glee party. Miss Ravenscroft accompanied. The band gave some selections in very good style. Mr. Edmund Leigh, Mayor of Over, occupied the chair.. SOUTHWORTAI-WITH-CROFT.

BOIRD Scatm.—The annual prize distribution and enter- tainment took place at ON school on F, iday evening last, under the patronage of the School Board. he school-room, as in previous years, had been beautifully and tastefully decorated for the occasion by the headmaster, teachers, scholars, and a few friends, with evergreens, artificial roses, texts, Chinese lanterns, &c, and a platform had been erected to seat upwards of 50 children, whose pleasant faces and clean and neat appearance added greatly to the admir- able arrangements of the school-room, and presented a most pleasing sight. There was a very large audience, the school- room being crowded, and the rector, the Rev. T. P. Kirk- man, M.A., F.R.S., chairman pf the School Board, presided. The following programme, consisting of songs, readings, I recitations, &c., was given in excellent style by the teachers and scholars, under the conductorship of the headwaster, Mr. F. A. Ball, who accompanied some of the songs on the harmonium :—Part first: Song. "Come .gather around ; " reading, "The skaters and the wolves," Master R. Stead;• song, "The forget-me-not ; " recitation, "The Saxon and the Gael," Master T. Burch ; song (solo), "The whistling • farmer bay," Master J. Ball; song, "Soft music is stealing;" dialogue, "The truants," Messrs. F. W. Ball, J. Waywell, L. Daintith, J. Ball, J. Hatton, J. Pemberton, T. Burch, R. Stead, and R. Sanderson; song, "Present time;" reading (Lancashire dialect), "Betty Podger un th' Encyclopeelia chap," Master J. Pemberton; round," Come follow, follow;" recitation, "The shipboy's letter," Miss A. Thomason; song, "The crow and the pitcher ; " action song, "The burlesque band" (boys). Part second: song, "Little acts of kindness;" reading, "A bad boy's diary," Master J. Hatton ; song," Tbe

slug, rsolOT "-1:116 a .ng. " Winter r dialogue, " The King and the of inefield," Messrs. J. Ponberton, L. Daintith, and T. Bu-ch ; round, "The Five Bells of Osney song. "The Burial of Sir John Moore ;" recitation, ',"The Milkmaid," Miss B. Whiston ; song, " King Christmas;" recitation (Lancashire dialect), "Cure for th' Tooth-warch," Master L. Daintith ; song and chorus, "The Schoolmaster, or A B C," Mr. Ball. Great credit is due to the teachers and scholars for the excellent manner in which they rendered the songs, &c., several of which were loudly applauded, es- pecially the songs given by Miss A. Stretch, Master J. Ball, and Mr. Ball, the last named receiving a hearty encore. The action-song, "The Burlesque Band," by the boys was also encored. The readings and recitations created much amuse-, ment, especially the Lancashire reading by Master J. Pem- berton, who was heartily applauded. The dialogues were also very well rendered, the respective characters being well sustained. At the conclusion of the entertainment the chairman distributed the prizes to the scholars, which con- sisted of beautiful and useful books, after which a hearty vote of thanks was given to Mr. Ball,. on the motion of the chairman, for the excellent entertainment he had provided, and to the children themselves for the creditable manner in which they performed 'their duties. On the motion of Mr. Hatton, cheers were given for the chairman for presiding, and on the motion of Mr. Ball, for the remaining members of the School Board. The National Anthem having been sung, the proceedings terminated, all being highly pleased with their evening's entertainment. The children were sup- plied with coffee, buns. &c. WHITLEY SUPERIOR.

STRA.YING ON THE HIGEWLY.—At the Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Josiah Wright, farmer,. Antrobus, was summoned for allowing two heifers and a bull to stray on the highway at Wkitley Superior on the alst ult., and was fined is for each animal and costs. Defendant said the bull did not belong to him. POACHING AT WHITLEY SUPERIOI2.—AI the Dareshury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, James Earle, labourer, Antrobus; was summoned tor trespassing on land at Whitley Superior, in the occupation of Miss Neild, in search of game. Mr. Percy Davies prosecuted, and Mr. Moore defended, and pleaded not guilty on behalf of his client.—lt seemed that Mr. Kerr, wire manufacturer, Stretton, has the right of shooting over land belonging to Mr. Neild, and in the occu- pation of Miss Neild. On the day in question, Saturday, the 27th October, Mr. Kerr found defendant on a small occu- pation road, where he had no right to be, with a min in his hand, and with a dog which captured a rabbit in his pre- sence.—Mr. Moore, in defence, contended that this pit or road was used by the public, who brought their cattle to drink there. On the day in question defendant had a gun awl was on his way to Mr. Whitshead's farm, where he had a right to shoot. There was a dog about but it did not belong to him, but to a man named Plumb; a machine feeder.—Plumb was calledand deposed that he had a spaniel dog with him at the time stated. He did not know whether the public had a right to the road, but they went there.—Mr. Davies pressed the case, as defendant had been previously convicted for stealing decks and threatening with a gun.—The magistrates fined defendant 20s and costs, or a month.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

WESLEYAN ENTEETAINMENT.—An entertainment given in the Wesleyan Chapel, Winsford, on Thursday last, for the new chapel scheme, passed off very well. Great credit is due to Mr. J. Stocks, who had exerted himself very much to make it what it was. The young folks whom he had trained sang and recited their very best, and will feel they have an interest in the new chapel which has to be built, whenever that event occurs.

div.head: CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE
div.p: CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE

SOCIETY- MEETING AT THE PUPLIC HALL, WARRINGTONb Under the auspices of the Church of England Temper- ance Society a public meeting was held in the Public Hall, Rylands-street, on Monday evening, when the building was crowded in every part. The Ven. the Archdeacon of War- ringten presided, and there were on the platform the Mayor and Mayoress of Warrington (Alderman and Mrs. Harrison), Mr. Clarke Aspinall (coroner of Liverpool), Rev. J. R. Eyre (Rural Dean of Toxteth, Liverpool), Rev J. Hirst (organi- sing secretary), Rev. S. Wilkinson, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Rev. A. M. Mitchell, Rev. W. H. Williams, Rev. E. S. Jack- son, Rev. W. Vernon, Mr. and Mrs. W. Beamont, Miss Nay.l lor, Mrs. Feirclough, Alderman Webster, Councillor Dr. Maokie, Councillor Dixon, Mr. John, Fairclough, Mr. R. Garnett, Mr. D. Garnett, Mr. R. A. Naylor, Mr. W. Roberts, and other gentlemen. Mr. Gilbert Legge presided at the organ and gave one or two recitals. A special selection of hymns was sung. Letters of apology for absence were read from several gentlemen who were unable to be present. The Vera. CHAIRMAN, in his address, remarked that the society had a dual basis. He knew there were some who were prepared to say that no one ought to enlist in the tem- perance movement unless they were total abstainers; but looking back on the work of the society he was prepared to say that they made very little progress until they estab- lished the dual basis. He congratulated them upon the progress which the society had made throughout the coun- try. Twenty-one years ago they wanted a president. They wrote to the bishops here and the bishops there, and they could not get a bishop to he president except one in the north-west of America. Now there was not a bishop on the bench who was not a member. Even if they looked at the question from the narrowest grounds they found that their cause had progressed. During tlee first few years of the society's existence its income was only about £sooi but now it had aa income of £7,000. In referring to the drunkenness among women, he remarked that 10,000 women were apprehended in Liverpool in one year for drun- kenness. And what did they read in the local newspapers? Young girls of 15 or le:standing at tbe public-house bar and drinking until they had to be brought up for being-.drunk and disorderly. He trusted that in Warrington there would be such an opinion formed against the practice that would put an end to the drinking amongst the young women of the town. (Applause.) Mr. W. Bnaatcm, who was received with applause, moved the fallowing resolution :—" That whilst the vast amount of drunkenness, even among the young in the town of War- rington, is so much to be deplored, and calls for increased and vigorous efforts -on the part of it inhabitants, the thanks of tha Church of England Temperance Society are nevertheless due to and are hereby tendered to the magistrates of the borough for their efforts to suppress this evil, the main cause of so much misery, vice, and crime in our midst." Mr. Beamont said that no lan, gaage of his with reference to the great evil they had met that _evening to do their best to suppress, and the words which had been used in calling it a plague and a pestilence walking by day and by night, were too severe a description to ghee. It was the duty of all of them to do their best to suppress the evils of intem- perance. It was hydra-headed, and the legion that was cast out of the demoniac would not equal the number of sins that great evil lead to. Ho was happy to think that in mordern times there had risen up a littlenrmy. There was was the Band of Elope—(applause)—which gave them hope, and would certainly lessen the evil. The Blue Ribbon Army had done a great deal of good. Then there were the followers of Jonadab, the son of Rechab and he hoped they were doing a good work. There were also the Teinplars. They ought to be pure, as they came from the temple that took their name from it. He might also name that great society whose interests they had met that night to promote—the Church of England Temperance Society. (Applause) He concluded by moving the reso- lution. e Councillor Dr. MACKIE in seconding the resolution, said he could not help remembering that he bad appeared o n a higher platform than that during 20 years, and that was the platform of total abstinence. Circumstances he need not relete, but which be trusted did no discredit to him, the action of medic ml and other authorities, caused him to have to retire from the teetotal platform. With him it was abso- lutely a question of health and strength, and he looked for- ward to the day when he would return to the ranks he so delighted to be in. He lamented that they had such a sad tale to tell of the young women of Warrington. He bemoaned it, and he was sure all their townsmen did. Some- how this drinking among the young women had worked it- self in in a manner they seemed to know little about. They were driven to their wits' end to know how to get rid of it. Their thanks were due to the magistrates, who had done well. But they had not done half of what they must yet do. They had net exercised half of the power with which the present law armed them. If they had not power to put down Sunday drunkenness, and week-day drunkenness too, he was sure they would be willing to go to Parliament and beg that greater power might be given. (Applause.) The Rev. J. R. EYRE supported in an able speech. The Rev. S. WILKINSON then moved the following resolu- tion :—" That the society, conducted as it is upon a broad basis, is worthy of the support, and 'demands the sympathy of all classes of Churchmen ; and that the clergy of the town and neighbourhood be invited to form adult and juve- nile branches in their respective parishes, and to give as much prominence as possible to the work and operations orthe society." He said that the resolution was a pratical one, and if they could carry out the sugges- tions it contained they would hare effected the object for which that vast meeting had been called together. He urged upon them to make up their minds to be more diligent and earnest in the great work of rescuing men and women from the soul-destroyiog vice of drunkenness. (Applause.) Mr. R. A. NAYLOR seconded the resolution, after which Mr. CLARKE ASPINALL delivered an eloquent and earnest address. Referring to moderate drinking, he said he would advise all who called themselves Moderate to go through the little process of self-examination, and ascertain really if they came up to their own description; and if they did not he asked them to be honest to themselves and others, and let their moderation be something of a more definite and defined character, and there would be more truthful men in the future than there had been in the past. The doctors would not have so many rang-tangs et their houses as they had, the chemists would not have to dispense sedatives sal often as they did at present, and wives would not have the worry they had bad to bear. (Applause.) The Mayor here took the chair, which the Von. J. W. Ba.rdsley was obliged to vacate in order to catch a train. A vote of thanks, on the motion of Mr. PIERPOINT soeon- ded by Mr. John Faincnotrog, was then accorded the Ven Archdeacon Bardsley, the speakers, and the organist. The Mayor sail that while listening to the speeches be had not only been instructed but amused in the right way, and he should go away from the meeting deeply impressed with the forcible manner which the great truths that hid been propounded bad been placed before, them. The sub-

. _ ally to his pleasure. flotsaver, be thought that the gentie- men NA° had come from a distacce would go auav deeply inrere,t,ed with tke fact that a favourable itnpression had b ,en made. (Applause.) A:1 u Aon ii id aeen made to the melancholy fact that a number of young girls in Warrington had taken to drink and were frequently to be found at public-house bars. It was a fact that some few girls had been found in that condition, but he did not hesitate to say for the honour of Warrington that the matter had been greatly exaggerated; and that, instead of it being a reproach- to Warrington that these things had been discovered, it was rather a credit than otherwise, be- cause it showed that the authorities were vigilant in their endeavours to detect crime and misconduct of that kind and to bring it to condign punishment. That such a state of things existed in other towns was beyond doubt; in fact he did not think Warrington was half so bad as other towns which had not been so reproached. (Hear, hear.) It was only his duty to say that much. He hoped they would all appreciate the noble work in which the Church of England Temperance Society was engaged—temperance not only in the use of drink but in all things—and if they did that the result could not be other than a blessing to the whole human race. (Applause.) The meeting shortly afterwards separated.

div.head: BLUE RIBBON ARMY SCANDAL AT
div.p: BLUE RIBBON ARMY SCANDAL AT
WIDNES.

ALLEGED IMMORAL CONDUCT OF TWO OFFICERS. Widnes Police Court on Wednesday Wa S crowded with a large number of people who had assembled to hear a charge of using defamatory language which was preferred against an old man named Janes Heath by William Francis Eitues and Hettie Whitehead. About a hundred persons, who were unable to gain admittance to the precincts of the court, were congregated round the building, and appeared to be labour- ing under some excitement. The case was not called on until nearly one o'clock, when all the other busineso• of the court had been discharged,. and the magistrates then eittiug on the Bench were Mr. George Pilkington and Mr. F. H. Gossage. The summons charged Heath with having un- lawfully, falsely, and maliciously uttered offensive and de- famatory language reflecting upon the character of the com- plainants, and asking that the defendant might be hound over to keep the peace.—Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens, appeared for the complainants, And Mr. J. W. Knowles was for the defendant.—Mr. Swift said Elmes wa3 a staff-captain in the Blue Ribbon Gospel Army stationed at Widnes, and Miss Whitehead was also a captain in the same army. Until the end of iaet month she was stationed at Widnes, but she was now located at Edge Ihil, Liverpool. Elmes was a married man with a wife and four children, and Miss White- head, he thought, expected to be married shortly, and there- fore any suggestion of immorality between them was a very serious matter to each of them. The defendant was a labourer, and lived in Oakland-street, and for some time Miss Whitehead lived with him: On the sth November the , defendant called to a man named Pierce, who worked 'rah , him, that he had something to tell him. He then told him that Miss Whitehead and Elmes had been in the front room of his house; that they were cc the floor together; and that the blinds were drawn down. Of course that could cnly mean one thing, and to make it clear beyond all doubt what the defendant did mean, he told another man the following Wednesday that Elmes had been up to his games again, and that he had been caught in the very act. The defendant also told Pierce that Miss Whitehead and Elmes had been caught behind a brick-kiln at 54te1mersda1e at 11 o'clock at night. Elmes, Miss Whitehead, Pierce, and a man, named Holden, went to see defendant about his assertions. He then said he was not going to say anything about Skelmersdale, but with reference to the other allegations, he called Elmes a rogue, a scoundrel, and de- clared that he would not have his house turned into a "bawdy house." This language was highly likely to lead to a breach of the peace even if it were true, and the assertion of such acts would be unjustifiable. But both complainants stated the assertions were uttnly untrue, and he should be able to prove them untrue. The defendant through his so- licitor stated he had never made the statements attributed to him; and the only queation for their worships to con- sider was whether the defendant did or did not.

George Pierce, of 13, White-street, Widnes, said in answer questions by Mr. Swift, that he was a member of the Blue Ribbon Army. On Monday, the sth November, he was working at Mr. Gossage's works, where the defendant was also employed. The defendant told him that Miss White_ head and Elmes had been on the floor together in his par- lour, and had the blinds down. He said it happened before Miss Whitehead went away—he believed on the 2.4 th Octo- ber. Ha also told him that there had been a great row about Skelmersdale, where Elmes had been be- hind a brick kiln with Miss Whitehead at eleven o'clock at night. He .',witness) asked him what he would have done if anybody had said anything to him about Miss Whitehead. He replied that he would have given him a "smack aside the chops," and would not have believed him. He (witness) reported this conversation to. -Elates. On Thursday he went with,Elmes, Miss Whitehead, and Holden to defendant's house. Defendant said he would not have his house made into a" bawdy shop." By Mr. Knowles: The defendant said his neice had told him about the parlour. Mr. Knowles: Did he tell you that his neice had caught Elmo kissing Mias Whitehead on the sofa? Yes he told ' us that. Did he say the blind was down? Yes. Did he say that Elmes must not enter hls door again? No, he never said anything about the door. Did he simply ask you, as a friend of Elmes, to tell Elmes about the parlour so that he could get to the bottom of the matter A Yee. sir. Why did you make it public? L never mentioned it Co anyone but Elmes. Did my client say a word about immorality taking place? He said he would not have his house male into a " bawdy shop." He never said anything more scrious than kissing? No, sir.

Mr. Swift: On Monday he told you something more seri- ous? yes. He began by telling you you, were Captain Eline's fancy man ? Yes, and said I must go and tell him. George Sweetman, labourer at Messrs. Goseege's, stated that on the 7th November he met Heath, who said "limes has seen at his game again, George, and be ni caught in the act." What defendant meant he could not say. Mr. Swift: You don't mean to pretend you don,t know what he meant by that? It is not for me to say what he meant. I cannot read a man's mini. (Laughter.) By MreKnowles : The defendant never asserted that any immorality took place between the complainants. ' William Elines then entered the box, with a jaunty airy, and having been sworn, folded his arms, and leaned forward. He was ordered to stand upright, and was then examnined by Mr. Swift. He deposed to Pierce informing him of the defendant's statements, and visiting defendant's house on the 7th November. The defendant, in addition to the other allegations sworn to. said he (witness) had been in the par- lour with the blinds down, and had " Captain " Whitehead on his knee, with his arms round her, and kissing her. He said his granddaughter had told him. He several times called him a rogue and a scoundrel. Ihe defendant refused to give him satisfaction, and he commenced these proceed- ings. There was no truth in the defendilit's assertions.— Mr. Knowles: Were you ever in the Salvation Army? Yes. —What made you leave that army? That has nothing to do with you. I shan't answer the question.—l will just give a little extract from a newspaper : " The plain fact is , that the person Elmes (the captain in charge of the Hereford Barracks (the same captain who went to gaol, and in three or four days de- sired to be released) and his lieutenant have been withdrawn from the Hereford after due inquiry for miscon- duct with .a woman belonging to the Army." Are you that man ?—Witness: I fun that men.—Were you tried by court martial ? Indeed I was not.—Were you every tried by superior officers in the Army, and then expelled? I don't know that I was expelled from the Army.—You are the person accused of misconduct with some woman in Here- ford? Yes, lam the person.—When you came back from Hereford I believe you went to Mr. Heath's house? I did.—How long did he keep you? A week or two—Did be charge you anything? No.— Why are you going on with these proceedings? Because he would not apologise.—Are von afraid of Mr. Heath hitting you? Indeed lam not, no more than I an' of you. —Mr. Pilkington : Stand properly, and answer the ques- tions in a proper mannerf—Mr. Knowles: You don't feel inclined to hit him? No, certainly not.—Do you remember the granddaughter of Mr. Heath coming to the parlour door when you and Miss Whitehead were alone? No.—Had you on the 2nd October Miss Whitehead sitting on your knee in the parlour? No.—Was the blind down ? Not that I know of.—Did you on that day kiss Miss White- head? No.—Did Miss Whitehead when Miss Norcott entered the room want to get off your knee? She never got on.—Didn't Lizzie Norcott say she would tell Mrs. Elmes about it? Never.—Didn't you say to her, "I know, Lizzie, you won't; I can trust my life with .you ?" I never said such a word.—Didn't she go to the kitchen and tell your brother, and your brother shouted, "Keep them, apart; we can hear them ' mouching ' in the kitchen ?' (Laughter.) No, I never heard him say anything of the sort.—Do you remember on the Satan:lly in that week being in the parlour again? No, I don't remember the week at all. I may just is well say that I have been in the habit of going into the parlour twice every week to do business with Miss Whitehead—Monday or Tuesday...—. Did Mrs. Heath ever say to you that you must remove Miss Whitehead from their house? No, never.—Did yefu say" Mrs. Heath, would to God my wife had died while she was ill, and all the devils in hell should not shift Hettie Whitehead?" No, I never uttered such a word out of my mouth.—Did you ever take a photograph of Mise White- head from the album? I did.—And did Mrs. Heath say you must not take it, because your wife had torn two be- fore ? No, she said she wanted it herself. I never saw my wife tearthern.—Do you know a woman named Mary Nor- cott ? Yes, rather too Will.—Do von remember her coming into the house the hack way six ;veeks aere when you were sitting on the sofa with Sliss Whiteheed on your knee? No, never with Miss Whitehead on my knee. H. e denied that he had ever taken improper libertie3 with AlmsWhite- head.—lf a woman comes here and says you have, is she swearing falsely? She will.—Do you remember staying at some cocoa rooms in Skelmered.ile with Miss Whitehead ? Yes Were you there si!tins with your arm round the shoulder of Miss Whitehead ? .7ee.ver.—And you had an apple between you—first one had a tote and then time other? Never, sir—.Do you remember walking up Waterloo- road with Harry Corwell to the post-office about four Nreas

ago, and that you said to him, "Harry, I know I can trust you. I have had Miss Whitehead on my knee. I have ' clipped and kilserh her, and we dropped the corner blind." Did you make that statement ? Never, if God strikes me dead—lf that man swears that, will he be telling lies ?He will he tellieg lies b:fore God.—Mr. Swift: Have you ever heels guilty of immorality with Miss Whitehead? No, sir. —Miss Whitehead saki she had heard the evidence of Cap- taiu Elmes, and he had spoken the truth.—Mr. Swift: Have you ever ,at on his knee? No, sin—Have your ever bean -on the floor with him in Heath's kitchen? No, site—. Have you behaved improperly with him at Skel- mersdale ? No, sir.—Have you ever made an improper use of Heath's home? No, sin—Mr. Knowles cress-examined witness in a similar manner to Captain Elmes, but she strongly denied the accusetiene.—bo you remember on Sunday morning, the 15th Ssptember, hearing Elmes shout to you at your bedroom door, "Morning star, are You getting up ?"(Loud laugteer.)—No.—Witness denie-el that she had ever walked arm in arm with Elmes,— Mr. Smith: Are you engaged to be married ?—Ys.—Hive you ever with Elmes given Your lover reason to be jealous ? —No, sir.—Has Elmes ever done anything with you that his wife might not have seen ?—No, William Holding, a flannen livine, in Mersev-road; corro- borated Pierce's evidence. He said Heath called Elmes a Brigham Young. Walter Elmes, the brother of the complainant, having bsen examined and sworn that he had seen nothing itnproleer take place between his brother and Miss Whitehead, Mr. Knowles addressed the Bench for the defence. His client instructed him that he never mid, any asser:lon of immorality against the complainaote, and Mr. Swift had simply preduced a certain amount of evidence which he said suggested immerality. Ei3. client was a respectalole man. He had been employed at one firai for 30 years, and he did not wish it set out that he was an untruthful man. If he- wonlcl have made ast apology that would have ended the matter, and even if he had that morning pleaded guilty, • and paid a few shil- lings.—Mr. Swift: I never asked you to admit that he ie guilty or to pay a few paltry shillings. If the m in had said he never intended to inmly immorality there would have been an end of the matter. Tne essee is fought on spiteful grounds. Mr. Knowles said he was pre- pared to show that his client had never said there had ever been anything immoral between the complainents. He told Pierce what had taken • place net in a spirit of scandal, but as a friend of Elmes, so that he-could tell Drees an ascer- tain if it was true. If it is tree," he sa'd, "he must net enter my door again." This -.7as an ,etion which every honest upright man ought to take. The defendant was there to answer a charge of ut7.ng larguege calculated to provoke a breach of the peac3. But the man Elms said he never felt inclined to strike Heath and Wes not in fear of Heath, so that there could be no antic:pation of n. breech of the peace, and he asked for the defeohlant',, dismissal on those grounds. Mr. Knowles then referred to what had taken place at Skeltnersdale, bat Mr. Swift ob'emed, and Mr. Pilkington said he did not see how the La-ing of as apple had anything to do with the case.—Mr. Knowles: It shows how they were carrying en there. The defendant was Then put into the witness box. He said be was 70 years of age, and hat had a family of 17. (Laughter.) He said on the TA November he told Pierce to tell Captain Elmes to keep out of his house, for he had transacted that in his parlour that no other man ever had. Pierce told Captain Eitnes, who sent him (the defendant) a note stating that he would fetele a summone for Mrs. :".;later, and that he would have him for a witness. He eould not read the letter himself, so he gave it to his wifo. He never told Pierce that Elmes had been cell& on the floor with Miss Whitehead. He never said any immoralit7 had taken place between them. He -!crleade Elmes his house.—Mr. Swift: You told Pierce that they had the blind down? No, sir, I didn't. I never mentioned the blind to him.—l think you tad Pierce he was Eleaes' fancy-man ? • Yes, I did.— You were very friendly over it ? Yes, sir; we are now. (Laughter.) He denied • that he ever said he would not have his house made into a`thawdy house."—Why did you call Elmes a scoundrel anla scamp? I called him that for making my house—into what he did do.—Well, don't stam— mer over it.

Elizabeth Nercott, granddaughter of the defendant, said she had seen Captain Whitehead sitting on Captain Elmes' knee in the front parlour- She said to Calatain Whitehead "How can you forshane. to sit cn a married man's knees. I shall tell Mrs. Elmes." Captain Whitehead said "I hope you won't. I dare trust my life with you." She (witness) told Elmee brother Walter that they were sitting in the front room like a young couple (laughter) —and asked him to come and see. "No," he replied, "I might get chucked out." The complainants went on kissing, andEltnes' brother shouted "Aent they giving them smouches." She replied they were. Miss Whitehead said if Mrs. Dales 'anew she would be jealous, and witness-said that was true.—ln reply to Mr. Swift, witness said LaZie and Miss NVhitehead parted r;uite friendly. Mr. Swift submitted that even if the allegations were true, it would be no defence. The only question was, did the defendant use language calculated to pr-ovoke a breach of the peace? • Mr. Knowles saki he had sufficient witnesses to prove that the defendant was not guily of any false or defamatory language. The defendant said he sinaply forbade Eltnes,the house in consequence of the kissing and so on. Henry Corwell said he was the leader of the Skelraersdale Gospel Temperance Mission Band. He deposed that Cap- tain Elmes had owned to him that he had had Miss White- head upon his knee, that he had Eased and clipped her when ; they had the blind down in the ;a:lour. He also told him that Miss Whitehead bad said she loved him. and that if they waited 40 years they would wait of each other.— Mr. Knowl:-A: I believe you are aourting defendant's grand- daughter. Was he afraid of her tolling? I don't know. I suppose be must have. been.—Mr. Swift: Yoe were under Stlff-Captain Elmes at Skelmersdale ? Yes.—li.)elieve he sent a report about you to headlual-ters ? I don't know. He never told me.—Were there complaints about your conduct ? Yes.-. Wore the complaints that you had been telling lies ? I don't know.—Do you know that Elmeswas the means of your removal ? Elmes and Cot. ford were the meana.—You name to Captain Dimes on the 6th November ? Yes.—W you supposed to be courting Misa.Norcett ? Tgat is not the qucstion.—Did you hear her say In the box you ? That is nothing to you. lam not going to tell you.—You are not going to admit it for fear of an action for breach of promise of marriage ? Wit- ness: Speak to me in a gradely manner will you.—Mr. Pilkington : Just remember that you are in a court of jus- tice, and conduct yourself properly.— Mr. Swift : While you were at Heath's did you write a letter proposing marriage to Miss Whitehead ? It was merely done for a bit of fun.—A bit of fun arranged between you and Misa-Norcott ? Yes.—. And that is the way you chaff young ladies, is it?, Neve. r mind.—You are a creditable young man. Captain Elmes made you his confident at the time he was trying to get you removed from the army? Yes.—Do you wish us to believe that ? He did; he told me walking along the road. Thelr worships refused to hear the evidence about the alleged Skehnersdalo episodes ; and Mr. Knowles said the case was concluded then. After a short deliberation, the Beach bound the defendant over for his good behaviour for tb:ea inc;nths,laimself in £5 and one surety in £5.

SHOCKING APFAIR.—AR extraordinary affair was inves- tigated on Thursday afternoon by the coroner, for Stroud. An aged couple named Smith resided in a cottage at Kits. combs, and on Wednesday the house was found locked. The neighbours, on forcing an entrance, found the old man, aged 71, dead in a corner of the bedroom, and his wife dying at the foot of the stairs. It is ly2lieved that the ccuple bad quarrelled and fought, inflicting fatal wounds upon each other. The inquest was adjourned.. THE LEICESTER ANTI-VACCINATORS —About 2,000 per- sons assemb'ed at Leicester Gaol on Tuesday morning to witness the libnation of an anti-v-accinationist,narned Ball, who had undergone a week's imprisonment in default of paying a tine for net having his children vaccinated. Ball was received with great cheering, and resolutions were passed condemning the acts under which such proceedings were possible. There is great excitement, as the guardians have ordered 1,000 prosecutions. WEAVERS' WAGES.—At a very large nanaber of mills in North-east Lancashire the notices of a reduction of 5 per cent. in Weavers' wages have been posted. It is reparted that the leaders of the operatives are "waiting upon events," choosing rather to allow the workpeople to select their own course of action than to dictate what policy shall be adopted. A great majority of the weavers are in favour of striking against the reduction, but with mere funds at tbeir dis- posal, and considering the approach of winter, many of the older hands look doubtfully upon Vas prospect of 3 general cessation o sn i support rwoorrtko. f t hThethe r e d employersuetod a n are practically unani- mous the final decision of the operatives will be ascertained by means of district meet- ings to be held during the ensalug . for the On Oract THE APPROACHING NEWRx. Special trams will leave Armagh city at 10-45 a.m. for Newry, and seats have been taken for 1,000 people. A handbill hen been issued stating that as Newry has been proclaimed, the brethren are cautioned not to display firearms, or allow anyone else to display them. The meeting is to be of a semi-religious kind, and the County Grand Lodge of Armagh is anxious to give no unnecessary offence to any opponent. Orangemen, now as ever, are anxious to uphold the law and observe the sanctity of the Sabbath. It is duty, and duty only, of an urgent kind that calls for this unwonted display. It is of the utmost importance that Orangemen keep together. No man should wander away. They are to bring colours, and, if possible, a copy of Sankey's hymns. In conclusion the brethren are exhorted to come in full feree. The Nationalists have resolved to hold their meeting mVsltie the town. Three hundred police and four troops of Dregeons will nrrive on Saturday. The excitement is in- creasing, and the Orange placards have been torn down. The speech of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN at Bris- tol, and that of the Marquis of HARTINGTON at Manchester, were awaited with peculiar interest, and it is not surprising that the utterances of both have been eagerly scanned and criticised. These gentlemen represent the two conflicting elements in the Cabinet, but there appears to us to be no reason to fear a collision so long as the pace of each is slackened and increased according to the necessities of the hour. The President of the Board of Trade, it is well known, holds opinions more advanced than those of any other member of the Government; whilst the Secretary for War represents the views of the more moderate section of his colleagues. On, most questions pressing for solution there is, we dare say, a general agreement among members of the Administration; but it is im- possible to disguise the fact that on the pro- posal to equalise the franchise and to extend it to the dwellers in the counties there is a wide divergence of opinion, which our Tory friends hope it will be impossible to recon- cile. We need not say that we do not share the idle anticipations of our Conservative advisers, who, by the way, have always proved themselves to be the opponents of all Reform. his because in Mr. CHAMBERLAIN and the Marquis of HARTINGTON the differ- ence of opinion to which we have. referred is so distinctly marked that so much interest is attached to the words of both. Mr. CHAM- BERLAIN, we all know, has again and again declared himself in favour of manhood suffrage as the basis of our electoral system. He recognises the suffrage to be the right of every citizen, and he would not hesitate even at the present time to confer a vote upon all who are now unjustly deprived of it; but knowing, as he does, the times are not yet ripe for such a step, he wisely subordinates his individual opinions to the wishes and aspirations of the majority. The Marquis Of HARTINGTON, on the other hand, is a long way behind Mr CHAMBERLAIN. His Lord- ship is agreed with all Liberals that it would be wrong to any longer deprive county house- holders of the vote which householders in the boroughs enjoy, but he would not by any means be so thorough in his Reform schemes as Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. The g latter can see "two benefits to be conferred and two wrongs to be developed. The first wrong is the injustice done to many countrymen who have no votes at all; the second is the injustice done to those who have votes, .but whose political influence is nullified' by the excessive weight and power which is given to the smaller constituencies." To confer those benefits, and to right these wrongs, Mr.CHAM- BERLAIN would very unceremoniously brush away every obstacle to their accomplishment. The Marquis of HARTINGTON, again, would ponder over uny difficulties which might arise in the ordinary course, and conjure up others in his mind. What Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN would at once give as a right, the Mar- quis of HARTINGION would concede as a matter of expediency. This is a weakness which his Lordship betrays when he deals with Reform; and his attitude is one we would much rather were absent from any suc- cessor to the present PREMIER. Caution is a very commendable quality in every man, and more especially is it so in a Statesman, for it is a quality which inspires confidence; but on the Reform question the noble Marquis seems to us to push his caution to extremes. It is a pleasure to know, however, that the diffi- culties he foresees are not unsurmountable, that he will loyally assist in removing them, and Will conform to the wishes of the majority of his colleagues. Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN, therefore, in subordinating his demands to what is practicable, and Lord HARTING- TON, in making an advance towards that

Sir James Hannen has been compelled to do a deed which • his soul abhors. I question whether the Doge of Venice allowed Shylock his pound of flesh off Antonio's breast • with more disgust than Sir James Hannen acceded to Mrs. Weldon's application. The President of the Divorce Court is an austere and logical judge. On the bench he conveys the impression of disliking the special work which the court over which 'he presides supplies him with in such pitiful abundance. And then be is very logical. Painful as it was for him to hear the miserable squabbles of this ill-assortei couple, it was more painful still to put the law in force. Mr. Weldon offers an establishment, an income, servants, an independence, to his wife, aud she in- sists on more, she claims a restitution of conjugal rights, or in eater words the presence of her husband in her house. There are few women who would have the courage to try and ferce a man who disliked them to live with them. But 1 Mrs. Weldon is that one woman, and Sir James Hannen has to administer the law, not to make it. Poor Mr. Weldon may :take his choice. Two mercies are offered to him and he must select between them, the society of his wife at her own fire-side, or the solitude of one of Her Majesty's prisons. Sir James Hannen will assist him in every way in his power, but then he has no way in his power. The most he can do is to suspend the law for a fortnight, and he does do that. But a fortnight flies very quickly. It will be about in the middle of cattle show week, when London is getting its first practical suggestion of Christmas coming, that Mrs. Weldon may apply to have the law put in force. I have heard men called the strong sex, and have been told that one reason why women are so much to be pitied is that thdayrauts are their law-gtters. Both statements may be tested by the result of the proceedings in Weldon v. Weldon.

There is a very general opinion that Sir James Stephen behaved with unnecessary cruelty to the unfottnnate War- den. No doubt his crime was great, and I suppose his sen- tence was not teo severe; but the sternness of the Judge certainly brought *ith it no dignity to the administration of justice. Sir James was Ina great hurry to pass sentence. / He might have listened, and having heard Counsel, still have adhered to his own opinion. Sir James Stephen is the last Judge on the Bench who could be accused of popularity jut/Ith, /g, hitt there was something very sensational ip the way 11Q 6WOoPecl dom.' on *retailed convict' ...,cought up for sentence. I think I never saw any human being look so miserable or feel more acutely a terrible situation. His conduct in the box when he was examined as a witness for the prosecution.in the proceedings against Watters was very dignified, and when in cross-examination he was asked how he managed to steal the securities, he replied with a simple impressiveness that seemed to tell on all the court. Even the learned judge prefaced some enquiry about the theft by telling the prisoner he did not wish to give him unnecessary pain. Warden did mot look at all like the 3.ccustemed Old Bailey swindler. He did not seem to h-rve either the braes or the brains of a thief on a large scale. The sentence on Watters was also a surprise, the judges having long since laid down the rule that the receiver is as guilty as the thief.

The whole profession got a scare or a fillip by the an- nouncement that the Bill for establishing District Courts was drafted by Lord Selborne. Indeed it was pretty gene- rally stated not merely that it was drafted ty one Chancel- lor, but that it was baciced by another, asti so was perfectly safe to pass. There as a great deal ef patronage involved, important positions with big salaries. For a day rumour was busy Cling them up, and one ,or two Q.C.'s were reckoned perfectly safe of prometirs. And now it tarns out that Lord Selborne knows :lotting about it. For all that a bill dealing with the sul*tt must sooner or later be made law. Big measures mar thrust little ones ov.t into the cold, but law reform is a ;nec,slity and we shall cer- tainly get it.

The sthasme of the new Ittderground railway is loginnltsr to provoke opposition. A tff,rst, nothing was said agairst it. The parties interested would ba compensated fat the devotion of their property, while the general public would gain 'Vac convenience of a new route from. Paddington to Westminster. But there are always people who gzurnble and prophets who proptesy gloomily. The public eeent to have gone mad on the subject of low holes. They don't Mind having the !Veda torn up to sait tramwaytempanies, and they acquiesce it the London lame poste being made advertisements for varions kinds of gas burners and electric lights, but they are tolerant of blow boles. *lad now we are told that the part of the line which arts tend‘ar the Park must either he constructed near. the surface or very deep dors under it. If it is built near the surface the trees is the Park will be killed. If it is built so low down as to •-bear the roots of the trees—blok: holes. It is curious to hear this solici- tude abut trees end to find so little donezow&rds planting them. Portland Place might be made as 'handsome as the BoulevardsV Faris for a few sovereigns, tut the residente won't allow it. Trafalgar Square could ~be carpetted with grass and enlivened with shrubs—but ;it is left with its greasy fountains shooting up the warm, dirty, soapy water that seems to come straight from the pu'alic baths behind the National Gallery. It is astonishingbow much the Lon- doner will tclerate, but it is possible to- go too far. When you mention,l)law holes, the citizen and the ratepayer is wronged.

In producine a new play the one great, element which must be pleaesd, but which eomehow cannot be safely .1 either prophesied or provided for, is tee influence of the public. "Never forget your fat grocer in the pit" is advice which I heard a great dramatist now dead give to a young dramatic anther now very famous. 'But !rot never can tell how your "fat grocer" may take the play. The one thing that seeres certain is that stage -managers are quite fallible. They bring at Ora most absolute failures with unexampled splendour of dresses and scenery. and the "fat grocer" ton&emns without a moment's iscvaation. I remember Marie DElapite the great actreso of the Gymnist tellinr me of the play, I think Dumas had written it, from which the greatest things were expected. .All the actors were ready with their parts. The manager counted on an enormous -success. A fortune had been sunk in costumes and detfarations—and, the result, absolute failure. The fat grocer shook •hit; head. "And," said the actress, "are every one of us felt that the verdict was right." The rankness of the piece was noticeable the moment it was acted before an audience. For that reason I think Mr. Wilson Barrett was right in invitinv. ,nn Wednesday night the critics to a dress rehearsal of the new piece. Critics are not exactly an audietsce, still the sears feel the presence of the public and sec where they may emphasise what Eses well, and correct what goes badly. Another things that the public is accuatomed to read the morning after production the critics' verdict of the night before. A ner pixy is rarely over till midnight, and it is rather hard to write a. column which shall largely affect fthe destiny of the play hurriedly and .without consideration. For that reason I think there ought lwars to be full dress rehearsals, at which the critics should be present when the first .night of the play is not on a Saturday. I mentioned in my hut letter how Gillette at the Royalty was nearly dismiized and almost all for the want of adequate rehearsal. I saw the piece last night. It went well. I should not pronounce it a boisterous succesti, but it was amusing. If it had been put that way before the public it would have been a success. Mr. Barrett is not in scab a hurry as Miss Saatley. When he rehearsed his piece on Tuesday he found it did not go at al/ well. He put Off the dress re:Gml before the

1 critic!, and the first night cf the play will not be till next 7bnraday. We are just approaching the !waggon of cheap sales and alarming sacrifices. They always set in with the first days of December. Already the shop windows are crowded with doubtful bargains. I saw to-day two very ingenious systems of advortisernent put in practice. Otte advertiser was a cheap tailor in Tottenham Court Road. There was a crowd round his shop that occupied the footway and extended into the road. The shop itself was closed, but from the bedroom and garret windows a flight of small balloons were seat I forth. They were about three timed the size of those given away at the Louvre in Paris and had Printed on them the name, address, and calling of the cheap tailor. The wind was south-easterly, and this flock of gas-inflated advertisements issued forth towards Hamp- stead, Highgate, Watford, wherever the wind carried them. Meanwhile in the road below a procession .of six large vane tumbled along, heavy laden with large packing cases. Each of the vans and each packing case in every. van was label- led with an enormous placard, "Salvage stock from the

wreck of the-," and then followed the name of the linen 'draper to whom these damaged wares were being consigned for cheap and immediate sale. The packing cases were of course empty, and the vans wcre merely on a profitable circuit of advertisement. •

A fresh topic has been discoverel by the newspapers,and there is quite a ferment of discussion about it. It is with respect to the kind of examination papers that are set to small boys. The questions are very abstruse, and it would puzzle their fathers to answer many of them. Very hard things are said of the examiners, and we are treated to all

the old argunients about cramming and a dissertation on Dr. Blivaber. But I think most of these questions have been put to break down cramming. The aaswers are lot to be had cut and dry. Most of the boys would miss most of the questions, but they wauld try most of them also, and it is exactly in their treatment of the subject that their relative abilities would be shown.

IThe news of the dastardly attempt to wreak the express on the Great Western Line created a great deal of excite- ment here; but, notwithstanding the sensational posters of the evening papers, it was not believed that Mr. Gladstone's life was intended to be attempted. Somehow the outrage has net been attributed to the Fenians, and it has not been suggested that Government should offer a reward. It is amusing to see how every novelty in London is safe to be imitated and reproduced. In picture exhibitions it was a new idea collecting the seeks of a living man, and thas setting forth his artistic biography in his lifetime. Now the idea is being rapidly developed. Mr. Dowdeswell will open a gallery in Bond-street with the water-colours of Mr. B. J. M. Donne, an artist who has contributed
excellent work to the Grosvenor, and the Dudley,
and the Academy. A few doors off is Mr. Agusw's
gallery, and its main attraction will be some SO pictures of Mr. Keeley Halswelle, chiefly Thames landscapes. I think no painter ever made so sudden and determined
" departure " as Mr. nab/Irene ; unless, indeed, J. C. Hook, when he left figure subjects and painted the sea coasts of
DevoNSbire, For years Mr. lialswelle was known for
Itaßan subjects, very smooth, very perfect, and very unin-
teresting. Almost without a period of transition hi took to

English landscape, which he treated poetically and broadly. I have been told that the change was due to his anxiety to write after his nante..the letters A It A. tHe saw that in figure painting there WM tO9 mach competition. It gi.:Linit all hi e own way with landicape!,

RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. TUESDAY—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge.. . _ .

Thomas Walker, of Oldham-street, Liverpool,' formerly of Frodsham, sued the Court of Independence Foresters' Friendly Society for £4, being the balance of sick pay due to him under a rule in the constitution of the society.—Mr. Dodd, barrister (instructed by Mr. Henry R. C. Dausen, of Liverpool), appeared for the plaintiff; and the society was represented by Mr. Thurnham.—From Mr. Dodds' opening statement it appeared that the plaintiff had received from the Order of Foresters 16 weeks' sick pay at 5s per week. He had accepted that from the society under protest, because he was entitled under rule 13 to the full sick pay of a free member at lOs per week. Mr. Dodd understood from Mr. Thurnham that the society did not dispute that the plaintiff was a free member, and had been for the past 49 years. The one question which his Honour ivouiti' uziVC t? (.Ifq.*l9 Tr4s one which he was toid his tionotir had already decided. But he thought he should be able to show his Honour that there was an entire difference between this case and the one de.

cided on the 29th May, in the case of John Fletcher agninst the same court. His Honour then decidel that chronic 'heart disease was a contlat3ii.l illness, In this case the dis- ease was bronchitis, which was recurrent. The 13th aule of the socilety was to the effect that any free member who was 'ficic, blind, or infirm, was entitled to 10s. per week 142.: 12 months, ss. per week for the second 12 months. The plaintiff from October, 1882, to the end of January, 1883, received 103 per week, but after that the soclety reduced it to ss. The plaintiff contended that he was entitled to 10s. .per week on the ground that he mast have been continuously 11l for 12 months before his sick pay could be reduced, and ho further contended that he was not so ill, but was able to follow his employment a portion of the year.—Dr. Dawson of 26, Rodney-street, Liverpool, was called, and stated that he had attended the plaintiff for three years. The plaintiff had suffered from bronchitis, but he cared the first attack. He was subsequently attacked with the disease, but between these attacks he was perfectly free from the disease. In chronic bronchitis the disease was sometimes entirely ab- sent, and the disease would not recur unless excited by ths first cause.—Mr. Thurnham addressed his honour for the defence, contending that it was an analagous Case with the one his Honour decided in May. He called Dr. John Robinson wbo said in chronic bronchitis the mellows membranes of the bronchial tubes were snore or 1 ss in- flamed, and any little cold would soon induce the bron- chitis again. The complaint was never entirely absent. From the evidence of Dr. Dawson he should sly the plaintiff suffered from chronic bronchitis. SUPPOSED ATTEMPr TO WRECK
RAILWAY TRAINS NEAR WIDNES.

What is supposed to have been a dastardly attempt to wreck railway trains on the Cheshire Lines Railway, be- tween Hough Green and Hale-bank, was discovered on Thursday morning. On Wednesday night the platelayers had removed their trolly from the lines between those statious, and following their usual custom had removed the top of the waggon from the wheels, which were locked with a padlock. Near the same spot there was also a large, heavy wooden lever, about 12 feet long. When the men went to their work next morning they were astonished to find the wheels of the trolly lying broken in the "four foot," while in the other "four foot" lay the lever, also smashed. That these things had been pl iced on the metals—one on the up and the other on the down lines of the direct route of the trains from Manchester to Liverpool anl vice versa—with the intention of obstructing the progress of trains there cannot be the least doubt, but happjly the at- tempt was unsuccessful. It is not yet known what trains came into contact with the obstructions, but evety inquiry is being made, and it is t.) be hoped the miscreant who placed them will be discovered. Several passenger 'trains mast have passed over the soot.

div.head: NEW SERVICE OF SONG AT RUNCORN.
div.p: A NEW SERVICE OF SONG AT RUNCORN.

"Pilgrim Street," a new servico of song, compiled by our townsman Mr. Richard Moore, was performed for the first I time on Tuesday evening in Runcorn Public Hall. We re- gret that a larger andience'did not assemble to applaud the merits or condemn the faults of the compilation, but the poor attendance can only be ascribed to one cause—the un- usually high prices which were charged for admission. As its name implies, the service of song is founded on ihe story " Pilgrim Street," from the pen of Hesbe Stretton.. It is a pathetic and graphic narrative of the lines of two Manchester street arabs, but to bring it within the limits of a service of song considerable condensation has been neces- sary. On the whole this difficult task has been well per- formed. In one or two instances, however, the thread of the narrative has been somewhat rudely broken, and the connection imperfectly restored; but it nevertheless possesses great interest, and may be read with pleasure. The musical excerpts have been chosen upon the usual lines, and ,consist of seal known anthems and hymns, and the Cara- piler is deserving of nescant praise for the admirable way in which they are adapted to the story. In the work are included two original compositions. The first is a hymn tune by Mr. John Holford, who, we understand, has lent valuable aid to Mr. Moore, and the second is a tenor lola by the compiler. The latter is harmonised as a chorus br Mr. Graham, of Liverpool. Of both pieces we may safely affirm that they are harmonious and tuneful, and as first attempts are meritorious productions' Mr. Ho`lord's music is wedded to some lines of his own conception, which he has prefaced with the title Kindly guard the youthful footsteps." poetry the piece may have little value, yet -tiiil:t=tlhileanl is pure and tender, and possesses the merit of being very appropriate to the episode which it is meant to music illy illustrate. Mama in its entirety the service of tong is quite equ.l to other productions of this description, amongst which, we have not the least doubt it will take a prominent pneiiion, and: bring credit Wits compiler, Mr. R. Moote. The audience on Tuesday evening was very favourably impressed with the service of song, which was rendered by an excellent choir, assisted by a number of instrumentalists. Guided by the baton of Mr. lioltord the choir acquitted themselves in admirable style, and the various anthems and hymns they were called upon to render received full justice.
