div.head: X-etteo to the gilitor.
div.p: X-etteo to the gilitor.

THE TRADE INTERESTS OF ENGLAND. Sir.—l beg to thank you for the fairness with which you treated my last letter by allowing its appearance in your paper. When facts are before the public, they have then an opportunity to judge for themselves. It, however, not unfrequently happens that they are told only as much as yeet:i suit a particular purpose The public pay the piper arltave a right to call the tune. Your readers will please note that I am not actuated by a political feeling in this matter, but rather by a desire to obtain a parliamentary en- quiry into the present trade interests of a country, whose chief support has hitherto been derived from manufacturing industry, beleiving that the consequences of Free Trade are now beginning to be more keenly Colt than at any previous date. With these preliminaly remarks, I beg-to clairn your indulgence by allowing me space to reply to the letter written by Mr. Whitham, which appeared in your paper of Saturday last. Ido not know that any necessity arose to cause Mr. Whitharn to inform us that he was a Radical politician, a term which by this time must have caused even Mr. Gladstone more anxiety than that of his honour- able opponents; nor do I see a reason why Mr. Whitham should bring local firms much less individuals, into a national question, thereby compelling me to reply more pointedly than good taste would perhaps dictate. In the letter to which Mr. Whitham alludes I wrote "British manufacturers cannot compete." This term applies to manufacturers generally; the statement is the re- Salt of conversation and information gathered from manu- facturers of various articles. Perhaps, howevet, Mr. Whitham is not aware of the extent to which American calico, French boots, German clothes, and German soap, is sold in our own, and more particularlY the neighbouring towns, the general public for the most part being kept in happy ignorance of the fact. Mr. Whitham informs us that thousands of pounds worth of drawn wire is yearly im- ported into Warrington," which amount must consequently be paid by Warrington to the country from which the wire is imported, and paid for by cheque also; certainly not a very cheering piece of information to the wire-drawers, rod- rollers, puddlers, general iron-workers, and colliers of this district., but is a good and sufficient reason why every man engaged in these respective employments should at once de- cide againet Free Trade. But oh! what a picture for a once independent people to see German drawn wire brought into Warrington, and sent out again as English manufactured. It is only a question of this becoming generally known amongst England's best customers, when they will at once say that they see no reason why they should not buy the wire direct from Germany, if in the end they really get German and not English iron. If German goods are sold, most as- suredly trade will at last gravitate towards Germany, the seat of production. British orders and conse- quently British money, has assisted Germany to its . present manufacturing position, a position which is likely to take that which England once so proudly occupied. Mr. Whitham inquires, suppose we tax German imports, how will that enable British manufacturers to ob- tain foreign orders?" I think your readers will admit that considerable use has here been made of the corkscrew; there is a decided twist about the question, seeing the object before U 8 is to secure home orders to our own country. I will first straighten the question, and afterwards deal with the twist. I will ask, "Suppose we tax German imports, bow will that enable British manufacturers to obtain home orders ?" If we placed a duty upon foreign manufactured articles coming into Englana, equal to the amount of dif- ference between the price at which they can supply and the price at which our own country could honestly manufac- ture at, we should secure home orders instead of losing I them as at present. With respect to obtaining foreign orders, I do not see how the taxing of foreign finished manufacthred articles coming into our country could pre- vent our taking orders in a country which already taxes our goods. England as a country would have the same natural facility and ability to manufacture and export her own pro- ductions as she has now. If, therefore, by placing a duty upon manufactured imports we could thereby secure home orders :o our country, and leave our position respecting manufactured experts the same as at present, in the name of common sense we must be better off to the event of home orders secured, which are worth many million pounds sterliog annually, and is at present paid to the foreigner. Manufacturers are moreover often willing to incur some slight loss upon a -por- tion of their business, or work to cover expenses, if they can see a profit upon the whole, which, however, it is hard to secure in an entirely export manufacturing trade, and so foreign manufacturers having a home trade to depend upon, are often ieduced to sell gocds wholesale cheaper in England than in the land of their production. To a great extent I would take nature as my guide, and allow all raw materials which we actually require, and also all things which nature has, not given ua, such RS cotton, natural oils, tea, coffee, arc •to come here duty free I hope your readers will so far have understood my ideas upon Fair Trade. There would he a degree of patriotism also dieplayed by following such a ccurse as I have described, but patriotism is a name which must for ever be unknown in connection with Free Trade. Te use a familiar expression, I obj,ct as a rule to talk shop in public, still lam obliged to touch OR the matter. First, then, wire-drawing rods might be called unfinished iron as an import term, and I have yet to learn that Germany can deliver fencing rods at English prices in Warrington ; in the next place English steel rods can be bought at a lower price to-day than German best iron rods. (I am now writing for my country's benefit and not for individual curiosity.) We have therefore English rods of different qualities cheaper than foreign rods delivered at Warrington. Mr. Whitham is now brought to the basis of the wire-drawing trade. How is it, then, that these thousands of -pounds worlle of foreign drawn wire, which he tells us, happen to come somewhere into Warrington? If the price of English wire-reds is favourable, hew does it happen that German wire, number 18, can be sold £2 per ton cheaper than Eng- lish in our country ? One cause is because German wire- drawers work for less wages than English wire-drawers. How are they able to work for less wages ? In a previous • letter I stated it was because the cost of living was higher in Eneland, but Mr. Whitham asks, "Would anyone believe it." Well, if this is not the reason I fail to see what is unless the Germans are more intelligent workmen, in which case they will most likely find their way over here in time. We place a duty upon tea, coffee, (az., whereas the Americans declare these articles duty free, but tax manufactured goods, and thereby secure labour to their own country. Wire-drawers have already been forced to submit to one reduction, and it is far from unlikely that they will be compelled by circam- stlnces to abide another, unless manufacturers by protec- tion are enabled to obtain some compensation from home orders. The workman may suppose that there is no neces- sity to reduce wages, and look upon the wealth of his em- ployer with jealousy; but accumulated capital is the re- sult of past profitable trade and careful investment out- side the manufacturer's own business. There is very. little present gain; indeed there is not any manu- facturer, unless he has a speciality, who iè at present earning above fair interest upon his invested capital. Ido not think it good to reduce wages if it can be avoided, and a substitute found ; to reduce wages is to reduce the purchasing power of the British workman, which in turn tells against our tradesmen. Indeed at, a nation we live in a circle, it is therefore to our interest to protect the whole against foreign attack. Fair traders wish t° Benre home orders to our own manufacturers, re- membeel. ee ag that a penny saved is a penny gained, or that a eve er .ed tons of wire sold in England is as Yood a sale as a clredred tons sold in some foreign country. 'The arguments -4prlicable to the wire trade equally apply to every other tr,tde in England. A lady enters a shop and purchases a pair of French boots, perhaps a thousand others follow her example, never for a- moment thinking of the result. Follow the boot through its different stages,and see the cow, the calf, or the kid reared in another land; the butcher fol- lows the farmer, and the tanner comes after; there is the twine, the nail, the wire, itind the cloth manufacturer all robbed of employment, in addition to the English bootmaker. We might follow all other industries in the same way. British workmen unite in trade unions, as they think to aro.:ect themselves against their own employers ; but if they would unite to protest against foreign manufacturers taking orders and employment from them, they would show more wisdom. The railway rates in England may be higher than manufacturers would wish; still if given at all they ought to be quoted correctly. If the figures named by Mr. Whitham refer to carriage of wire, and the public will conclude they do, then the rate named to London is over 100 per cent. more than the actual rate. It is a great pity there should often be so much attempt made to mis- lead the public, even by persons who lay claim to the name of gentlemen; no more striking instance of this can be given than the way in which our imports and exports are mis- represented. Individuals would not receive such statements in regard to their own business ; why then should they credit them in connection with the trade of the nation? It is well-known that our imports or requirements far exceeds our exports or sales to follign countries; and the only way to square this would be by manufacturing home orders our- selves, thereby reducing the amount of our imports. Any person ought to see this who has not determined to remain eneceavinaed. The amount of our imports and exports is

neither more nor less than the addition or united amount of so many individual purchases and sales. If the amount of a baker's flour bill was in excess of the value of his bread sales he would at once know that his business was going wrong; and so on with every other trader. Then why should the simple addition of a million such transactions be doubted? The cause of every bankruptcy is the fact that the value of goods received is greater than the value of goods sold. The fallacy circulated and so misleading to the pubic, that the produce imported into England is interest upon railway and other investments made abroad, is no more correct than that the pigs broug4it by Cheshire farmers into Warrington market, were brought in payment of the annual dividend upon the London and North-Western Railway shares. The American and other nations do not pay railway fares with barrels of flour any more than we do ourselves. The simple ' fact is we are giving our home orders to the foreigner, and thereby increasing the amount of our imports. All goods are represented by a money value, and if the consumable articles required, purchased, and imported by the people of England are in excess of their sales to foreign nations, united England must square the balance, just as any in- dividual member would, out of an already accumulated capital. I have already encroached to far upon your space, or I would have given many statistics showing the decline of different industries in Great Britain and Ireland pro rata with the increase of population, and also showing the steady increase of the same in foreign protected countries. This letter appears in a public cause, but I must hereafter res- pectfully decline to reply to any letters which may be writ- ten for a private motive.-1 am, sir, yours respectfully, Wirrington, Nov. 27th, 1683. S. LAWRENSON. P.S.—Free Traders are strangely inconsistent their avowed object is to get everything cheaper and cheaper ; yet every man amongst them would be delighted if an ad- vance in price of the article he sold took place to-morrow, ta fact became dearer. -

div.head: REV. JOHN YONJE ON "THE RIGHT OF
div.p: THE REV. JOHN YONJE ON "THE RIGHT OF

PRIVATE JUDGMENT." Sir,—On reading Mr. Yonge's sermon in your last issue, I at once came to the conclusion that the last half was a contradiction of the first. After showing "that a man ought to be his own authority in religious matters, and ought not to be led by any human authority," Mr. Yonge deals very largely with the "rights of conscience" and asserts that it ought to reign supreme—" My conscience binds me," being a grand motto for every man. Up to this point Mr. Yonge made a clean and able defence for the right and competency of man to think and judge for himself in matters religious: but after speaking so ably and unre- servedly in support of the "right of private judgment," or, as I would prefer to call it, "freedom of thought," Mr. Yong° begins to use his "human authority" and limits this freedom, saying, "thus far shalt thou go and no further." Is there such a thing as limited freedom? It does sound paradoxical, far the fact of fixing a boundary at all does away with freedom altogether. If a man doubts, or even rejects, what another man takes to be facts, don't condemn him, or say that he has formed no judgment, and don't call it intellectual indolence or moral cowardice. Perhaps he is as anxious to arrive at the truth as anyone, and very likely he has studied thon so-called facts more than the person who has accepted them. Upon the same principle that I take every man to be honest till he is proved to be a thief, I give every man credit for honesty of doubt and sin- cerity of purpose till he be proved otherwise.-1 am, sir, Warrington, November 243 th, 1883. CONSISTENCY.

Sire-es-Tread the Rev. J. Yenge's sermon, published in your last issue, on "Private Judgment," with great pleasure, not unalloyed altogether with the halting which he strangely exhibits in his application of the noble theme upon which he discoursed. Luther risked physical torture and the sacrifice of his life in the assertion of this great right, while others endured the one and lost the other over mere differences of detailed beliefs. In a mild form, the condi- tions which brought about this state of things still survived —the concession is granted as to freedom of belief, but freedom of unbelief is denied, though tolerated. Mr. Yonge quotes the Rev. Dr. Dale as insisting that it is obligatory upon every person "to strenuously and laboriously enquire," so as to arrive at the acceptance of religions , dogmas or the assent of religious faith. Neither of these , worthy gentlemen, it would seem, know anything of the humanity about them, or they could hardly be serious in , urging that any such monstrous and impossible condition could form one of the already too many onerous and crushing problems which weigh upon /he human race. Such an obli- gation has only to be mentioned to be swept aside. And that it Is an impossible element in the maze of human effort is proved by the fact that the religious multitude accept their religion as it is offered them by priests, or as it comes to them by inheritance. It is not impossible to conceive a relenting disbeliever confes- sing te a rigidly impartial believer that he should like to choose a chapel or church in which to satisfy his newly- awakened emotions; and that his friend would honestly confess that he was unable to take such a great responsi- bility upon himself—heiwould no doubt modestly add that he worshipped at a Baptist chapel, or some other, as the case might be, that one neighbour was a Churchman and another a " Free Jerusalem" man, and so on. Then carrying our quite reasonable supposition still further, let us assume this honest friend saying " Suppose you exercise the same in- dividual choice ?" the reply might very possibly be "I don't know how." Quite true, and then he falls into the hands of the first religious strong man he comes across, ending in worshipping the Virgin Mary perhaps, or in denying the sonship of Christ. In this way he rises above the odious badge of scepticism, but only by weakly yielding to the beliefs of others, not having the self-reliance or capacity to choose for himself. Thus he becomes the victim of a corrupt church or of a heretical church, in Mr. Yonge's opinion—a result which can hardly give him much satisfaction; but the perplexed seeker has satisfied the religious teacher's demand, that you must not remain outside all the various organisations, ordinary and extraordinary, that the religious sentiments has given em- bodiment to. Then cui boric from the orthodox point of view. If Mr. Yonge concedes private judgment, he must not attempt to draw the line and exclaim "Thus far and no farther." The responsibility of scpeticism, agnosticism, is entirely that of the individual embracing one or the other; and it shows, in my opinion, considerable weakness and • timidity for anyone who has made his own choice in his reli- gious belief to be pointing his finger at those who, in the exercise of the same right, diverges from the rut unwar- rantably assumed to be the on 1), right one. Men in Mr. • Yonge's position should concede cheerfully to others the • claim they make, that they have conscientiously and with care made their choice; and to reflect prejudicially upon such is to drag us back to the dismal times of mental en- thralment, release from which Mr. Yonge has shared in commemorating. It is setting up the Pope afresh. I know hardly any higher pleasure than the searching out for one's self, individually and solely, the religious principles that shall satisfy one's own soul and guide one's own life; but that is a very uncommon experience, I think.—l am, Sze., Warrington, Nov., 1883. MORE LIGHT.

Sir,—The Rev. John Yonge in the pulpit is to be admired for his pluck if not for the soundness of his logic. His sermon reported in extenso in your last issue is a bold step,- and the example one which it is high time should be largely imitated. The subject is broad and attractive, and one in which all are interested, and so far is in direct contrast with the themes upon which we are accustomed to hear the old platitudes. But a perusal of Mr. Yonge's discourse is disappeinting, and only shows the hopelessness of looking for a thorough .examination of the arguments under such circumstances. About the early part of it, dealing with historical matter and the establishing of the principle of the rights of private judgement, nothing need be said. Mr. Yonge, however, commences to dogmatise at once. The right of private judgment on masters of belief must, he says, be limited according to the teaching of the Bible. Let us take Mr. Yonge's argument in support of this. A man is not at liberty to think as he likes on this subject; he must think according to the facts." Certainly, but then what are the facts? Looking round at the whole of Christendom, we find an infinitude of sects each ready to assert that it does interpret these soccalled facts according to the teaching of the Bible' and yet all are at variance on vital points of doctrine. We believe that each and all of these, from the Roman Catholic to the Unitarian, will be ready to show that they base their particular and distin- guishing views on Bible teaching. What then are the facts upon which such differeuce of opinion is possible. And granting Mr. Yonge the measure of toleration in these matters for which he would have us believe he contends, what is his attit tideand that of his church to his brethren so differing from him in belief, and how are such differences reconciled? The limiting of the right of private judgment is thus found to be impossible, because of the initial difficulty of ascertain- idg what constitutes the facts. Mr. Yonge's sneer at the self-conceit of the young man of the times who " thinks as he likes on matters of religion" is all very well and very proper. There is, however, this to be said even for him, that he is quite entitled to ask from. Mr. Yonge and all others equal credit for sincerity in the investigation of truth and the putting into practice the biblical text on which Mr. Yonge founds his discourse. But there are men of higher mettle than the young men of whom Mr. Yonge speaks so charitably at work on the subject of these contradictory beliefs and the conclu- sions to which a study of them points. We hear a deal now-a-days about the antagonism of science and religion. It would appear that there is quite as much caing for reconciliation in the ranks of religionists them- selves. Certainly the conflict there is much more real, as in the long run, time may prove. The agnostic worthy the name makes no parade of his opinions, or the want of them, nor of any intellectual superiority. He is the product of our nineteenth century spirit of investigation, and is horn of a conscientious desire to " Prove all things, and hold fast to that which is good." Looking around him at the diversity Of opinion on matters of belief amongst professing Christians, he discerns no limit to his right of private judg- ment. Examined together and separately he finds that the holding Of this or that theological dogma is non-essential to the end which retieion has in view, viz, the furtherance of the happinees of himself and his race. While engaged in a war of creeds, sheta sere m riesitacwtv work kt neglected in proportion to the time so wasted. Preferring then his passive attitude on matters ei:n this a tl• eolo,:ical he is free to recognise the truth and force of that lettereiay ecripture which teaches that "God helps these who help thenesi Ivee." The ignoring of a Ppecia I providence or divine interference of any sort as a factor in the governing agencies of the world is rapidly becoming more general. Utilitarianism, rightly comprehended, is the basis of all reform, as it can be shown to be the true guid- ing principle of individual conduct. It is seen to be pos- sible to perfect a science of ethics, pointing clearly enough

div.head: EXAMINER. 4 TURDAY, DECEMBER 1, 1883. ROBBING PETER TO PAY PAUL.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. 4 TURDAY, DECEMBER 1, 1883. ROBBING PETER TO PAY PAUL.

to an ultimate paradise on earth from the relations of man to man. It becomes a question, indeed, whether the agnostic cannot •claim to be as sincerely religious as the professed Christian of whatever distinguishing shade or colour. By their very differences in ritual and doctrine it is seen that the various religious beliefs have nothing in common ex- cept the single fact of the acknowledgement of the Author of the Universe to whom homage is to be paid. Recognising, as the agnostic does, the futility of all efforts to formulate a new and consistent creed, or to reconcile existing ones, he contents himself with a devotion to the practical end in view. Swendenborg has tersely put it that "all religion has relation to life, and the life of religion is to do good." Accepting this precept as his guiding principle, may it not be claimed that the agnostic's life and conduct shows as truly a religious spirit as that of the most orthodox. Only when the one arrogates to himself the right to preach doc- trine and to lay down limits to principle does the other claim the equal right to examine the arguments for and against. And this must be done dispassionately and without bias. The right of private judgment can have no limits except those which can be established by reason. Granted the right to hold a mental reservation on a single subject of Scripture history as actual fact. allegory, or pure fiction, who shall set the bounds of selection, rejec- tion, or interpretation? And yet thus to push the principle to its logical conclusion Mr. Yonge considers " as sinful as it is lawless," two terms of condemnation which it would be interesting to have an exact explanation of. Mr. Yonge quotes an eminent preacher of his own church to the effect that "To doubt is to be ignorant." Let it be so. "There's far more faith in honest doubt than half the creeds." A suspension of judgment seems inevitable under the circum- stances, and this is surely no "cowardly attitude, nor an apology for mental indolence." Amongst the leaders of scientific thought and the writers of philosophy who grapple with these questions are men whose transparent singleness of purpose lifts them high above calumny such as this. No, the Rev. John Yonge in selecting a subject like "the right of private judgment" is to be commended for. the implied intention of investigating the truth. But con- ditioned as he along with ministers of all denominations is, it is idle to expect that much real advance will be made. His particular 'dozy must be defended and maintained no matter in what direction the logic of argument or of fact may lead. And until there is some radical change in the constitution of religious bodies it seems probable that this must remain so. Debarred, in his public utterances at least, from keeping apace with advancing knowledge and from giving a more intelligible explanation of the faith that is in him, the orthodox expounder of creeds must be content to see the processes of thought carried beyond the bounds pre- scribed for him by those less trammelled by fixity of opinion. Apologising for intruding so largely upon your valuable space, I am. Sir, itc., A MODERN THOMAS SURNAMED DIDYMUS. Warrington, November 27th, ISM.

Bi,—The right of private judgment was, I see by your paper, powerfully championed by the Rev. John Yonge on Sunday week: bat there is one allusion he made which set me thinking. He said that it is a mistake to suppose, as some do, that we can think as we like. Subject to correc- tion, I think he treated this point imperfectly. We certainly possess the power to think as we like, and it is undoubtedly freely exercised. .If he had supplemented it by saying that that exercise carries responsibilities or consequences, as in every action of our lives, I could have understood his aim. But now as to the practical application in another sphere of doing as we like—that of disposing of or giving away our money. That right seems to be abso- lutely conceded by society; yet where its the difference considered as a right? May n't the latter result in harm, as well as the former? Let me apply the analogy more pertinently. If, in response to Mr. Yonge's appeals for funds towards the London Missionary Society, any wealthy gentleman in this town were to hand him £120,000, would he hesitate to receive it, and deny the right of the giver to do what he liked with his own? It could be plainly shown that there are want, misery, and heathenism sufficient in this very town of Warrington to absorb that sum for the alleviation of all that destitution; then has any one ale moral right to do as he likes with his own, to the virtual impoverishment and abandonment of his helpless and woe- stricken neighbours. I hope a reply will be forthcoming, , because the Issues are obviously of importance. ENQUIRER.

BY JOHN SAUNDERS, Author of " HIRELL ; 011", LOVE BORN OF STRIFE," "ABEL DUANE'S WIFE," "ISRAEL MORT, OVERALAN," &C., &C.
CHAPrER XLVIII.—STEPREN'S BITRTHPLACE. Stephen's emotion as he marched with the troops along
he road towards Goa!Wore where (as he had learned so

strangely), his mother and brother now were and with them Miss Vandeleur ; so affected him that ;or the first time in his military career he brought upon himself a sharp reproof from his Sergeant, for some neglect of duty in guiding the men. How coulu he fail to be moved when so suddenly carried back in thought to the hone he had so long left ; to the _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ .

whole series -of dissatisfactions with himself and all his sur- roundings he had there experienced; and to the events in which they had at last culminated ;—his break with Miss Vandeleur, and his consequently cutting himself adrift feom his home and from all his friends and acquaintances to enter upon the life of a private soldier ? And now he was advancing to the very place, where, if he did not carefully guard himself, all the weary and useless round of suffering and discontent might have to be again gone over with its life of weak indulgence, vain hopes, cruel and bitter disappointments. It was a curious fact that within the last few hours he had suddenly become conscious for the first time that he was forgetting home, so far as its dangerous influences or temptations were concerned ; was becoming reconciled to the life he had chosen provided he obtained in it the rank he sought, and so on the whole was doing well ;—the ex- periment was, so far, successful. Now everything was changed or changing, through the Colonel's news as to the residents of the place the troops were going to protect. And that place itself was one to deepen the effect of all that migh happen therein, so far as he was concerned. It was his birthplace. As he grew calmer under the self-control evoked by the Sergeant's warning, he ironically reminded himself that he was anything but a gentleman visitor on the way to Gault- more; that there would be no liveried domestics as of old, coming forth to meet and welcome him after any prolonged absence; that in all human probability, whatever he might wish or fear, he would not be able to catch even a single glimpse of his relatives; that even the attempt secretly might bring down a still more humiliating reminder from his I superiors, perhaps even before his relations, and at the very 1 moment of mutual recognition. But did he want to see them? His mother ? Yes. He felt his conscience was not at rest with regard to her. He knew he had left her, when her weak health might cause his departure to have the most serious effect. The Earl, his brother? No. He should not much care if he never saw him agaih. But the harshness of this first Impulsive thought died away as he reflected that after all, it was rather their external relatioas that made them so hostile, than any deeper influences springing from vital differences it the hearts and minds of the men themselves. Perhaps, had he been the earl and elder brother, he might have been an equally hard judge of the younger one's aber- rations. And thus, practically, he came to the conclusion that it would not very much matter whether he did or did not see Lord Harlaxton—whether he was or was not re- recognised by him—so far as he alone was concerned. But, Miss Vandeleur ? Ah ! he began once more to falter in thought, in purpose, in aim, as her image came back to him as last seen, her expressive face fall of the most in- tense emotion that the wounded modesty of woman, per- haps, had ever shown, but more beautiful in her outward restrained anger towards him—a thousand times more beautiful than he had ever seen before. Then, as .if a dash of cold water had been thrown sud- denly in his face by her, he shrank back from the glowing picture he was summoning up, as he reminded himself— " And she is now, perhaps, engaged to the Earl! Was he likely to lose the chance my folly and recklessness had given him ? " That sobering thought again sent him back to the pos- sible meeting with his mother— 'Would she not determindly press upon him his retreat from the army, through his discharge, which she could so easily procure? "Could he resist her appeals—if made in her own behalf —if she toid him her very life was bound up with his return? "And yet what a laugh for his companions at the clubs, in the Row, on the race cource, if he did yield! How eloquent they would be on the courage and grandeur ..of his project, till he tried it, and then the poor devil got his mother to clear him, and bring him back 'a sadder but wiser man' to the old haunts, and the old life, and the old apron strings!" He was interrupted in these unpleasant cogitations by the first aspect of Gualtmore across the Park, and a strange aspect it was. Every window frame, every chimney moulding, every bit of tracery on the surface of the wall was brought into strong yet soft relief by the snow, which found in thote dellcate hollows shelter from the wind, and nestled there., But it was the fading sunlight that gave such inexpres- sible char,m and colour to these delicate snow lines, suffusing them with an exquisite rose tint ; so that for a few moments Stephen could only stand and gaze at the spectacle wrapt in its beauty. "Shand !" cried the voice of Major Etheredge, summoning him to his side, and speaking to him in low tones, "there is likely to be work for us here to-night, if all that I have heard from the Comte and his wife be true. We shall stay here some hours, get thoroughly fed and reeed, then proceed on the march some time before midnight; but only to return in silence and secrecy, to take up our position in the mansion, there to wait. "Meanwhile there is a bit of very important work which I confide to you. There are three points—at some little dis- tance from the mansion, end from each other—where sen- tinels must be posted, so that no one will be likely to see them under the trees, and from whence every possible ap- proach to Gualtmore is commanded. "On this paper is a rude but capital plan, marked with three red crosseg. Those are the spots where I want you to plant three of our best, most intelligent men, reserving your- self for constant communication with them, and to watch for our return in strict silence. "The order is, that no one be allowed to pass (unless by volunteering the countersign). Should a number of men appear, too many to be stopped, fire on them, and retire through the trees to the mansion, firing continuously as you go for the more effectual warning. I have little doubt, the attack if made will be late enough for us to be ready to respond. If not, there will be some strength inside. But we mast seem to go, which involves some absence, or they will be too much wary to move at all. Beware of their scouts. We can trust no one that we do not ourselves know. Remember the scouts of to-day !" Stephen's animated face showed how he felt the import- ance of the work given to him—and how he was affected by the confidential manner in which the whole position was shown. So that his few, earnest words of assurance that he would& his duty, were not needed te tell Major Esther- edge he could have chosen no better man. And it must be said that all the Major's previous inclin- lugs towards Stephen, as a good and extremely promising young soldier, had been intensified a hundredfold by the belief he owed to him his own life. As Stephen left the Major. he too could not but think of all this, adding to the remembrance of the Major's curiosity in the camp about himstlf and family, the thought, 'What would he say, could he now know the truth, who I am, an 4 what the people are to rae whom I am to aid him to protect?"

But scarcely had the Countess made the best of things, and persuaded one of the guests to take Miss Vandeleues place, before that lady herself returned, and with a smile said aloud, " Pray forgive me. I felt suddenly as though I should be ill, but it is quite gone ; " and therewith, without even a word of suggestion that would certainly have led the guests to change the song, she sat down at the piano under the tearful but admiring eyes of the Countess, and again sang, and delighted all who were present with her refined and in- stinctive sense of humour, as much as she had done by her pathos a few minutes before. Dancing succeeded the music, and was kept up with spirit till the time came for the departure of the troops on their pretended journey. When the Majer left the drawing-room with Lord Har- laxton, the latter said: "Will you be back in time to continue our dance—that is, supposing you have not another kind of dance, a sword dance, to engage in ?" "I wish," was the reply, " you would keep it up, if only at intervals, till we come back; as helping, if there are traitors on the watch within or without, to make them sure you can be safely attacked." "I understand, and will do it. I have everything ready to arm a dozen of my servants, should you want them." "Keep them to guard the ladies and your guests, other- wise my first anxiety must be for them."- "Thank you, but I have places in which to put them where no harm could reach.'

• "That then is a good work accomplished, well say. And now, my lord, farewell, for two or three hours only. Please don't fire upon us when we come stealing in like so many thieves in the night." And with that jest, which Lord liar- laston received with a smile, they parted. Presently, however, the Earl followed to watch from some point of vantage the Major's skilful, and to him somewhat novel method of marshalling his small army in view of the necessities of the case.

The infantry were in column in the middle of the road, with the cavalry long drawn out on each side as if to shield them, but really in order that when they reached the bye road through which the former was to return, the cavalry should go on slowly to a certain point agreed on as the place whence, in case of need, they could easily be recalled, but as if the infantry were still marching with them, after they had in reality passed away. If Fenian scouts were near they would be obliged to keep a certain distance to prevent themselves from being dis- covered. That fact and the darkness it was thaug,ht would make the ruse successful.

LONDON MISSIONARY SOCIETY. MEETING AT WARRINGTON. On Sunday sermons were preached at Wycliffe Church, Warrington, in aid of the above society, when there were large congregations. The morning preacher was the Rev. J. D. Thomas (Ruecorn), there was a special address to , young people in the afternoon, and in the evening the Rev. G. Cousins (recently returned from Madagascar) delivered lan interesting address. The secretary announced that ' during the year the collections and contributions amounted to about £27, which was some £4 less than the year pre- vious, and he hoped they would consider the matter and I raise a larger sum next time. On Monday evening a public meeting was held. The Rev.Jolen Youge presided in the unavoidable absence of Z. Armitage, Esq., J.P.; and the Rev. W. C. Willoughby (Central Africa) and the Rev. G. Cousins (Madagascar) attended as a deputation. On a table in front were a num- ber of interesting objects brought from Central Africa, and such as were in use by the natives, besides maps of Africa and Madagascar. The CHAIRMAN expressed his regret at the absence through illness of Z. Armitage, Esq., S.F., who was an- nounced to hive presided, and, referring to the missionaries, he siid he had hoped that the intereet which was excited in Warrington at the beginning of the year in the Made- gascer question would have resulted in a much larger gathering than the one assembled that evening. They would remember in January last they had a visit from the Malagasy Envoys, and the cordial reception and entertainment the latter received at the hands of the Mayor and Corporation. No doubt many of them had followed with a great deal of interest the events that had since hap- pened in Madagascar. He was sure all of them deplored— most deeply deplored—the action of the French Govern- ment in relation to that island. It must appear to them an action almost insane, and certainly very inhuman and un- necessary, which had been pursued, and they could only .trust that He who ruled all things according to His will would before long show them what His great purpose had been in permitting what they in their shortsightedness felt was a hindrance to the progress and prosperity of the island of Madagascar The rev, gentleman then spoke of their last missionary meeting when a resolution was embodied to Lord Granville asking the Government to use their best endeavours to bring about an amicable arrangement of the Madagascar question. It was some credit to them as a Christian congregation that they were the first in the whole country to send such a representation to the Foreign Office, and he had the personal pleasure of receiving an acknow- ledgment from the chief envoy when he was here. (Ap- plause.) Regarding their help to the London Missionary Society during the past year, the Chairman said they had not contributed so much as they ought to have, and not so much as they might have done, and he encouraged them to better efforts. He then called irpon the Rev. W. C. Wil- loughby to address the meeting. (Applause.) The Rev. W. C. WILLOUGHBY commenced his address by referring to the fact how at the beginning of the present century so very little was known concerning that great con- tinent of Africa, but through their great explorers, the names of whom were as "household word'," light lead penetrated the darkness, and men had gone forth with hearts filled with love for those races for which God had died to redeem. The result was that the great blank in the interior had given way; the travellers bad brought to light new tribes, new nations, and had linked them to the nations of the civilised land, as they knew more of Africa so much they do for Africa. They must show e greater interest and endeavour to send the Gospel of Christ out to the mis- sionary centres. The speaker in describing life in Central Africa adverted specially to Tanganyika (Urarribo), the station where he was engaged. It might be asked why they did not start from the coast, but if they could establish Christianity at Urambo it would transfer itself to the coast. Where the native African came in contact with the civilised trader, there they found the worst specimen of the native At Zineiber, where were to be found traders from all coun- tries, the natives were infinitely more demoralised and so much lower in the ecale of civilisation than those to whom the trader was unknewn. That was the reason they began at Uearnbo instead of along the coast. Mr. Willoug- hby then proceeded to speak of the great dangers of mission- ary work in the interior, and gave an entertaining ageount of the manners and customs of the people. Then they came to the question of the result of their work in those parts. He had been asked as to the number of conversions net had made, and what was the result of all that labour and expense in which they had been involved. The world went on so fast nowadays that if the Church did net go the same pace people soon became discontented. They must consider first, how they had to begin, and must remem- ber levees only just four years since they began actual work among those people. They had to select suitable sites for missionary enterprise and to prepare the soil. They bad only yet explained the fundamental truths of Christianity. They had left their mark, but it was not the result of their teaching, for they had not taught, but they had established a reputation for honesty and thoroughness among the natives. There were signs of success from their work, but they were so smell that he could not describe them in sucn a way as to excite their enthusiasm. He was there that even- ing to plead for his comrades labouring in the missionary field. It was a pleasant feeling to work in the harvest field. The work was bard, but the harvester shouted for joy at the appearance of the golden corn. There was joy in the harvest field, but there was nothing of the kind in the ploughing and sowing. His comrades were ploughing and sewing out yonder; there was no joy of the harvest field foe them, and for those he had to plead. By their prayers wed their sympathy did they show their interest in those noble men? He entreated those present, in conclusion, not only to afford pecuniary help, but to give their hearts and souls to the work of the Master in Central Africa, (Ap- plause.) The Rev. G. Corsters then addressed the meeting on the subject of Madagascar. He observed that so interested hid ha been with the details of native life as described by Mr. Willoughby that he had been scarcely able to think much about his own subject. Their mise sionary work in Madagascar had been going on for 65 years, and during Mr. Willoughby's address

he could not help thinking how different the story of ale missionary from Central Africa would be 65 years henoe-- of the glorious progress and success of Christianity and of Christian cburches springing up everywhere. But, as had been pointed out, the work there had Only just cousniericedr the language was yet unknown, and the Africans did not _ .

know What-the Gospel really was. But they had been work- ing in Madagascar for a long time, and when the mission- aries left, God took up the work, and in spite of persecutiens Cnristianity had been maintained. He found, however, as he travelled about, notwithstanding the interest that was he- ing evinced in Madagascar, that there was still a certain amount of ignorance as regarded the real state of things- People did not realise how large the island was. It wan nearly a thousand miles long, and only a small portion had been really touched by Christianity—chiefly that inhabited by the Hovas. Wherever the Hovas went they took the Gospel, and they were as little lamps in the surrounding darkness. Speaking of the country as a whole, it was heathen and dark. But that must not be misunderstood, as he could tell of much progrees that had been made. They had a college for the training of the native ministry, and which had been veil, successful. No less than 280 men had passed there since its commencement in 1809. His chief work had been as a tutor at that college. About 100 young men were nearly' entirely occupied in Christian services. Then there were fifty who held important positions in the State Government, and had been selected as enlightened and educated men' The Minister of Education and others were from the Col- lege, and some of the goveraors held important positions e Tamatave. They had also developed the independent spirit of the people especially in the matter of church life. TheY had a Congregational Union, which was a powerful means of inculcating Christian principles and developing native talent. Their society had gradually introduced the Free Church system in Madagascar, and it had educated the people to be somewhat independent in political as well as religious matters. They knew, however, mil they had no doubt felt in eignant when they heard it that now their work in Madagascar was threatened, and to a great extent upset, and all English speaking and reading people in the world had been displaying a particular interest in Madagascar through the wicked and cruel action of the French, which was quite new in the history' of that island. A few months ago people did not knovi such a place as Madagascar, but it had lately been brought to the front owing to the French having gone there and ad- vocated certain claims. The French spoke of their "general rights "over the whole island, and that necessitated inquiring into the past. Formerly France had extensive rights in Madagascar, and unless they remembered that they could, not understand what was meant by the " general rights! Eighty or ninety years back they had several stations in Madagascar. Taraatave, which tbe French were tryinq le seize, was a French name, and was used as a French stations but that and the others were deserted and were handed oVer, to the rising Hove power, and the British Government aid all that they possibly could to strengthen the hands of ,the , Hove sovereign. All that had been accepted, and they bad rejoiced in it until the last few months' when quite a different view had been taken. The French made a treater with the Sovereign of Madagascar, and held him respell; sinle for everything that happened to their subjects. le the French suffered from the wild independent tribes the, inhabited certain parts of the island they calla° on the Hove Government for remnneratioes and only last year they claimed an indemnity of 9,000 &is lars for what they said was an insult to the French flag: which the Government paid. The French said the islana had been theirs since 1841, which was rather a strange statement to make after the matter of the indemnity. The whole thing was strange, and the natural question to be asked was "How has it come about ?" He could not answer the question very satisfactorily' but he could tell them the motives of it, the stages of theditficailty, and of the results as far as at present were ascertained. As to the motives, lte was a hard thing to say—it was rather a shameful 0105 to say, but it was nevertheless true that the prime motive of the whole of this business in Madagascar had bee 2 jealousy to Great Britain. He was sorry to have to stare it, but he would not be honest if he did not tell the Ow unvarnished truth, that the jealousy was first of all religionsi The fact was that the Protestants were winning the day, aree the Jesuits were losing ground. The Protestants went wile' the open Bible which the people were glad to accept a! against the teachings of the Romanists. And instead being con4ned. to a religious jealousy, througit. some mixing up, it had become nation; The rev, gentleman spoke of the various stages which bee led up to the present claims, and remarked that ee tbe Freol, could not state their daB6 openly, because If they did tb would appear ridiculous' they had therefore resorted to pretexts. Having entered fully into the action of the Frencbi he seld they could not but boil with indignation at Oa' had taken place, and when they were asked whether it vias a sight thing to do, all that they could do was to hangdoWil. their heads in shame and confess that it was not a righ; thing to do. They had heard of what the French cal't "The success of their arms." The French were about give medals to soldiers for knocking defenceless forts le pieces, and taking forts which were never protected. It 10_ a sad thing for the future of the world when such thiege were taking place. The Hovas had retired inland, the FrenCP were there but they were perfectly isolated. • The Malagas,; were trying—whether they would succeed, who could tel —to defend themselves against the wanton conduct of the French. The Hovas would be safe until the French sent t great military expedition to the capital, and that could ne, be done yet, and he hoped in the meantime better counge would prevail. As regarded their missionary work, rale; had had to be given up, and it was in considerable dangeit* He wished it to be understood that the missionaries had ne come away from Madagascar on account of the French vasion, as it was arranged before the war broke out Oa' they should leave this year. None' bad shown the while feather. (Hear, hear.) They must not be allogether &Aril; cast as to the future of the island. As to the political ieeti,a of it, he did not feel very hopeful. He wished he con,. b -Hove that tbe French would retire from their presellii false position. He could not hope that the Malagasy wall t yield, because they had right on their side, and his bear went with them. (Applause.) Christianity would, holy: ever, stand its test, as it had already done so. If the Frenv. culled out their schemes, and the Jesuits obtained power' such as they had not hitherto possessed, he believed Prole' tantism would stand its test. (Applause.) God had de.: fended His awn in the past, and would do so in the futer'e Mr. Cousins, in conclusion, appealed on behalf of lb society, and asked his hearers not to go backward but fori ward and assist in bringing the whole world to the feel ° Christ. ( A ppl au se.) Rev. J. EGLINTON proposed a vote of thanks to the ucli,r sionaries for their interesting addresses, and wished to kiln', of Mr. Cousins as to the veracity of the rumour concerninn the fate of the envoys whom they had met in WarringtO some time since. a Rev. J. D. WARNOCK seconded the vote of thanks, 0, paid a warm tribute to the self-sacrificing work of tling' labouring in foreign parts. The Rev. G. Canisters replied to the compliment, and said that with regard to the rumour which Mr. Eglinton had re: ferred, so far as he was concerned he did not for a raceno'lli credit it. It was just barely passible that something 'nig have occurred to give rise to such a report, but it was all°: geyser unlikely. Their latest information was of entirelf contrary character. The source from which the runlet' came was Bourbon, and nothing from Bourbon was te believed for an instant unless it was confirmed by 111; telligence from Tasnatave or Antananarivo,where the lieVa were. (Hear, hear.) The meeting closed with the singing of the Doxology.

COMPULSORY EDUCATION AT Si. HELENS.—A large number of persons were summoned before the St. Helens bench on Monday for not having sent their children regu- larly to school, and in most cases-a flue of 5s (including coins) was imposed. FORTUNATE DISCOVERY OF A Fall& A fortunate dis- covery of an outbreak of Sre was made at Burtonwood, on Saturday morning last. It appears that about half-past five O'clock a Mr. C. Broster, residing near the Wesleyan school, came downstairs for the purpose of proceeding to his work, and before leaving the house he used a lighted candle. The candle was placed on a table, and after Mrt Broster had left by some means the- table-cloth and table became ignited. A neighbour who was passing happened to see the light inside, and "knocked up" Mrs. Broster The fire was then extinguished; though not before the table had been considerably damaged.. BURTONWOOD WESLEYAN CAAPEL : A GENEROUS OFFER.—About 100 persons sat down to the annual tea which was held in the Burtortwood Wesleyan School,. on Saturday evening last. The tea was greatly enjoyed. The subs.quent proceedings took the form of a meeting, for the purpose of eliciting or bringing abeut the best means of raising a sum of money for the purpose of enlarging the Sunday school, which is becoming too small for the increas- ing number of scholars.—Mr. B. Walker, of Earleatown, oc- cupied the chair, and after the reading of the year's report by the Secretary, the Chairman said he should like to see a new chapel erected, and the present place of worship used as a school, and if four of the leading " citizens " would con- tribute £5O he would give another £5O; and if they could not meet with success in that direction, he would give them £lO towards the school. (Applause.)—The Rev. J. %Velma- ley, of St. Helens, addressed the meeting, observing that the circuit would assist them as far as they could.—The Rev. J. Fairbourne, of Earlestown, also spoke, and the meeting was brought to a close by the singing of the Doxology.

div.head: CHAPTER L.-STEPIIEN'S MIDNIGHT ADVENTURES.
div.p: CHAPTER L.-STEPIIEN'S MIDNIGHT ADVENTURES.

Meantime action again, as had so often happened before, vras proving an effectual sedative to Stephen's disturbed thoughts. Perhaps, too, he saw with secret satisfaction that the duties assigned to him presented favourable opportunities for an occasional glance into the interior of Gualtmore, without danger of recognition. He chose and placed his men, by the aid of the map, without having occasion to make a single inquiry ; warn- ing each to whistle only as a first signal to him, re- serving fire for those who would not stand and wait till he , came.

And then he sought out, and found the best, the shortest, and the most secret paths through the tress by which to go from one to another of the sentinels at frequent intervals, and from there to the mansion. That done, he took his post to watch at the back of the mansion, which remained in complete darkness, for the re- turn of the troops. At some little distance from the doors at which they were to enter, stood a group of magnificent cedars, whose lower branches swaying to and fro in the wind often startled him into the belief he saw the forms of his comrades emerging from the obscurity. And when at dead of night they did arrive, their ad- vance was so noisless, their march so like a march of ghosts bent on some supernatural errand, their disappearance in single file through the gloom of the open door as into a tomb, so impressive, that Stephen could hardly satisfy him- self to take the fact on trust that they were his comrades; and not the very enemiea whose presence was so expected and provided for. But absolute silencehad been enjoined. Hesould there- fore only wait and watch. It was quite a relief when the man who was the last to enter, spoke to one in advance, saying "Well done!" and knew the voice to be the Major's. After paying visits to his three men and finding all well, the sounds of music drew Stephen towards the mansion, and to one of the windows of a long room on the ground floor, brilliantly lighted by chandeliers. He found as he expected, dancing going on, and his heart began to beat as he saw a pair advancing towards, and then passing the window, where he was; and he fancied the lady to be Miss Vandeleur. That was a mistake. He waited some time thinking she , mast come. But still he saw nothing of her. And that ' small fact served him for large inferences. She was not inclined to dance—she was, perhaps, still thinking how often she had danced with him—she was sad ; she still cared for, still thought of him, and him only in full for- giveness. A whistle cut short his reveries. He hurried to the sen- tinel, who had signalled to him in order to say he had heard some rustling among the adjacent trees; and believed a man had passed into the wood, who either did not hear or would not acknowledge his challenge, and was gone before he could make up his mini to fire, thinking he might be one of the gamekeepers of the Earl, Stephen made him point out the place from whence the ; sounds had seemed to issue; and thither he went, moving with stealthy step, his bayonet and rifle in position ready, from one sheltering tree trunk to"another ; and at last saw something that brought him to a stop, just as he was about to emerge on a little open place that had been cleared for the purpose by the woodcutters. What was the something? At one moment it looked like a rude pillar. The next be fancied it the trunk of a broken tree. But in an instant more he decided it was a man, standing as if in doubt what next to do, and unable to decide. " Stand ! " cried Stephen in a stern voice, and he ad- vanced with a levelled bayonet towards the figure. Suddenly he saw a movement as of an arm, armed na doubt with a revolver, and quick as lightning he leapt for- ward and plunged his bayonet into the obj,ct before him. What was his wonder and annoyance to find by the shock he himself received (enough to have broken his weapon) the nature of his antagonist It was a broken tree; of which only a single branch remained and was blown occasionally to and fro by the wind; and this in the darkness and mys- tery of the night, was converted by Stephen's imagination into the arm of a Fenian lifted to destoy him. With a laugh that was not the least mirthful, and some- thing like an angry oath following, he called himself an egregious ace; and was thankful he had not been tempted to fire, and so brought the sentinels to his aid in such an ex- tremity. - - -

At that very moment, when his heart seemed burning within him for something to do that might make him forget this ridiculour blunder, he, too, heard the sound of rustling near him of which the sentinel had spoken. "Now I shall, if I don't mind, commit the opposite and worse folly, and fail to act when action may be a matter of life and death. Still I most take my chance, so here goes !" Going to the sentry, whose whistle had warned him, he bid him follow, and walk where he moved, and as noise- lessly as possible. Listening with bended head, be could hear the faintest possible sound of rustling leaves, as if under some one's feet. _

Following the direction of the sound, and warned by that of his own and his comrade's danger from the leaves, he trod with careful step where he fancied there would be fewest, about the elevated roots of the trees. The pri- vate did the same, and both succeeded in moving silently along till they were on the edge of the bye-road, along which the retur_ning soldiery had come. This road con- tinued past the mansion, and presently joined a high road about a hundred-yards or so away. There they became aware of the sound of wheels, coming from the same quarter as the returning soldiery, and they advanced into the road to see who was passing.
A ear drove up, in which Stephen could just make out the forms of four men.

Not an instant did he hesitate, although knowing that if they were armed their lives might pay the forfeit of their audacity; he shouted to them as he leaped into the middle of the road, " Stop ! or I fire !" Thus hailed the car did stop. Stephen sent the Private to the horse's head, and then opening the 1?ull's-aya lantern he carried, examined the inmates;: at first cursorily, to identify their number,and see if they had weapons in their hands, or near them. " Who are you, and where are you from ?" he first asired _ _

the driver. "Shure now, I'm the driver of the car, and I'm from —," mentioning the name of a place where there had been a pig fair that day. "And who are these with you?" "Oh, very honest gintlemen—pig jobbers." "All of them ?" "I believe so;. but, shure, you can inquire for your- self."

" Do you know either of them ?" "Certainly I dei.anl for many a year, and by token of many a job—and handsomely they've paid me when I was hard put to it." "Which of them do you know ?" "This one," oaid the driver, touching the arm of one of the men. tand Stephen pawed the stream of light on, his fale.

"And this one," continued the driver, pointing with hl3 whip at a second of the men. in the ear. Again Stephen looked at the man in the fierce light of the lamp, and when he spoke it aeemed as though he had Seen nothing mare serious than pig jobbery in the face of either. "And as to the third ?" demanded Stephen, directing- h.is lamp for an instant at the driver's countenance. "Oh, he's been at the Fair, too; but walked on, thinking some friends would pic-a- hial up, and that's just wha.l- hap- pened." Where ?"

" Oh, not far off. But he's all right. Good nig'at !" He shook the reins to go on, but Stephen stopped him with, "If you don't want my comrade's bayonet in your horses belly, and a shot from his rifle in your ewn brains, yon'll stop where you are till I bid you proceed." The driver lowered his whip, and Stephen, going round to the other side of the car, where the third man sat, levelled his bull's eye :at him, and saw a agure with a thick shawl round his neck, wearing a cap with ears that came down and partly covered his lam

"It's all right, pig jobbing all day, and wanting to be at home and out of the cold at night," said the person in question, with a half laugh. What with his natural care to guard against the cold, and his genial comment, he and his fellow-travellera might in a few seconds more have been allowed to pass, for Stephen had been told of the Fair, and of the probability that some, and possibly tipsy men would be passing in the night. But there was a peculiarity in the voice that he seemed to remember—though where or under what circumstances he could not for the life of him recall. So thinking, but with no idea in his mind that be was about to elicit anything offsnoment, he said, "I seem to remember your voice. Have we met before ?" And again the light streamed on the man's face.
Another thought now startled Stephen, and caused him to say,_ _
l'Be so good as to remove your shawl and take off your cap," he said.
"What, in a night like this ?" was the rejoinder. The answer was Stephen's rifle and bayonet pointed at him.

He removed his shawl and cap, and Stephen lowered his rifle, but kept careful watch, with his bayonet in his right hand, while using the lamp with his left. Readers may imagine his emotion when he beheld and recognised the face of the Three Days' Fenian—the man in whom he had been so interested in the train to Holyhead; and who was, doubtless the mysterious rustler of the leaves in the wood; and engaged,in all probability, in the very busi- ness of the night for which the troops waited. I "Al,, is that you ?" he exclaimed, in joyful surprise, or what was made to appear very like it. "Descend," said Stephen sternly and abruptly. Then turning to his comrade, he said— " Bullock, come here !" "Why, my good fellow, what is the matter ?" asked the Three Days' Fenian. "Descend !" again said Stephen, with still more dangerous tone and accent.

The Three Day's Fenian accordingly descended. "Turn out your pockets!" was the next command. "Bul- lock, help him!" And again he was obeyed. "Feel that one in the breast-lining of his coat," said Stephen to the Private.

ihe Three Days' Fenian put his hand to his breast, hesi- tated for a second or two, as if feeling for it, looked at Stephen, who held his bayonet ready for the slightest sinis- ter movement, and drew forth a revolver.
"Take it," said Stephen to his companion,-and to him was quietly given.

"Ascend the car ! " As the Three Days' Fenian was retaking his seat; Stephen sent the Private again to the horse's head, taking the revolver .from him. He looked at it and at its owner, and asked— "ls it loaded?" "You had better try," was the sullen response. Reviewing the position—four men before him, one of whom he was certain was dangerous, while they might all be connected—and with the means of escape in their hands, could they, by a rush, pass and overpower him, he was half- tempted to shoot the horse, but could not decide on so pain- ful a step except in the last necessity. Suddenly the Three Days' Fenian snatched the whip from the driver, tumbled him off by a violent blow, and, lashing the horse with the utmost fury, would in a few moments have escaped. But Stephen's comrade was too quick for him. He fired —the animal fell and kicked convulsively, se the soldier thrust his bayonet into him, and relieved him by death. Then qtephen turned to the baffled Three Days' Fenian, who was rising from the ground, to which he and the other men had been violently thrown, and said, "I think you had better try no more experiments." Both the other sentinels were now heard running, roused by the shot, and presently joined Stephen. "Guard these men—that man especially," he said, in- dicating the Three days' Fenian. "Shoot them if they attempt to move, Igo to report to the Commanding Officer."

When he had gone a few spaces he stopped, returned, came to the man whom he was now convinced was any- thing but a Fenian of three days only; and said to him, with much feeling, "I could wish any other Ittzt tne had this duty to per. form; but, as it is, farewell ?" He turned, and passed away. (To be continued.)

div.head: CHAPTER XLIX.-MISS _NrANDELEUR'S SONG.
div.p: CHAPTER XLIX.-MISS _NrANDELEUR'S SONG.

Gaultmore reached, the troops*fcund the doors wide open to receive them, for the Comte had sent a swift messenger in advance to inform Lord Harlaxton of their approach to the castle; and how he, the Comtesse, and the commander of the troops had taken counsel together, and he was happy to say the latter had welcomed the double opportunity of protecting Gualtmore, and having, as he hoped, another brush with the Fenian s' that might end ,differently from the last.

Nothing could exceed the satisfaction of Lord Harlaxton to be so relieved of the anxiety he had felt for his mother and Miss Vandeleur through the excited state of the district around, and on account of the threatened attack by the Fenians, about which he had managed to keep them in ignorance. Some guests-were in the house, whe, like the Countess and Miss Yandeleur, knew nothinz of any special danger. To keep them all still unsuspicious, Lord Harlaxton had made nse of the season (just before Christmas) to keep up all possible festivity. The troops now found themselves the objects of a recep- tion that was likely to be only toa hospitable, but for the forethought of the Major; who warned all his sub- ;ordinates to be on their guard, and stop on the instant everything that looked like license, or unseemly, or dan- gerous indulgence. When he had, like all good officers, seen to everything with his own eyes, he rejoined the Earl, who led the way to the drawing-room, where the Ko.jor was introduced to the Countess and to Miss Vandeleur. _ _ . _

He presently became the centre of a wide circle, the chief speaker in a sort of all-round' conversation that left the family and the guests deeply interested in the young sol- dier whose aid bad been so timely. As to the Major,. he became so impressed with the beauty of the two ladies in person, mind, and character—that he hardly knew -which he admired most—the age of the one, or the youth of the other. _ _ - -
As the evening drew oa,tha Countess went to the piano, and called on Miss Vandeleur to sing._ _ _ -

This she did with emittleite taste and feeliag, and in sweet but not powerful voice, that charmed the guests, who all, with the Major, pleaded for another song. Her first had been a ballad, "The Miller's Daughter ; " and she was again about to stop in turning over the leaves of her music, at some equally sad strain, but the Countess, who watched, said in an undertone to her, "We should chter, not sidden, our guests, and for that matter our very hearts too. Sing "Impudent Barney O'Hea." Miss Vandefeur paused, seeme,l to hesitate as if in diffi- culty, but turned the leaves once more, and summoning whatever of humorous feeling might remain jn her not very happy life of late, was about to comply, when she suddenly burst into tears, and murmured to the Countess. _ _
" ay lam not well," rose and hurriedly left the rQOIII.

Mr. LATtLeta took exception to a clause in the report in reference to the utility of the Agricultural Holdings Act, and asked what benefits it had conferred upon the community. He moved that the clause should be left out. The question was put to the vote, when eight were in favour of and eight against it. The chairman gave his casting vote in favour of the adoption of the report in its entirety. It was resolved to hold a special meeting in January next to discuss the merits and demerits of the Aericultaral Holdings Act. CHI SHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY. The annual meeting of this society was held at the Crewe Arms Hotel, Crewe, on Wednesday, Mr. H. J. Tollemache, M.P., presiding. The annual report and statement of ac- counts were adopted. A deputation, consisting of Messrs. Moore, Totall, and Moreton, attended on behalf of the Middlewich and Not thwich Agricultural Society, and in- vited the Cheshire Society to hold their next show at North- wich. In consideration of this, the local society would be prepared to amalgamate and raise £lOO towards the expenses of the county society. There being no other invitation be- fore the meeting, it was decided to accept the offer, and to hold the next show at Northwich, on Saturday, September 30th, 1884. Lord Delamere was chosen president for the ' next year, and the usual officers were reappointed. The revision of the prize list was left to the general committee. between the above clubs was played on the ground of the , Pagefield Club, when Pagefield were again successful in lower- ing the colours of the Sbanters. The Pagefield were the victors by one goal, five tries and eight minor points to nil. Thorpe, Yates, and E. 31asou played well in the backs, whilst the forwards pla3 ed with spirit. For Runcorn Howard, rye. and Owen distinguished thrriselves. t.T. HELENS V. Isovei, (25D TEAMS )—These teams met on Saturday last, on the Aspull ground, for the first time this season. Owirg to the late arrival of the visitors, play was confited to twenty minutes each way. she Aspuilites were victorious by 1 try, 3 toucbctowns, to 1 touch in goal. The teams afterwards partook of an ample repast at the Hare and Hounds Inn, kindly provided by the home team, to which it need hardly be said full justice was .cl,..sne. The cloth being removed, the Et. Helens captain was called to the chair, and the Aspull captain to the vice-chair. The chairman spoke of the very kind manner in,which the Aspull team had that day treated them, and also hoping they might meet on many occa- sions in the same friendly and gentlemanly spirit, remarking :hat the game was entirely free from discord. The vice-chair- man replied in suitable terms. COWLEY MIDDLE SCHOOLS FOOTBALL CLUB V. By. HELENS RECREATION Juttroes.—This match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday last. On sesing the small dimen- sions of their opponents the Juniors became highly elated. ex- pecting an easy victory, but great was their dismay on play being o mmenced, for they found the School team more for- midable than they had anticipated. During the first half the score was nit. In the second half the hall got very near the school goal, where it was received by Pennington, who for- warded it to Mather, the latter dribbling it to the Juniors' goal, and passing it to Makin who succeeded in kicking it be- tween the uprights, thus scoring the first goal for tile School. The ball was again kicked, off by Turner, and returned by Willacy; the `!invincibleT. owton, then took charge of it, and got it through the School forwards; but he was at once arrested by Johnson. who took it to the opponents' goal, where it was sent under the bar by McNelly. It Is only fair to state that the Juniors played without one of their best men, R. Glover. Score Cowley Middle Schools, two goals to nil. WARRINGTON WANDERERS (2ND) Y. LATCHFORD (IST).—This match took place on the ground of the former at Arpley, when some very good play was witnessed on both sides. The visitors came with an unbeaten record this season, but the Wanderers are the first team to lower their colours. The teams on both sides held their own in the paeked scrimmage, but the borne team exeelled them in the loose and dribbling department. The backs of the visitors played feebly, excepting Sudlow and Burgess, while on the other bane the home backs played agood game, Calland making some of his strong runs. After some give-and-take play Mather secured the first try, the kick at goal failing. Graham followed up quickly and secured another try. Lightfoot crossed the visitors' lines: After change of ends both sides played vigorously, Cannon securing a try for the visitors. The place by Hough was a failure. Flay being resumed, the Wanderers' forwards rushed the leather over the lines, when Graham scoured another try. which Appleton con- verted Into a goal. Flay shortly afterwards ceased, victory resting with the Wanderers by one goal, three true Graham two, Mather and Lightfoot (one each). four minors to one try (Cannon), and three minors. WrireitB V. RuSIIOI3IE.—ThiS match was played at Rusholme last Saturday, and ended In a win for Rnsholme by one goal to sae try and minor points. Doh team played 14 men. Rus- holm° were without Maurey. Emery. and Lowther, forwards, whizit considerably weakened the front rank. Widnes kicked adt.-aud-Rushohne.w.nra.pressed for some few minutes, but the backs removed the danger, and the first half was productive of nothing but minor points. After chaDglng ends Faulkner kicked off, and from 14 scrimmage in front of the Widnes posts Hamilton kicked a goal. From the kick off Widnes scored a dead ball. After the drop out play became very fast. Rusholme rushing the ball down the field but could not score, mainly ow- ing to the good defensive play of the brothers Briggs. Harrop st cured the ball and passed in mistake to Kendrick, who had on a Rnsholme jersey, and a try was got between the posts. Morris failed at goal. After this nothing but good defensive play was shovn by each side, some good tacking being shown. "No side" brought a fast game to a close. Teams :—Rusholme : A. Dickson. back R.
