-PRESENTATION TO SUPT. BARNETT, LATE OF WIDNES. On Wednesday afternoon a well attended meeting was held in Widnes Police Court for the purpose of presenting to Supt. Barnett, of Asbton-under-Lyne, who was recently promoted from Widnes, a testimonial in recognition of his many services to the town. Mr. F. H. Goesage, JP., was voted to the chair, and there were present the Revs J. Wright Williams, George Bond; Dr. Cooper, Dr. McLennan, Messrs. J. W. Cerlile, la Wright, S. B. Stringer, J. White, W. Treecy, F. H. Pankharst, C. U. Lewin. Tighe, J. B. Imison. J. M Winn's, E. Martley, J. W. Knewlee, J. Ankers, A. Carlile, J. Hulme, Forsyth, T. Atherton, J. Hough. superintendent Barker, Inspector Wood, and a good number of officers were also present. Ma JAMES WHITE, as secretary to the Testimonial Corn' enlitee, made a financial statement. He said the total sub- iptions received amounted to £34 13s 61 The expenses am -anted to £1 19s 3,1, leaving balance of £B2 14s 3d. it woald perhaps be only right to say that the committee had stO attempted a regular organised canvas throughout the teem, other Wise they might have obtained a much larger sum. -Very many subscribers had come in without solicitation, and some had been paid into bank. The only attempt at canvas hid been amongst the menufecturere, and this had been accomplished by Mr. Car- laa with very great success. He (Mr. White) did not think be had seen so full a subscription list; for there were only two firms in Widnes who had not contributed, and these firms were limited companies, and the managers would have to get permission. The fact that Mr. Gossage was present to take part in the proceedings added materially to the value of the testimonial. (Applause.) Mr. J. B. IMISON then read the following address:— To Superintendent Barnett, isi,!•.n.under Dyne Division o.sunty Constabu:ary.—Dear Sir.—We, the manufacturers, teadesmen, and Inhabitants of Widnes and neighbourhood tender you our hearty congratulations upos your recent promo- ti n ; and at the same time desire to record our appreciation of the exceptional tact and ability with which you discharged doles as Inspector during the seven years you were . stationed amongst us. Tkis period was an exceptionally trying o and we rec.rd with satisfaction the fact ttitt on all noes- si sa,, when the re:ations bAween chrses political or otherwise hive become somewhat strained and property and life endan- gsred, your firmness, discretion, and devotion to dutv largely vtr.ktributea to the speedy restoration of law and order. In token of the esteem in wh!ch you are ho:d by us, we ask your aPteptance of this address and purse of gold, and assure you we shall always remember with pleasure your so j •t.irn In ligtilites.—Wishing you a happy and pro,perous career, we are, dear sir, on behalf of the subscribers, yours sincerely. JoTpi 11/LATTIIEWS, JAMsS WHITE. WM. TREA.CY, and J. B Ixtsox.— Wtdaes, liovembe • 28th, 1883. • Tha addross, which was beautifully illuminated by Mr. J. B. Imison, was enclosed is a handsome gold frame. The CHAIRMAN said as one of the subscribers to that tes- timonial he had the greatest pleasure in presenting Superin- tendent Barnett with that substantial testimonial that had been subscribed to him by his fellow townsmen. (Hear, hear.) That testimonial showed him the esteem in which he eats held by every class of the population in Widnes. By the exercise of his ability Mr. Barnett had succeeded in placing Widnes in a different position than it had occupied for many years. (Applause.) He admitted that for Wid- nes the number of subscribers-282—was very small, but there had been no regular canvas, no advertising' or ex- traneous method adopted to raise the testimonial to a ve:y high figure. It had been left entirely to the good feeling of his fellow townsmen—(hear, hear)—to show how substantially they appreciated his efforts to what was, after all, simply his duty as inspector of police in that district. Mr. Barnett had been inspector in the town seven years, and he (the chairman) had been a magistrate five years. When he came to the Bnech a perfectly unfledged magistrate, he found Mr. Bernett there to assist him in his duties. He (the chairman) was forced by his position en rota to be a very prominent magistrate in the trial of the persons impli- cate,Tl in that most wretched Treacy murder case. He was on:y expressing the feeling of the local magistrates, and perticularly of himseld, when he said their thanks were due to Inspector Barnett for having sifted that most wretched case to the bottom, and having with consummate ability. brought the evidence to such a termination as to prove that there csuld not be the slightest doubt of the drssdfegüilt of the persons who were cortvi,ted, and some of whom were executed, (Applause.) The local magistrates regretted the loss of Mr. Barnett, but they rejoiced in his promotion, and Vusted that the people of Ashton-under-Lyne might find him as good a man as they in Widnes had done, and that he might live happily long, and that his ability to do that which was right might never diminish. (Hear, hear.) The Chairman, amid-applause. then handed Superintendent B it- nett a purse containing £B4 163 3d, the address, and a book Containing the names of the subscribers. Superintendeat BARNErr, who received quite an ovation on rising to respond, was evidently much affected, and spoke with considerable feeling. He said he could scarcely ex- press his feelings on that occasion. He was not a nervous person generally, but after hearing the very flattering re- marks of the chairman he felt quite embarrassed. He feared that his services and abilities had been considerably over- estitnate,d. He was proud and grateful to find that his ser- vices as Inspect:o'r of Police at Widnes, during the last seven years had been so much appreciated, and had given such general setisfaction to the magistrates, and the res- pectable and peaceable portion of the inhabi- tants of the town as to cell forth this sub- stantial and handsome testimonial. During the past seven years there had bean meny occurrences of a some- what serioas nature which required great patience, tact, and- perseverance on the part of the police. In performing his duty as Inspector, which he did to the best of his skill and ability, ha was ably assisted by a body of good and effi- cient men —(hear, hear)--and he was also well supported by the respectable and law-abiding inhabit Ants of the town (hear, hear) for which he begged to take this opportunity of returning his sincere and hearty thanks. He had also to acknowledge in the most sincere in inner possible the kind- ness and courtesy in which the magistrates of the division always received hi. He had to thank the subscribers for the kindness they had shown to hinnand especially for that liberal testimonial, for which he hoped to cherish a grateful remembrance for a long time to came. (Loud applause.) Superintendent BAUEER, then presented Supc. Barnett with a very handsome silver tea and coffee service, one of the articles bearing tl:e following inscription :—Presented to Mr. Superintendent Barnett by the officers and men of the Prescot Division, upon the occasion of his promotion to Ashton-under-Lyne. September, 1883. Mr. Barker made the presentation in a neat speech, observing that every officer had subscribed, and he had not the slightest doubt all wished him a long and happy life. (Applause.) Superintendent BA.RNETT suitably responded; and on the motion of Mr. D. WRIGHT, seconded by Mr. MATTHEWS, a hearty vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Goesage for presiding. In replying, the CHAIRMAN said it was always a great pleasare to preside at any meeting which forwarded a good cause—(hear, hear)—and he thanked them for their cordial reception of him that day. They bad known Mr. Barnett whom they had lost, and he thought that if their present ' Inspector was left with them for a number of years they would find out his virtaea. (Applause.) If he could only inspire the law-abiding with the same respect that Mr. Barnett inspired, and if by any possible method inspire tie non-law-abiding with a greater respect and fear for him than Mr. Barnett he thought he would be a very clever man. (" Hear, hear," and laughter.) That be might be able to do so4bey all wished, and before closing the pro- ceedings he might say they all wished Inspector Wood every success. (" Hear, hear," and applause.)

div.p: 01:7TBREAS OF SCARLET FEVER AT WILDEESPOOL.

The MEDICAL OFFICER, in a special report, informed the Board of an outbreak of scarlet fever in the row of cottages near Tom Payne's Bridge, Wilderspool. The patient, Wm. Knowles, a carter, was now convalescent. The usual pre- cautionary methods of isolation and disinfection had been carried out. The source of infection could not be ascer- tained, but the patient's occupation took him to Warrington daily, and tkis fact might furnish the requisite explanation. No fresh cases were reported. CHARGE OF POACHING AGAINST RUNCORN the Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Wm. Hitch= Robert Moores, and John Skelton, labourers, of Runcorn, were charged with trespassing on land at Acton Grange, on the 21st instant, in the occupation of Thomas Ball, and taking certain game, to wit three hares.—The defendants, with three others, were found on the land on the afternoon in question with greyhounds, and having secured their booty they made for the river, where a host was in readi- ness for them. The gamekeeper followed to the river, when he was told by one of the men that if he came nearer it would be the worse for him.—Mr. Hitchin, of Runcorn, who defended, contended that his clients were not concerned in the poaching; but the magistrates considered the case risarly proved, and fined Moores, who was an old offender, fOs. for trespassing and £2 for taking game, and casts. ritchin and Shelton were fined 20s. and costs for each

COOKERY BY GAS AT RUNO )11N- INTERESTING LECTURES. The first of a serie3 of lectures on cookery, practically illustrated, was given in Bethesda School-room, on Tuesday afternoon, by Mrs. Thwaites, of Liverpool. There was a large attendance of ladies. The lectures have been arranged for by the Runcorn GAS Company, who hive shown them- selves very enterprising in bringing under the notice of the public the economy which would result from an extended use of ges for heating and domestic purposes. Mr. F. Rigby, J.P., in the absence of Mr. W. Hayes, chairman of the Board of Directors, occupied the chair, and amongst those present were tha Revs. W. Preston and J. D. Thomas, and Mr. James Handley, J.P. The CHAIRMAN, in introducing Mrs Thwaites, expressed regret at the absence of. Mr. Hayes, and said the reason way they were there that afternoon was perfectly obvious. They were about to enter upon an experiment which he hoped and believed would be a successful one. He thought after the ladies of Runcorn had kal the advantage of a series of lec- tures an cookery' with which, he had no deubt, they were to a certain extent familiar, that they would have derived a sensible and distinct advantage. But the Runcorn Gas Co., he must say, speaking honestly, did not pose before them as humanitarians or put)!ic benefactors or philanthropists, but simply as traders. They asked the public to come there to learn and sitisfy themselves of the fact that cooking by gas was not only wholesome but cheap. They were perfectly satisfied that everybody who had gas at hand would be glad to avail themselves of the chance. Lest year, about the same month, the Gas Compeny availed themselves of an op- portunity to test the cost of cooking by gas a dinner which they gave to a great many residents in the tewu, but at which, unfortunately, the ladies ware not present. There were about 70 gentlemen assembled and a din- ner of live courses WAS cooked on that occasion by gas. It was not, however, cooked by an artist as the dinner at that place would be cooked that afternoon, but simply by the vendors of the stoves. Therefore it could hardly be t tken as dinner of superlative excellency; still it was a good dinner; and estimating gas at 3s. 61 per 1,000 feet, which was then 61. higher than it was now—(the gas was measured and the meter was read off before and after the dinner)—the cost of cooking the repast was only 23. Id. He thought it was perfectlyplain that if they could cook a dinner of five courses for 2s. Id. for 70 people, the cost per week or per e ncitun ma small or a large household could not be very excessive. There was one point to which he wished to call their attention and that was the advantageous terms at which householders could now be supplied with gas. At this period last year there were differential charges in res- pect to the large-consu:ners and the small consumers. The large consumm; by wb.orn he meant the owners of works, hid an advantage of 6d. per 1,000 feet. That advan- tage they had been relieved of, and every consumer, be he large or small, was charged 3s. per 1,000 feet. The gas company rather wished to take advantage of this oppor- tunity to blow their own trumpet because they really had a trumpet to blow. The price 3s. was a very low one. Out of 118 gas works in the country there were only 33 which sold gas under Runcorn. Of these 33 towns he might men- tion taking them haphazard, very few could be compared with Runcorn. There was Birmingham, Darlington, Hali- fax, Huddersfield, Leeds, Manchester, and Liverpool. But Liverpool only sold the gas 3d. per 1,000 cubic feet less than the smallest consumer rot it at Runcorn. Therefore the Runcorn Gas Company bad reason to say they sold their gas very cheaply indeed. They had another advantage over many large companies, and that was that they sold very good gas. It had been tested and proved beyond doubt that the gas at Runcorn was really incomparably good. For in- stance, if they took the whole ef England and Wales—he was not giving the ipse dixd of the company, but figures collected from official returns laid on the table of the House of Commons—there were only 16 towns which supplied 20 candle gas, and Runcorn was one. Of these 16 London charged 33 Id, Huyton 53, Liverpool 2s od, Oakengates Sc, Ruthin 45 7d, and Stretford 2s 2d, so that Runcorn com- pared favourably with every other company. There was another fact which he would like to mention, and that was that at the last exhibition a great many people purchased stoves. Within a month of that exhibition the company sold MOO worth of cooking gas stoves, and if it were neces- sary they could obtain testimony to the effect that every parchaser was more than pleased with their purchase. He concluded by asking the audience to pay the strictest atten- tion to Mrs. Thwaites, who would demonstrate as fully as she could the advantages of cooking by gas, and remarked that he could not sit down without testifyihg in the sincerest possible manner, on behalf of the directors, the able and energetic manner in which Mr. Frith had contributed to the success of the company. (Applause.) Mrs. THWAITES, who is a member of the Ladies' Sanitary Association, London and the authoress of "Fish cookery," then proceeded to deliver her lecture. She observed that it was quite possible for a lady to cook a dinner by gas without soiling her hands, and cleanliness was one of the chief elements of success in cooking. High class cookery WAS Mrs. Thwaites' theme, and by means of a gas stove she cooked a great variety of dishes in a most finished and artistic style, interspersing her operations with many valuable hints, which many of the ladies present recorded in note books. She also gave the recipes, which were also eagerly recorded by the fair auditors. Mrs. Thwaites continued her lectures on Weineedey and Thursd iv. She has been favoured with large audiences, and on Thursday evening quite 250 people were present. A. special lecture to the wives of workingmen will be given to- night (Saturday), and a series of lectures will also be given next week.
PROPOSED NEW WESLEYAN CHAPEL AT FRODSHAR.

A meeting was held in the Five Crosses Chapel, on Wed- nesday evening, to consider the proposed erection of a new chapel. Mr. John Simpson, of Dunsdale, Frodsham, pre- sided, and there was a good attendance. The proceedings commenced with singing and prayer, after which the CHAIR- MAN called upon Mr. Allen to make a statement as to the proposed new chapel.—Mr. ALLEN stated that the present chapel at Five Crosses was the gift of the late Mr. Thomas Hazieburst in the year 1859. The growth of its congrega- tion and school had at length made enlarged accommoda- tion a necessity. A school of 200 children was conducted in a small room without class rooms, and in which the chil- dren were packed as closely as possible back to back, all the seats in the chapel were let, and there was no longer accommolation for new corners, the extension of the good work was thus checked. Five Crosses was no doubt incon- veniently near Frodsham, and at Trinity Chapel there was space enough for a large increase, both in school and con- gregation, but the people who had chosen the smaller chapel had become attached to it, and having it near their homes were not likely to be p3rsuaded to walk the distance to Frodsham. It might be inconvenient that the congregation should have grown up so near to Frodsham, but grown it had, and they could not coerce it to go else- where. Its church membership was nearly equal to that of Trinity Chapel, Frodsham, its school was quite as large. and it was necessary and just that they should have adequate accommodation, particularly as the population of the neigh- bourhood was increasing. It was thought a chapel seating about 300 would be needed, thus providing about 100 seats more than the present building. At present they had no t definite plans for meeting this want, but a general convic- tion seemed to prevail that it would be best to retain the present building for school purposes and erect a new chapel on some adjoining site. A chapel to seat 300 would pro- bably cost less than .-C1,300. As to the means of raising this sum the rev gentleman stated that the Extension Fund Committee would probably grant £6O. The ladies of Five Crosses_ and Frodsham proposed to com- bine in collecting materials for a bazaar which must be m Ade to raise 300 if possible. By strenuous effort the occasion of laying foundation stones and the opening services might be made to realise £l5O. These sums he ventured to expect towards the scheme, but there was upwards of .£7OO remaining, which must be col- lected in subscriptions. The committee would not feel safe in going forward unless promises for something like £5OO were forthcoming at the meeting. The scheme might be extended 21. years, and what was promised might be paid in instalments during that period. It WAS important, how- ever, that as far as possible cash should be paid at the be- ginning of the work, in order that it might not be ueces- safy to borrow money to meet the builder's claims AS they became due.

The meeting was afterwards addressed by the Chairman, Rev. F. F. Mmonds, Mr. W. B. Gibson, and Mr. Samuel Walker. The following subscriptions were promised during the meeting, viz :—Mr. John Simpson, £100; Mr. W. B. Gibson, £5O; Mr. J. Littler, £5O: Mr W. H. Colliuson, £3O; Mr. Peter Booth, £5O; Mr. W. H. Pickering, £25; Mrs. Yond, £25; Mr. John Walton, £2O; Mr. J. C. Sutton, £10; Mr. Joseph Berrington, £10; A Friend, £10; Mr. Bennett, £10; Mr, W. Robinson, £10; Mr. S. Barnett, £10; Mr. S. Pickering, £5; Mr. J. C. Hinson, £5; Mr. Joseph Knibb, £5; Mr. Samuel Walker, *£s ; Mr. S. Moss, £2; Mr. Henry Limbert, £2; and promises for small amounts, £ll 10s.—total, £465 10s. The above result was considered to be highly satisfactory, and offered a sufficient inducement to the Building Committee to go on with the scheme. The singing of the Doxology brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: EXAMINEE, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 1, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINEE, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 1, 1883.
WARRINGTON TEMPER kNCE UNION. 1

LECTURES BY MR. G-. R. TWEEDIE, F.C.S. Three very interesting lectures w9re delivered in the Workmen's Club, Market-place, on Tuesday, Wednesday. and Thursday evenings, by Mr. George R. Tweedie, F.C.S., of London, and formerly of the late Royal Polytechnic In- stitution. They, were profusely illustrated by diagrams and brilliant chemical experiments, and were throughout listened to with manifest interest. Oa Tues lay evening the subject was "Alcohol and alcoholic drinks!' The Rev. John Yonge presided. and there was a moderate attend- ance.

'rue rev. CHAIRMAN Said the lecturer was going to ap- proach the subject of temperance in a way in which it was not very frequently approached, at any rate in Warrington. That was from a scientific stand- point. He had no doubt that the lecturer would be able to show them that night good aeientifio rea- sons for total abstinence, and that when they had listened to him they could be in possession of solid reasons why they should abstain from intoxicating drinke, reasons differ- ent perhaps from those which were generaliy put forth at temperance meetings. It was argued that total abstinence was a prevention of drunkenness. He would not he sur- prised if the lecturer told them that night that there were better reasons than that—that it was essential to health Perhaps he would tell them teat the notions they had had about alcoholic drinks were very n.ietaken notions. A great many people had grown up in tOe idea that their system required the use of stimulants, and that if they were to abandon the use of stimulants they would suffer in their health. He had no doubt that the lecturer would tell them that that was a fallacy, and that health was more likely to be attained by total abstinence than by the most moderate or diticreet use of intoxicating drinks. (Applause.) The LECTURER said his task that night was to lay before them a chemical history of the substance known as alcohol. Alcohol was made from grape sugar, and they could not have alcohol unless they had grape sugar itself or something that could be converted into grape sugar. But grape sugar could be made out of an infinite number of things. He could make a good glass of brandy, judged in the usual way, out of that old duster which he held in his hand. First, he would have to get from it the grape sugar, and then from the grape sugar the alcohol. Beer was made from barley. The barley had to be made into malt, then the starch which was in the malt had to be converted into grape sugar, and then the grape sugar into alcohol by means of fermentation. Ferment was a kind of fungus or tiny vegetable seeds which were moving about in every atmosphere. When the ferment was nut into the malt, or rather infusion of malt, the seeds began to grow, and in growing they had to feed upon the barley. In the fermentation was lost the nourishing starches, and a great deal of the muscle-forming substance that was in the barley, these going to feed the ferment. He showed to the audience a specimen of grape sugar which had been converted from the front page of a Times newspaper, and said that grape sugar could be made from rags and paper. Some temperance advocates Would get up at a meeting and say that alcohol was entirely useless. He was a total abstainer of life-long standing, but he was also a dliGitist, and his idea about alcohol was that it was an extremely useful substance. He did not object to the use, but to the abuse of it. The varnish maker, druggist, and perfumer would be able to do very little without it. There were many essential oils which could only be dissolved by alcohol. The manufacturing chemist used alcohol very largely for the preparation of other substances. It was useful to the anatomist and the collector 01 ant;quities, and it was used in chemical analysis. But the right place for alcohol was On chemists' shelves and not in our cupboards still less inside our bodies. Alco- hol found in wine was produced from the grape sugar, aed it destroyed to a great extent the muscle-forming substance that existed in the grape. He then referred to artificial wines. About four years ago he was staying at a well- known north of England town, and there chanced to be staying at the hotel with him a well-known American chemist. This gentleman had with him a case of chemi- cal, and he undertook to produce by means of the contents of his bottles almost any kind of wine they liked, and give the wine almost any desired ago. If they wanted five-year- old port he could produce it, and if they wanted it ten-year- old he would put in a few more drops of something and make It apparently that. And there were a certain num- ber of individuals known as wine, merchants' chemists, who undertook to furnish all kinds of materials necessary for the production of artificial spirits. He was at Cork some time ago, and met with a gentleman who told him he was in the wine and spirit trade, and thought that he might be interested in a circular he had received from a certain firm in Brussels. The circular re- ferred especially to the fabrication of artificial champagne. One qualification put further was: " By the aid of these substances you can provide champagne at sd. to 61. per bottle, aid sell it at ss. to 6s. per bottle." - (Laughter.) That substance was very largely used. The analytical chemist knew these things before, but the puolic had to a large extent been kept in the dark. Passing on to die- tiled spirits, the lecturer said that brandy was mere than half alcohol. The word brandy came from two German words which meant burnt wine, and brandy was formed by burning some kinds of wine or refuse of wine. In a very large proportion of the public-houses the brandy now sold was made from a very c Arse whisky, or from what was called silent spiriis. This coarse whisky was coloured with coarse sugar and flavoured with cayenne. Gin was not the strongest alcoholic liquor, but owing to the fact that it contained the oil of juniper berries it was exceeiingly harmful. In London it was essentially the drcnkards' drink, and its effects were very rapid. The English learned to drink gin from the Dutch. Gin drinking had spread to such an extent in 1736 that a special Act of Parliament was pulsed coiled the Gin Act. It was intended that the effect , of the Act should be to restrict the sale of this spirit, but there was a loophole in the Act. Tne apothecaries were allowed to sell gin as a medicine. People soon found out that they were poorly and wanted gin. The recipe was "Take two or three spoonfuls four or five times a day or as often as the fit takes you." (Laughter.) Gin was a curious subeance. and almost every mauufacturer of it had his own recipe, but however it was made it contained alcohol and the extract of juniper berries. Whiskey contained what was called amylic alcohol, a very dangerous substance. There eyes no doubt that the introduction of this pernicious whiskey into India had brought about the extermination of many an Indian race. The lecturer then demonstrated by means of experiments that beer contained alcohol and that brandy contained the same substance, the only difference being in quantity. He concluded his remarks by saying that beer should not be taken in however small a quantity, because the small quantity of alcohol it contained crea'ed an appetite for more and then spirits were resorted to. On Wednesday the subject of the lecture was " Are alco• holic drinks food ?" There was a good attendance, and the Rev. T. Rippon presided. The Rev. CHAIRMAN slid that they often heard his voice in the town of Warrington on the question of temper- ance, and he was thankful for once that it was his to have the luxury of listening rather than to have, as some times it was, the onerous work of addressing. They were to have, as he understood it, the physiological aspect of the tem- perance question censderecle and that by an expert in their friend Mr. Tweedie, of London. He had heard it said that alcohol was the devil in solution. He believed that assertion was put down to D. Richardson, but the coiner of that phrase was Mr. Walter, the proprietor of the Times. Dr. Richardson's. phrase was that alcohol was a bona-fcre• devil. He did not know what phrase Mr. Tweedie would coin, or if he had' coined one be would let them have it. This, however, was a question they might well ask themselves as intelligent men and women—" Is alcohol an article of food, or ought it to be treated simply as a medicine ?" That question he expected would be satisfactorily answered by the lecturer. This he thought might be said, that mnn who had to do serious head work and bard-handed work could do it much better without alcohol than with it. Captains who went to sea told him that their sailors could do their work much better and retain heat longer on coffee thin rum. The farmers had told him that in getting in their harvests their labourers could do their work much bettet on cold tea than beer. And since he had come to Warrington he had heard ironworkers say that they could work as well without strong drink as with it; others hilt said better. (Hear, hear.) This, he though, led them to this : that looking at the matter from a scientific standpoint, it was much better for them to be teetotallers than not. The drinking of to-day was to be summed up in the Quaker's honest expriession—" For the simple reason I like it." There were many people to-day who would-go on drinking and suffering from the effects of that drinking rather than give up the habit and be free from thooe effects. They would contribute to their health by their, having nothing to do with alcohol except—he supposed the lecturer would take this position—as a medicine, when under very serious circumstances in some cases it might even be a factor for good. (Applause.) The LECTURER said they would ham to enquire that evening what might be the food value of alcoholic drinks; whether the alcohol or the drinks which contained the al- cohol could be considered food. He explained that there was constantly going on within our bodies two operations, one being construction , and the other deatiruction, and if one of these operations were to cease, death would inevitably ensue. To carry on these operations with satisfaction to oureelves, we must have three things—air, water, and focd. He likened the body unto a steam engine, and said that in both cases, life or force was derived from the burning up of materials. By means of an experiment he demonstrated the presenco•of carbonic acid gas in his breath, and showed that burning and breathing were identical things. The body was there- fore continually burning away, and ceriseepiently food, wh;ch might be considered as fuel, bad to he taken in order to rep'ace the material which was burnt. Very few people indeed had any notion as to the enormous quantity of food which was consumed by one individual in a lifetime. and most people used a great deal more food than was necessary or good for the body. There was no dispute that that burning liquid, alcohol, in intoxicating drinks made them harmful, and that alcohol would not produce flesh and muscle. The reason was simple enough; flesh and muscle- forming substances contained nitrogen; alcohol contained carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, but no nitrogen. Twenty ounces of pale ale contained one ounce of alcohol. It was ' very evident that there were a great many other things in ale besides alcohol, and it was asked by some, "Might not I these be capable of forming flesh and muscle ?" The lec- turer here exhibited to the audience a glass 'tar containing a pint of pale ale and another containing the water which:was found in a pint of ale, and there appeared to be little dif- Jerence between the quantities of the two jars. He did not °bleat to the water being in the ale, but to the water being
spoiled. (Applause.) All the muscle-forming matter that was to be found in the ale was to be found in the solid
matter. Beer and barley were two totally different substances. Certainly beer had been made from barley, but it represented the destruction of what WAS best in the barley. _

A pint of ale was made from half an ounce of barley. Seventy-six pints of malt liquor contained about the same amount of muscle-forming matter as would be found in five pounds of bread. Port wine was said to be the most muscle- forming of the spirits. According to the authority of the Laneeta thousand grains of the very best port wine would only contain one and third grains of matter that could . .

be capable of forming muscle. Meat was 207 times as nourishing as these much Tainted wines. He pointed out the fallacy of the notion which some people entertained tkat taking spirits made the body warmer. When alcohol was taken into the system it sent heat to the skin, and thus it was lost, the inside of the body being much colder than before.l Wi7.7n a man was stout from drink, if they I examined his fat they would find that it was not what the I butcher would call prime; it was bloated and flabby. There were many large breweries at the east end of Landon which employed a fine-looking race of men, apparently the pictures of perfect health. The lives of these men in many cases were not worth a moment's purchase. 'They would go to the hospitals sufferinz from a cut of the finger, and amputa- tion might be necessary. Scores of these giants were carried away year by year by injuries of the most childish character, simply because they had ruined their systems with alcoholic drinks.—The lecture was applauded at the mclueion, and the meeting separated. On Thursday evening, the lecturer took for his subject "Fermentation and distillation." J. 11. Gomel], Reg , took the chair,and there was a good audience. The CHAIRMAN said that the medical profession was quite as desirous as the most ardent teetotaller to assist in pro- moting all efforts designed to suppress the abuse of alcohol. In Warrington they had an institution, the Fever Hospital, where alcohol was only used as a medicine, and he ventured to say that its statistics would compare favoutably with those of any other institution of a similar kind. There was evidence that drunkenness existed in Warrington to a large extent, notably among women. The people, he said, must have better homes, and sanitary laws mast be enforced, but side by side with this sanitary reform they must have the power of dealing with licensed houses, which in the town of Warrington were the direct cause of so much crime and poverty. He had had the pleasure of listening to the previous two lectures, and he cerdially agreed with the conclusion to which the lecture came—that alcohol was not flesh or muscle-forming, or gave sustenance to the body in a state of health. (Applause.) The LEGTURER said that civilisation never made so fatal a present to mankind as when she taught them the mode of distilling and drinking these drinks. Beer, as we understood it at the present time was very different from the beer of the ancients. The old barley drink of the Egyptians was not flavoured with hops, nor was the beer of the Saxons. The bitter principal in the hops served to stimulate a fagged appetite, but when it was taken with beer its effects were rather neutralized than otherwise, because alcohol disagreed with several of the digestive juices. Turning to wines, he said that they might be sumated up, when properly made, to contain a! mister° of alcohol and water, grape sant; Yert,hl2;clds,! tanning, colouring matter, and Various essential oils and ethers. Many of the home made wines, such as were knewn as raisen wine, elderberry wine, orange wine, Jec., contained alcohol; and no one could be a perfectly oeneistent abstaliler who was in the habit of drinking these wines. The Alcohol was produced by fermentation with brewers yeast. He then showed the process of distilling spirits. It was impossible, he said, to produce by fermentation alone a very strong al- coholic liquid, because after a certain length of time the ferment refused to do any more work. It was enly in the 15th and 16th centuries that distilled alcohol began to be looked upon as an exceedingly valuable drink. It was a sad thing that in the manufacture of these distilled drinks an enormous amount of good food was spoiled. He explained that in order to set free alcohol for commercial purposes the authorities had devised the plan of mixing with it what was called methylic alcohol, which had the desired effect of making it unpalat- able to drink. These alcohols when mixed were called methylated spirit. As showing the extremities to which the appetite for alcohol would sometimes drive a man, he gave an instance of a French polisher whom he had known to drink methylated spirits. In conclusion he hoped the result of his lectures would be to stimulate thought on the subjects he had dealt with. He referred to the remarks recently made by Mr. G. R. Sims respecting the hovels of London, and laid he thought more was attributable to drink than Mr. Sims appeared to admit. They could not bring about the reformation of the people by giving them new houses and plenty of fresh air. Give them these by all means, but before they did it try to bring about the reform- ation of the people. A sober man would soon, bY" some means, better his "burroundings without delaying for out- siders to do it for him. (Applause.) Mr. WILLIAM ROBERTS, hon. sec. to the Union, in moving a vote of thanks to tho lecturer and chairman, said that the holding of the lectures to a certain extent had been ex- perimental, inasmuch as it was a new thing to have the temperance question brought before an audience from a scientific standpoint, but on the whole he thought it had proved successful. He thought the worthy doctor that night was the right man in the right place. (Applause.) He hoped Dr. Gornall would long be. oparod to lahltir ana.,ns thorn and be all example in connection with the Fever Hospital to prove that alcohol was unnecessary even as a medicine. He would like to refer to the remarks which were made by their worthy Mayor, at the Public Hall, on Monday night. They all knew very well that for seine time past Warrington had been notoriona for the intemper- ance among its women. He believed that the statements which had appeared in the newspapers had not been exag- gerated. The Mayor thought that the statements had been grossly exaggerated, that Warrington was not as bed as other towns, and that it was a matter of satis- faction that these Cases had been brought before the Bench and dealt with. It happened at the very time the Mayor was making these remarks that a medical man of the town said to a gentleman in the hell, "Why, only to- night I passed one of our gin palaces a, seven o'clock, and it was crowded with young women." It was not, Mr. Roberts said, an exceptional thing to see droves of young; women walking through the streets in a state of intoxica- tion The other Saturday night he saw no less than ten young' women Come out of a public-house in Bridge-street, and he had no hesitation in saying that not one of them could walk straight. This state of things was discreditable to the town, and it was their duty as Christian and temper- ance people to use their best efforts in seeing that the matter was brought to the light of day, and that it should go forth that their mag;strates should not go on punishing the young girls who were the victims of the chink, but the Publicans who served them with that drink. (Applause.) the last licensing day the clergy of all denominations of the town presented a petition to the magistrates, and asked them to do all they possibly could to lessen the temptation for drinking. There was only one application that day and they were succassflef in stopping the fresh license being granted. Oalv a week previously, although the Chief Con- stable brought serious charges against three ;public-houses, although he proved to the magistrates that these houees had increased the drinking among young women, the magis- trates hod not the courage to withhold the licensee. He would say that if the the licenses had been withhel'd—he might remark that the houees were the property of the hon. baronet at Walton Hall—the whole town would have sup- ported the magistrates in their decision. (Applause.) He believed that the feeling of Warrineton was exceedingly strong on this question. Depend upon it that if this state of ,things continued they would neake a determined effort and do all they could to influence the magistrates to take upon ,themselves the responsibility of refusing to renew these licenses. He felt vary strongly on the question, and he thought that they were only dcing their duty in" bringing these faces to light, and in trying to do everything they could to stop the iniquitous evil of drinking among young women. (Applause.) He had pleasure in moving a yob& of thanks to the lecturer and chairman. Mr. TOFT seconded the motion, which was carried un— aninsouely. Ihe CHAIRMAN, in replying, eaid that with reference to what occurred oa Monday night at the very large meeting which took place in connection with the Charch Of Eng- land Temperance Society, the chairman announced that the first resolution was carried unanimously. He (the chairman): however, had the audacity to held up his hand in oppositicn to it. He certainly did not think the magistrates were de- serving of the thanks which the resolution conveyed, for hia experience was that all the magistrates had to do was the pitiable work of fining people for being drunk and dis- orderly. He thought there badi been many occasions op which, if the magistrates had shown a little backbone, they would have had the support of. every man and woman in the town. (Applause.) The LitCTURER having replied: the meeting was brougbli toa close.

Bedell presided, and there were also on the platform—the Rev. G. Cousins (who Las recently returned from. Made- gascar), and the Rev. W. C. Willoughby (from. Central Africa). The chairman delivered an interesting address on mission work, and Mr. Cousins gave an oatlins of the French trouble in Madagascar from its commencement down to the present time. Mr. Willoughby gave an inter- esting account of the work being done in the. Mission field, and the speakers were listened 0 with great attention. A number of assegai.s. drinking cups, ar.4 other African curiositiza wore on view.

Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers. 13, Qtven's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (Nov. 29th):— _ _ _

, Owing to rumours and fears of trouble an uncertain feeling has pervaded the share markets during the past weeks and prices in leading stocks have for the most part experienced a further declinn with, however. in not a few cases some recovery from the worst points reached. Foreign Funds are mostly lower, but the decline is not material in any instance save' Egyptian Stens, all of which mark a decided fall, though sh )wing sensibly better than lowest on better news frozu lgypt. and Lord Hartington's speech giving evidence of the. Intention of the Government being to detain troops there for the present. In two cases. viz., Mexican Three Per Cents. and Zussians, some advance is reaorded the former being fand the latter 5 higher. Argentine Hard Dollar Bowls have de- clined 4, and Italian, Peruvian, Spanish, and Turkish !Ramped are ali fractionally easier. Mexican Railways have again relapsed, and shows fall of about 64 on the week, besides the deduction from price quotation being now ex-dividend. Share- hollers want more guarantee to go upon than they got at the meeting, and when it is owned that an important piece of news relating to traffic was kept back, uneasiness is felt as to the ruling of their- affairs. The traffic return this week announces a decrease of £9,200. The aggregate of movement in the other groups of investments exhibits a fairly equal general balance.

THR LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADE.-The iron market continues- very dull, and apart from such influence as is exerted by the apprehended strike, the weight of busi- ness doing is small. Buyers Wee have anything like orders of importance to plaee prefer to wait unless they can secure some concession. For-local brands of pig iron quotations remain firm at 45s to 45s ed less 2i for forge and foundry delivered equal to Maachester, but no new orders are being got at these figures, and the few offers which come into the hands of local makers-are at about is to is 63 per ton under Their quoted rates. In•distriet brands the quotations of the leading Lincolnshire makers remain at 44s ICd to 45s 10d lees 21 delivered here: at 641 under these figures business is being done, but buyers are not disposed to pay the full rates. A moderate business is being done in the finished iron trade,' but there is a want, of steadiness in prices, rtad merchants are open to sell forward at under current rates. For de- livery iato this dietriot the average quotations far bat& remain at £6 2s &1 to £6 ss, but the average basis of selling prices is more nearly represented by the minimum figure ;- hoops do not average more than £6 7s 6d to 10s; and sheets £7 15s to £.1.1- 111 e ad per ton delivered equal to Man— chester.—The apparently determined stand which is being taken by the miners-with regard to their demand for an ad- vance of wages, and the certainty that the employers will not give wayeis-naturally tending to increase the anxiety on the part QI censumees to get supplieee in anticipation- of a possible strike. For actual requirements there is no real improeement in the demand, but daring the week there-has been quite a push of orders in the market for all cleans of fuel, and colliery proprietors in many oases have more-orders in hand than they can at present execute. Round coals are moviag off freely both for house-fire and manufacturing purposes, and for engine classes of fuel there is- a good demand.. The present pressure has naturally a teadency to cause a hardening in prices, and in a few cases higher rates have been obtained, slack espeeiany fetching mere money than sellers have been able to obtain of late, but where any material advance in prices has been asked buyees have held back their orders. It is probable that with the close of the month there will in the Manchester district bean announced advance of about 10d per ton on all classes of round coal, ' with some upward movement in engine fuel, and this may lead to similar action in °thee districts. List rates generally are so far unaltered, bet prices have hardened up to the full rates of 103 for best coals, 83 for seconds, is for common house coal, 63 for steam coal, 5s for borgy, with good slack fetching from 4s to 4s 6d, and ordinary qualities about 3s 6d per ton. The demand for shipment has been fnly quiet, and delivered at Liverpool or Gersten Lancashiee steam coal does net average more than 74 6d to Ss per tn.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was 11,1 d at the Workhouse on Wednesday. Present :—Messrs. Greening (chairman), Cooper (vice-chairman), Appleton, Blackharst, Brown, Broadbent, Darbyshire,Greenall, J. Houghton, Hunt, Jolley, Siddellev, Major Cartwright, Owen, Jeans and the Rev. G. F. Roberts. There was very little business of public interest before the Board.

E6I7E EGGS. • Mr. DAR3YSHIRE drew attention to a bill of <ls. for 20 eggs supplied to the workhouse, and thought they bad paid too much. He conedered they had enough poultry in the House without purchasing them—The CHAIRMAN: We don't keep poultry.—Mr DAREYSHIRE : Oh, yes we do.— The CHAIRMAN : They belbng to the porter.—Major CARTWRIGHT : And they are not laying at present. (Laughter.)—The subject then dropped.

_ SCHOOLS COMITTTEE. At a meeting held on the Oh, November it was resolved that at the first meeting of'the committee in e:.ch month a sub-committee of three be appointed to visit at their dis- cretion the institution until the appointment of their suc- cessors, and to report on their visits to the committee in a book to be obtained for the pnrpeae. Messrs. Brown, Cald- well, and John Houghton were appointed. Mr. Mines, superintendent, • submitted a series of rules he had prepared for the regulation of the schcore, and the same were approved subject to each member of the committee being furnished with a printsr's copy of the rules before the next meeting, and to the-remainder standing over until after the next meeting. The orders of Mr. Robert Pemberton and Mr. Stephen Moss for work in connection with hot-water supply, repairing mangle, and other laundry work, were considered, and that of MI-. Pemberton was accepted: An application by the Rev-. W. H. Williams for pew rents in respect of church seatareserved for the school chi:then at Padgate Church was deferred for the present. It' was agreed to purchase about 200 poplar and similar trees, and to set the same on ths-grounds.—The minutes were adopted on the motion of Mr. DARRYSEHRE, seconded by Mr. BROADBENT.

SOUTHPORT CONVALESCENT HOSPITA*L AND SEA-BATHING INFIRMARY. The Board of Governors wish particularly to °ill the atten- tion of the Public, and the Committees of Management of Hospitals and Infirmaries, to the advantages to be obtained by Convalescent Patients in this Institution. A haudsome addi- tion to the old Hospital, capable of accommodating 150 patients, and fitted with every modern appliance for heating and veati- lotion has recently been erected by the Committee of the Cotton Districts Oonvalesoent Fund, and the total number of beds in the new and old buildings now amounts to 370. During the winter months especially the dry bracing air of Southport is considered very beneficial in cases of incipient Phthisis, Bronchitis. Rheumatism, and Debility; and the Governors are anxious that the benefits to be derived by these classes of patients from a short stay in this Hospital shall be widely known. LATEST NEWS. THE TRIAL OF O'DONNELL. The trial of O'Donnell for the murder of the informer Carey was commenced at the Old Bailey, yesterday morn- ing. The Attorney-General having opened the case for the Crown, James Parish and Thomas Jones were called, and repeated their previous evidence, as did also Carey's son and Mrs. Carey. Young Carey, however, when examined, ad- mitted having been wrong in some ()ibis evidence at Bow- street, and said he could not remember O'Donnell's words in reply to Mrs. Carey. Nathan Marks. an hotel keeper at Capetown, deposed to seeing through the hatch- way Carey and the prisoner talking together. He afterwards heard a shot fired, and looking again thought he saw O'Donnell fire another shot. Re- plying to Mrs. Carey, prisoner said "I could not help it."— In cross-examination, witness said he thought O'Donnell was in liquor.—Robert Cubitt, a new witness, said he went out in the Kinfauus Castle to Capetown, and during the voyage Carey and O'Donnell were on friendly terms. At Capetown a publican gave him a portrait of Carey, which he showed O'Donnell, who put it in his pocket, saying in quite a pleasant manner "I'll shoot him."— The witnesses Beecher and Cherry were then called, and repeated the evidence given by them on previous occasions.—Fuperintendent Mallon,of the Dublin police, testified to supplying Carey with a revolver before leaving Dublin, and in cross-examination, said he considered Carey a desperate man, utterly regardless of human life. This concluded the case for the prosecution, and the court . adjourned at five minutes to seven. END OF A STRIKE.—The men of the Dalmellington Iron Company, who struck three weeks ago, resumed work yesterday at ten per cent. reduction. FRANCE AND CHINA: ENGLISH MEDIATION.—A Central News telegram, dated Paris, Friday, states :—The rumours of English mediation meet a favourable reception. GREAT FIRES IN AMERICA.—The Saxonville blanket factories, Massachusetts, have been destroyed by fire. The damage is estimated at s7oo,ooo.—The Windsor Theatre, New York,- with an hotel adjoining, were leurnt down on Thursday night after the performance. The damage amounts to half a million dollars. SHOCKING SUICIDE OF A CLERGYMAN.-011 Thursday, a suicide, surrounded by most mysterious circumstances, came to light in Dublin. On Wednesday last a young clergyman engaged lodgings at Heytesbury-street. He had no luggage, and took nothing to eat. The next day he did not leave his room, and the landlady, alarmed, had the door forced. A horrible sight met her gaze. Stretched on the bed, cold in death, la r the clergyman, and beside him an empty bottle of chloral, so that the mode of death was at once apparent. He had given no name, and was an Englishman by accent. On searching his pocket, pieces of a torn post-card were found, and when joined the following words could be de- ciphered :—" lam sent back a Protestant orphan. (Signed) HAMILTON." It was addressed to the Rev. W. G. K. Borough, and portions of it could not be read.

THE RIGHT OF PRIVATE JUDGMENT. air,—The Rev. J. Yonge in his sermon on the above sub- ject reminds me of the proverbial good cow, who, having given a pail of milk, kicks it over and spills it. He labours hard in the first half of his sermon to demonstrate the right Of private judgment in matters of religion, and then sets to in the latter half to demolish all that he has previously demonstrated. In one breath he tells his hearers to act ac- cording to the dictates of conscience; in the next breath he tells thin/ there Is a limit to acting-even according to con- science. It hi' E'lear to au unprejudiced mind that the Rev. J. Yonge has for eri63 Aseathed the ra,:: 9f the priest, and ventures to launch forth the Protestant bull, viz "You must accept the teaching of tile' Bible." I suppose there are some minds which cannot rest In matters of religiod without a visible infallibility, so the Romish Church meets the wants of the more mentally indolent clams of worshippers, and the Bible serves as a "traveller's rest" to the more active class; and to my thinking the difference between the two infallibles is like " tweedledum and tweedledee." I would like to ask the Rev. J. Yonge whether he really believes there is no sincerity in those of use who have discarded the whole system of modern theology. Does he really give us no credit for conscientiousness in matters of this sort. His quotation from Dr. Dale about "private judgment" and "private fancy" is simply throwing dust in the eyes of the unwary. Pray is Dr. Dale an authority as to what is "judgment" and what is "fancy" in the minds of those who in searching after truth have come to doubt those things which are regarded by Protestants as funda- mentals ? Why, all history attests the fact that the funda- mental truths of one age are rejected by the next age as un rustworthy, and altogether erroneous. With regard to "a man's thoughts about a thing" being "guided or governed by the facts about a thing," I think we are all pretty well agreed; and what some of us are at a loss about is that we cannot get at the facts about the problems uttered from the pulpits of our land. We certainly are not much perplexed on the whole as to what we should think about in matters of every day life, for we generally arrive at such facts as are sufficient to guide us in our determination to pursue in any given course. 35 at wnen we came to religion, "the curious and striking point is this: "—" Religion is the only subject on which some of us "claim unlimited liberty" to accept or reject the assumed facts set before us. And•why ? 'Sim- ply this—lts champions hive not yet settled between them- selves what are the facts. Until that is done, vre who ate branded, as those who claim to have a perfect right to think about religion as it seems good to us—will continue so to think, " lawless "as it may seem to do so. I have no doubt Luther was considered very "lawless" by the savants of his day, for the bold step he took then. Well we have gone a step farther in "the right of private judg- ment." Luther disputed the right of the Romish Church to fetter men's minds, as it did in his day. We dispute the right of the Protestant Church to fetter our minds in this our day. SINCERITY. •
